questions.promptHtml: Explain how a stack is formed in a coastal landscape. Use one or more labelled diagrams. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Waves attack a weakness such as a crack in a headland of resistant rock, for example the chalk at Old Harry Rocks in Dorset. Hydraulic action — where the waves force air inside the cracks, and the pressure widens them — enlarges the crack 1

The waves also throw rocks against the headland, which further erodes it (abrasion), and sea water dissolves soluble rock (solution). Together these processes erode the crack into a cave 1

Continued erosion deepens and widens the cave until it breaks right through the headland to form an arch 1

The arch is weathered at the top and eroded at the base, which weakens it, and it eventually collapses because it cannot support its own weight. This leaves a stack — a vertical column of rock isolated from the headland — which further erosion will reduce to a lower stump 1

✗ Naming hydraulic action and abrasion without saying what they are.
✓ Define each process as you use it — that is the difference between Level 1 and 4/4, according to the school's own feedback.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how spits and bars form along the coast as a result of deposition. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
The prevailing wind drives waves onto the beach at an oblique angle, so the swash carries sediment up the beach at that angle and the backwash returns it at right angles — the zigzag movement of longshore drift, which moves material steadily along the coast 1

Where the coastline changes direction, or where it meets a river mouth and the power of the waves is reduced, the sea loses the energy to carry the sediment and deposits it 1

Deposition continues, so the sediment builds up above sea level and extends out from the shore as a finger — a spit, such as Dawlish Warren at the mouth of the River Exe. Opposing winds and currents curve its end landwards, and the sheltered water behind it silts up to form salt marsh 1

If longshore drift carries the spit all the way across a bay it joins the far side and becomes a bar, trapping the water behind it as a lagoon — for example Slapton Ley at Torcross 1

questions.promptHtml: You have studied a coastal management scheme in the UK. Explain the effects of the scheme. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
I studied the scheme at Brighton, which protects 10 km of coastline from the River Adur to Brighton Marina. The wooden and concrete groynes trap sediment moving by longshore drift, so the beach has widened; a wider beach means waves break further out and their energy is absorbed before reaching the sea wall and the cliffs behind 1

As a result the high-value built-up area behind the defences is protected — hotels, restaurants, high-value seafront properties near Hove, Brighton Pier, the i360 and the Marina — along with the A259 coastal road, safeguarding tourism worth £5bn a year 1

There are negative effects too. The defences require continuous maintenance and expenditure: beach nourishment and reprofiling near Brighton Pier is repeated around every May, and a new £11m scheme of rock armour, a new sea wall, longer groynes and nourishment is needed to widen the beach further 1

The groynes also interrupt longshore drift, so the coast down-drift receives less new beach material and is more exposed to erosion — and there is conflict between locals, who want protection from erosion, and tourists, who may find hard engineering unsightly on a seafront whose appeal is the view 1

questions.promptHtml: Discuss the costs and benefits of hard engineering strategies for coastal management. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked: Basic 1–2, Clear 3–4, Detailed 5–6. At least two strategies, reference to the figure, a judgement with a degree word, and figures for Level 3. Plan:

Groynes. Largely effective on a drift-dominated coast: they trap sediment as it moves along the coast, widening the beach, which means waves break on the beach and their energy is absorbed before reaching the cliffs. A wider beach also benefits tourism. At about £750 per metre — Brighton's timber groynes cost £75,000 per 100 m — they are cost-effective 1

The groyne cost. But by trapping sediment a groyne deprives the area down-drift of new beach material. At Mappleton, rock armour and two rock groynes removed the risk to the village but increased erosion to the south; at Hornsea, down-drift beaches are so starved of sediment that even neap tides reach the base of the boulder clay cliffs 1

Sea walls. The most effective option for reducing erosion: a concrete barrier that reflects wave energy, durable for 30–50 years, and it creates a promenade used by locals and tourists. It also does not impede the movement of sediment along the coast, unlike a groyne 1

The sea wall cost. At around £10,000 per metre it is by far the most expensive option, it needs maintenance, reflected energy can scour the beach in front of it, and it can look obtrusive 1

Rock armour and gabions. Rock armour at £2000/m absorbs wave energy and lets a beach build up behind it, but the boulders are imported so look out of place and can shift in storms. Gabions — wire cages of rocks that absorb energy as water passes through the gaps — cost only £500/m, so they are a good choice for protecting something important but unvisited, such as a road or a power station, though they are not visually appealing 1

Judgement. Hard engineering is largely effective where the value protected is high — at Brighton it defends £5bn of annual tourism and the A259 for an £11m scheme — but its costs are real: it must be maintained indefinitely, and groynes transfer the erosion problem down the coast, which is why soft engineering and managed retreat are preferred on lower-value frontages 1

questions.promptHtml: Discuss the costs and benefits of soft engineering strategies in protecting coastlines. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked. The 2021 question, which the school answered on Medmerry. Plan:

What it is. Soft engineering manages erosion by working with natural processes to restore beaches and coastal ecosystems, rather than building artificial structures to control them 1

Beach nourishment and reprofiling — the benefit. Adding sand or shingle artificially replaces material removed by erosion or longshore drift, and a beach is a natural defence against both erosion and coastal flooding, because it absorbs wave energy. At around £500 per metre it is relatively cheap, and it blends into the environment — Brighton nourishes and reprofiles near the Pier each May 1

The cost. It requires constant maintenance to replace material as it is washed away, so the low price per metre is paid repeatedly; and on a high-energy frontage gentle intervention may simply not be effective 1

Dune regeneration. Rebuilding dunes and replanting marram grass stabilises the sand, allowing other vegetation to colonise and the dune to strengthen, with boardwalks preventing the trampling that destroyed it. At about £20 per metre it is the cheapest strategy on the spec — but it only works where dunes exist and it takes years 1

Managed retreat. Allowing the sea to flood or erode low-value land encourages the development of beaches and, importantly, salt marshes, which are valuable habitat and absorb wave energy for free. The Medmerry scheme cost £28m, so set-up is not free, and people must be compensated for the loss of buildings and farmland 1

Judgement. The decisive advantage of soft engineering is that it works with nature rather than against it and does not interfere with coastal processes elsewhere, so unlike groynes it does not move the problem down the coast — which makes it sustainable. But it is only appropriate where the land behind is of lower value, because people can lose homes and livelihoods, and it cannot defend a £5bn seafront such as Brighton's on its own 1

questions.promptHtml: Explain how different coastal landforms are created by erosion. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked. "Different landforms" means at least two or three, each with its own sequence. If a figure is given, use it as the structure — the exam guide suggests splitting a photograph into quadrants and finding a point in each. Plan:

The processes. Four processes of erosion operate: hydraulic power, where breaking waves compress pockets of air in cracks and the pressure widens them; abrasion, where sediment flung by the waves grinds the rock away; attrition, which wears the sediment itself smaller and rounder; and solution, where sea water dissolves soluble rock such as chalk and limestone 1

Headlands and bays. On a discordant coastline, bands of hard and soft rock meet the sea at right angles. The less resistant rock erodes faster and retreats to form a bay — Swanage Bay, in clays and sands — while the resistant rock is left protruding as a headland, such as Durlston Head in Purbeck Limestone 1

Cliffs and wave-cut platforms. The sea attacks a weakness at the base of a resistant cliff, and hydraulic power and abrasion cut a wave-cut notch; weathering weakens the cliff top; the overhang collapses under gravity and the cliff retreats, leaving a gently sloping rocky shelf — the wave-cut platform at Kimmeridge Bay 1

Caves, arches and stacks. On the exposed headland, waves attack a crack; hydraulic action, abrasion and solution enlarge it into a cave; continued erosion cuts the cave through the headland to form an arch; the arch is weathered above and eroded below until it cannot support its own weight and collapses, leaving a stack — Old Harry Rocks, in chalk at Ballard Point 1

Why rock type runs through all of it. Resistant rock holds steep cliffs and overhangs, so it produces platforms, arches and stacks; weak rock such as the boulder clay of Holderness slumps and retreats instead, so it produces rapidly eroding cliffs and no arches at all 1

Linking sentence. The landforms are therefore not independent: the headland created by differential erosion is what concentrates wave energy and allows the cave–arch–stack sequence to develop, while the sheltered bay beside it becomes a site of deposition 1

questions.promptHtml: "Coastal management schemes move the problem of erosion from one location to another." Do you agree? Using an example, explain your answer. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Level marked. The school's own mock question. Its mark scheme states there is no "correct" view and both sides can be credited if supported with evidence, but a named example is required for Level 3. Plan:

Agree — the mechanism. Longshore drift is a continuous conveyor: beaches are maintained by sediment arriving from up-drift. Hard engineering that interrupts it therefore protects one place at the expense of another — the mark scheme's phrase is that down-drift areas are "starved of sediment" 1

Agree — the named evidence. At Mappleton the scheme placed rock armour along the base of the cliff and built two rock groynes; Mappleton and its cliffs are no longer at great risk, but the groynes stopped beach material moving south and erosion south of Mappleton has increased. At Hornsea, groynes build up the beach protecting the sea front, but down-drift even neap tides now reach the base of the boulder clay cliffs 1

Disagree — not all strategies do this. A sea wall reflects wave energy without trapping sediment, and the school mat notes that sea walls do not impede the movement of sediment along the coast. Beach nourishment adds material rather than intercepting it, and the mark scheme is explicit that it "does not have a negative impact on coastal processes further along the coast" 1

Disagree — managed retreat does the opposite. Allowing low-value land to flood or erode releases sediment and allows beaches and salt marshes to develop, which absorb wave energy and benefit the wider coast rather than harming it; Medmerry cost £28m to set up for exactly that outcome 1

The Brighton case. Brighton combines both: wooden and concrete groynes over a 10 km frontage from the River Adur to the Marina do interrupt drift, but beach nourishment near the Pier every May replaces material rather than taking it, and the £11m widening scheme pairs longer groynes with nourishment — so the scheme is designed partly to offset its own side-effects 1

Judgement. I partly agree: the statement is true of groynes, which demonstrably transfer erosion down-drift, but it is not true of soft engineering or managed retreat, which work with coastal processes instead of interrupting them. The problem is moved only when hard structures interrupt sediment supply — which is why modern schemes combine the two 1

Agree — the named evidence. questions.promptHtml: Stretch — 9-mark shape. "Hard engineering is the only realistic way to protect a developed coastline." To what extent do you agree? (9)
questions.answerHtml:
Section C itself carries no 9-markers, so this is practice at transferring the material into the 9-mark evaluate shape — three paragraphs with evaluation inside each, plus a conclusion using a degree word. Plan:

Introduction — the coast and the stakes. At Brighton, 10 km from the River Adur to Brighton Marina is managed because it is a high-value built-up area: hotels, restaurants, high-value seafront property near Hove, Brighton Pier, the i360, the Marina, the A259 coastal road and tourism worth £5bn a year 1

Paragraph 1 — the case for hard engineering. Sea walls reflect wave energy, last 30–50 years and create promenades; groynes trap drift and widen the beach so waves break offshore; rock armour absorbs energy and lets a beach build behind it. On a high-energy developed frontage these are the only options that reliably hold the line 1

The costs are justified by the value protected: an £11m beach-widening scheme against £5bn a year of tourism is a strong ratio, and at £750 per metre groynes are cheap relative to the property behind them 1

Paragraph 2 — the case against. Hard engineering transfers the problem: groynes starve the coast down-drift of sediment, so at Mappleton erosion increased to the south and at Hornsea neap tides now reach the boulder clay cliffs. It also requires indefinite maintenance, and a sea wall at £10,000 per metre is unaffordable on most of the coast 1

It can also damage the asset it protects: there is conflict at Brighton between locals who want protection and tourists who find hard engineering unsightly — so on a coast whose value is its appearance, concrete has a hidden cost 1

Paragraph 3 — the alternatives, and where they work. Soft engineering works with natural processes, blends into the environment and, crucially, does not interfere with processes further along the coast. Beach nourishment at £500 per metre and dune regeneration at £20 per metre are far cheaper, and Brighton already uses nourishment and reprofiling near the Pier each May 1

Managed retreat goes further: allowing low-value land to flood creates beaches and salt marshes that absorb wave energy for free and improve habitat. But it needs land that can be given up — Medmerry cost £28m and required compensation — so it cannot be applied to a built-up seafront 1

The synthesis. The realistic answer is not one or the other but a combination matched to the value of the land: hold the line with hard engineering where assets are concentrated, and work with natural processes where they are not. Brighton's own £11m scheme pairs rock armour, a new sea wall and longer groynes with beach nourishment, which is precisely that combination 1

Conclusion that decides. I agree only partly. Hard engineering is necessary on a developed, high-energy frontage, because nothing else holds the line against destructive waves — but it is not sufficient, since it must be combined with nourishment to offset the sediment it traps, and it is not "the only realistic way" for the coast as a whole, where managed retreat is both cheaper and environmentally better 1

questions.promptHtml: Stretch — 9-mark shape. Assess the extent to which rock type and structure, rather than coastal processes, determine the landforms of a stretch of coastline. (9)
questions.answerHtml:
A "to what extent is X rather than Y" question: you must argue both and then decide. Use Dorset and Holderness as the paired evidence. Plan:

Introduction. The spec itself says distinctive coastal landforms are the result of rock type, structure and physical processes, so the question is really about which dominates 1

Paragraph 1 — the case for rock type and structure. On the discordant Dorset coast, resistant Purbeck Limestone forms Durlston Head and chalk forms Ballard Point, while the clays and sands between them have been eroded back into Swanage Bay. The same waves act on all of it, so only the rock can explain the difference 1

Rock type also decides which landforms are even possible: chalk is strong enough to hold an arch and then a stack, which is why Old Harry Rocks exists, whereas the soft boulder clay of Holderness slumps along a saturated shear plane instead and no arch ever forms 1

Structure decides the plan of the coast: discordant coastlines give headlands and bays, concordant ones give a straighter coast with coves — so the large-scale shape is geological before any process acts 1

Paragraph 2 — the case for processes. Processes do the work: hydraulic power compresses air in cracks, abrasion grinds the rock, solution dissolves chalk and limestone, and without them no landform forms at all, however weak the rock 1

Processes also determine the rate, and rates are set by wave energy, which depends on fetch, wind speed and wind duration. Holderness retreats rapidly because weak rock meets high-energy North Sea waves; the same clay in a sheltered bay would not 1

And depositional landforms are almost purely process-driven: a spit such as Dawlish Warren, a bar such as Slapton Ley, Chesil Beach as a tombolo, and the Studland dunes all exist because of longshore drift, the change in coastline direction and the wind, not because of the rock beneath them 1

Paragraph 3 — the interaction. The two are not separable, because each shapes the other. Differential erosion creates the headland; the headland then concentrates wave energy on itself and shelters the bay beside it; so the bay receives deposition and a beach while the headland develops caves, arches and stacks. Rock type sets the template and processes execute it, but the result then redirects the processes 1

Conclusion that decides. Rock type and structure determine which landforms appear and where, and are therefore the more fundamental control on an erosional coastline such as Dorset. But processes determine how fast and are the dominant control on depositional landforms, which owe nothing to the local geology — so the statement holds to a great extent for erosional landforms and only slightly for depositional ones 1

drill.intro:
What each command word actually wants

Paper 1 is 1 hour 30 minutes, 88 marks, 35%. In Section C you answer two questions from Coasts, Rivers and Glacial — the class did Coasts and Glacial — and each is worth 15 marks. The first rule from the school's exam technique guide: "Don't answer the wrong questions."

  • 1 mark — recall, multiple choice, OS map or data. Read the instruction; shade one circle only. Grid references (four-figure for a square, six-figure for a point), distance with the scale bar, area by counting grid squares, and mean / median / mode. These are a third of the section — don't lose them.
  • 2 marks — describe / compare / suggest. Point plus development, or two linked points. Use the data in the figure: the school's feedback lesson says "the best answers made use of the data in the table". For compare, use "whereas".
  • 4 marks — explain the formation of a landform. Level marked: Basic 1–2, Clear 3–4. The guide's four requirements: step by step in the order it happens; processes named and explained; explanation with nothing implied; key geographical terminology. If it says "use one or more diagrams", annotate rather than label, and explain the sequence in the order it occurs.
  • 4 marks — explain the effects of a scheme. Same level marking; needs the named scheme and its figures.
  • 6 marks — discuss / assess the effectiveness / costs and benefits. Level marked: Basic 1–2, Clear 3–4, Detailed 5–6. You must refer to the figure and write "in Figure…". Discuss at least two strategies. Make a judgement — fully, largely, somewhat, not at all. Level 3 is "detailed", so include facts such as cost or timeframe. A named example is required for Level 3.
  • 9 marks — not in Section C. The school's booklet confirms Section C has "only 6 markers on this topic, no 9 markers". D11 and D12 below are therefore marked as stretch: they drill the same material in the 9-mark evaluate shape, which is how Section B and Paper 3 use it, and they are the best possible preparation for the 6-mark judgement.

Twelve questions. The 6s and 9s are written as plans — AQA marks them in levels, so the mark points are a coverage target, not a tick list.

modules.title: Glacial Landscapes in the UK
modules.standfirst: Question 5 of Section C Physical landscapes in the UK on Paper 1 — the second of John's two options, alongside Coasts. The maximum extent of UK ice cover, freeze-thaw weathering, abrasion and plucking, rotational slip and bulldozing, till and outwash; the erosional landforms (corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, troughs, truncated spurs, ribbon lakes, hanging valleys) and the depositional ones (moraine, drumlins, erratics); then economic activity, land use conflict and the management of tourism. 15 marks in the same shape every year: OS map work, a 4-mark landform, and a 6-mark discuss. The example is the Lake District.

subsections.html:
What they actually ask

Paper 1, Question 5 (Glacial landscapes in the UK) in the five papers John has. The structure barely moves: a process definition, OS map and data work, a 2-mark describe, a 4-mark landform or tourism question, and a 6-mark discuss, for 15 marks.

  • The 4-mark landform formation question — corrie formation asked in 2023, 2025 and the school's own mock; the glacial trough in 2022. Learn the corrie word-perfect.
  • The 6-mark discuss — tourism or conflict in the Lake District in 2018, 2022, 2023 and 2025; landform formation in 2019 and 2024.
  • 1-mark process recall — every year: 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025. Abrasion, plucking, bulldozing, erratics.
  • OS map and landform identification — 2022, 2023, 2024 and the school mock: grid squares, grid references, tarns, ribbon lakes.
  • Ice cover and data work — 2019, 2022, 2025: describe the extent, complete a cross-section, measure a drumlin.
  • The 2-mark describe — 2023, 2024, 2025 and the school mock: a ribbon lake, a valley shape, a drumlin, a conflict.

And note: Section C has no 9-markers, so the 6-mark discuss is the biggest question here.

Every question from 2019–2025, with the exact wordings

Paper 1, Question 5 (Glacial landscapes in the UK) in the five papers John has. The structure barely moves: a process definition, OS map and data work, a 2-mark describe, a 4-mark landform or tourism question, and a 6-mark discuss, for 15 marks.

  • 1-mark process recall. "What does abrasion mean?" — the correct option was "rocks trapped beneath the glacier scratch and smooth the bedrock underneath" (2024, 1); "Which of these is a process of glacial erosion?" — freeze-thaw, plucking, rotational slip, transportation (2019, 1); "What is the name given to a large boulder transported and deposited by glaciers in areas with a different rock type?" — erratic, moraine, outwash, till (2023, 1); "Give one way glaciers move material" (2023, 1); "Which term is used to describe the process where a glacier moves forward and pushes material ahead of it?" (2025, 1); "Suggest one reason why the material deposited by a glacier is mixed in size and shape" (2022, 1).
  • 1-mark landform identification and OS map work. "Using Figure 18, which grid square shows part of a ribbon lake?" and "name one landform of glacial erosion shown in grid square 7112" — Snowdonia (2024, 1 each); a 1-mark grid reference (2023, 1); "Identify the feature shown at X" on a photograph of a retreating glacier — moraine, drumlin, truncated spur, arête (2022, 1); "Using Figure 1, identify the glacial landform at grid reference 347149" and "identify the grid square containing a tarn" (school Glaciers mock, 1 each); "Using Figures 1 and 2, what direction was the photographer looking?" (school mock, 1).
  • Ice cover and data. "Using Figure 19, describe the extent of ice cover across the British Isles during the last ice age" (2019, 2); "Complete the table in Figure 20 by calculating the range of sediment size, in cm, at location B" and "suggest one reason for the difference in the range of sediment size between location A and location B" — a till plain versus an outwash plain (2019, 1 each); "Using Figure 17, complete Figure 18, a cross section showing the depth of ice between X and Y" and "compare the maximum depth of ice over the British Isles with the maximum depth of ice over Scandinavia" (2022, 1 each); "Using Figure 17, what is the length of the drumlin from point A to point B?" (2025, 1).
  • 2-mark describe. "Using Figure 17 and Figure 18, describe two characteristics of a ribbon lake" — Llyn Ogwen, Snowdonia (2023, 2); "Using Figure 18, describe the shape of the valley and measure the width of the valley floor between points X and Y" (2024, 2); "Use Figure 16 or Figure 17 to describe the shape of a drumlin" (2025, 1); "Outline one possible conflict between tourists and farmers in the area shown in Figure 16" (2025, 2); "Describe one feature of the glacial valley containing Grisedale Beck" (school mock, 1).
  • 4-mark — landform formation or tourism. "Explain the formation of a glacial trough (U-shaped valley). Use one or more diagrams" (2022, 4); "Explain how corries form as a result of glacial erosion" (2023, 4); "Explain how a corrie is formed. Use one or more labelled diagrams" (2025, 4) — and the same question in the school's own mock (4); "Explain why there may be land use conflicts in glaciated upland areas. Use Figure 21 and your own understanding" — the figure listed tourism, quarrying, farming and forestry (2019, 4); "You have studied a glaciated upland area in the UK. Explain why this area attracts tourists" (2024, 4).
  • 6-mark discuss. "Explain the formation of different landforms of glacial deposition. Use Figure 22 and your own understanding" — drumlins and a terminal moraine in front of a retreating glacier (2019, 6); "Assess the economic and environmental impacts of tourism in a glaciated upland area of the UK. Use Figure 20 and your own understanding" — tourism statistics for Snowdonia, including 595 000 visitors to Snowdon annually (2022, 6); "Discuss the possible conflict between development and conservation in glaciated areas. Use Figure 19 and your own understanding" — concerns about a zip wire across the Thirlmere Valley in the Lake District, spoiling the view and bringing extra traffic to narrow roads (2023, 6); "Explain the different ways that glacial material is transported and deposited. Use Figure 19 and your own understanding" (2024, 6); "Discuss how different strategies are used to manage the impacts of tourism in glaciated areas in the UK. Use Figure 18 and your own understanding" — repairing paths in the Lake District and the Park and Sail scheme (2025, 6). From the school's booklet, outside these years: "The growing number of visitors to glaciated upland areas in the UK can only bring advantages. Do you agree?" (2018, 6, Lake District) and "Explain how glacial processes have created the landforms shown in Figure 22 — arête, pyramidal peak, corrie/tarn" (2020, 6). The school's own mock reversed the 2018 wording: "The increasing number of people holidaying in glaciated upland areas in the UK can only bring disadvantages. Do you agree?" (6).

The pattern that matters. Corrie formation has come up three times in five years (2023, 2025 and the school's own mock) — learn it word-perfect. The 6-marker alternates between landform formation (2019, 2024) and tourism or conflict in the Lake District (2018, 2022, 2023, 2025), so you need both. And as in Coasts, Section C has no 9-markers — the school's booklet says so explicitly — which makes the 6-mark discuss the biggest question here.

The spec for this module, in full

Section C offers three questions — Question 3 (Coasts), Question 4 (Rivers), Question 5 (Glacial) — and you answer two. The class did Coasts and Glacial, so Question 5 is the one to turn to. The spec runs: the maximum extent of ice cover across the UK during the last ice age; glacial processes (freeze-thaw weathering; erosion by abrasion and plucking; movement and transportation by rotational slip and bulldozing; deposition of till and outwash); erosional landforms (corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, truncated spurs, glacial troughs, ribbon lakes, hanging valleys); landforms of transportation and deposition (erratics, drumlins, types of moraine); an example of a UK upland area affected by glaciation; economic activities in glaciated uplands — tourism, farming, forestry and quarrying; conflicts between land uses and between development and conservation; and an example of a glaciated upland area used for tourism, showing the attractions, the social, economic and environmental impacts, and the strategies used to manage them.

subsections.heading: Maximum extent of ice cover across the UK
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · 2019 Q5.1; 2022 Q5.1–5.3

  • Nearly all of the north was covered — ice reached across Scotland, Ireland, Wales and northern England.
  • The southern limit — the ice sheet stopped roughly across the Midlands; southern England was never glaciated.
  • Describe with compass directions and named places — that is what the 2-mark version is marked on.
More detail

The 2019 paper gave a map of ice extent across the British Isles with the Shetland Islands, Scotland, Ireland, Wales, England, the Lake District and the Irish Sea labelled, and asked for a 2-mark description. Use the exam technique guide's structure for describing a map: the trend (the distribution is northern, decreasing southwards), the extremities (the far north entirely covered, the far south entirely uncovered), and named places as the evidence.

The 2022 paper took it further, giving a map of ice depth over north-west Europe and asking candidates to complete a cross-section of ice depth between two points, then to compare the maximum depth of ice over the British Isles with that over Scandinavia. The comparison is that the ice was deeper over Scandinavia, which was the centre of the main European ice sheet, than over the British Isles. The true/false statement in the same question tested two common errors: ice did not cover the whole of the British Isles, and the main ice sheet was not centred in southern Europe.

Why this spec point exists. It explains the geography of the rest of the module. The Lake District, Snowdonia and the Scottish Highlands have corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, glacial troughs and ribbon lakes because they held the ice; East Anglia has till plains and drumlins because it lay under or at the edge of the ice; southern England has neither. When a question asks why a landform is in a particular place, the extent of the last ice sheet is the first-order answer.

  • The uplands were the ice centres — Scotland, the Lake District, Snowdonia and the Pennines held the thickest ice.
  • Scandinavia held more — the main European ice sheet was centred over Scandinavia, deeper than over the British Isles.
  • This is why the landforms are where they are — corries and troughs only occur in the glaciated uplands.

✗ "Most of Britain was covered in ice." — one vague statement for a 2-mark describe question.
✓ "Ice covered the whole of Scotland and Ireland, together with Wales and northern England as far south as the Midlands (1), including the Lake District and the Shetland Islands, whereas southern England remained ice-free (1)."

subsections.heading: Freeze-thaw weathering
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · Glacial Landscapes Revision Mat; AQA List of Key Terms

  • Step 1 — water enters cracks in the rock face during the warmer day.
  • Step 2 — it freezes at night and expands by 9%, exerting pressure on the surrounding rock.
  • Step 3 — repeated freezing and thawing enlarges the crack until pieces break off.
  • Two landscape features — scree slopes and block-fields.
More detail

AQA's definition: freeze-thaw weathering, "also called frost-shattering… occurs in cold climates when temperatures are often around freezing point and where exposed rocks contain many cracks. Water enters the cracks during the warmer day and freezes during the colder night. As the water turns into ice it expands and exerts pressure on the surrounding rock, causing pieces to break off."

The mat's version adds the quantity and the repetition: "Water enters cracks in the rock face. It freezes and expands. This causes the crack to become larger by 10%. Subsequent freezing and thawing enlarges the crack causing rock to break away. Large blocks of rock can be shattered by repeated freeze-thaw weathering." The school's quick-fire list gives the expansion itself as 9% — that is the number to quote.

The two landscape features the mat names are scree slopes — accumulations of angular shattered fragments at the base of a rock face — and block-fields, areas of shattered blocks on a plateau surface.

Why it matters more than it looks. Freeze-thaw is not just a background process; it is the supply mechanism for glacial erosion. It shatters rock off the back wall of a corrie, which makes the back wall steep and creates the armchair shape; it supplies the angular debris that falls onto the glacier surface and down crevasses to become the sandpaper for abrasion; and it is what keeps the arête sharp once two corries have cut back towards each other. Mention it in every landform answer.

  • Also called frost-shattering — it needs temperatures oscillating around freezing and rock with many cracks.
  • It feeds the erosion — the shattered debris becomes the abrasive material carried by the glacier.

subsections.heading: Glacial erosion — abrasion and plucking
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · Glacial Landscapes Revision Mat; AQA List of Key Terms; 2024 Q5.1; 2019 Q5.4

  • Plucking — meltwater freezes around loose rock at the glacier base, and the moving ice pulls it away.
  • Abrasion — rocks frozen into the base of the glacier act like sandpaper, scratching and scraping the bedrock below.
  • Abrasion leaves striations — scratches on the bedrock that record the direction the ice moved.
More detail

The mat's definitions, which are the ones to reproduce: "Plucking — as a glacier moves over the Earth's surface, meltwater freezes around loose rock, pulling them away. Abrasion — rocks frozen to the base of a glacier act like sandpaper scratching and scraping the bedrock below."

AQA's own wording is close: plucking is "a type of erosion where melt water in the glacier freezes onto rocks, and as the ice moves forward it plucks or pulls out large pieces along the rock joints"; abrasion is "erosion caused by rocks and boulders in the base of the glacier acting like a giant file scratching and scraping the rocks below."

The 2024 paper tested abrasion as a 1-mark multiple choice, and the distractors are worth knowing because each is the definition of something else: "glacial ice moves in a circular motion causing hollows to form in the landscape" is rotational slip; "meltwater freezes beneath the ice and tears away pieces of loose rock" is plucking; "water freezes in cracks and expands, causing the rock to break down" is freeze-thaw weathering. The correct answer was "rocks trapped beneath the glacier scratch and smooth the bedrock underneath".

The link to make in a 6-marker. The two processes are in a feedback loop. Plucking pulls rock out of the bedrock along joints; that rock becomes frozen into the base of the ice; it is then dragged over the bedrock and abrades it; the abraded surface is smoothed while the plucked surface stays jagged. That is why a roche moutonnée has a smooth, striated up-ice side and a jagged, plucked down-ice side — and why saying "the glacier eroded the valley" scores nothing while naming the loop scores well.

  • Plucking — meltwater at the glacier base freezes around loose rock, and as the ice moves forward it pulls the rock away.
  • Where plucking acts — along rock joints, which is why it leaves a jagged, pitted surface.
  • The two work together — plucking supplies the tools; abrasion uses them.
  • Weathering is not erosion — freeze-thaw is weathering; only abrasion and plucking are glacial erosion.

✗ Picking freeze-thaw or rotational slip as "a process of glacial erosion" — the 2019 MC used exactly those distractors. The answer was plucking.
✓ Erosion: abrasion and plucking. Weathering: freeze-thaw. Movement: rotational slip and bulldozing. Deposition: till and outwash. Keep the four lists separate.

subsections.heading: How glaciers move, and how they transport material
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · Glacial Landscapes Revision Mat; AQA List of Key Terms; 2023 Q5.2; 2025 Q5.1

  • Basal flow — the glacier slides over the bedrock on a film of meltwater.
  • Rotational slip — the ice moves in a circular motion, eroding hollows into bowl shapes.
  • Bulldozing — the snout pushes material of all sizes ahead of it by the sheer weight of ice.
  • Three carrying positions — supraglacial (on the surface), englacial (inside) and subglacial (at the base).
More detail

The mat's account of glacier movement, which is the sequence to learn: "Snow accumulates in shady north-facing hollows in upland areas. It becomes compressed forming ice. Gravity causes it to flow over the lip. The glacier slides over the bedrock on a film of meltwater, a process called basal flow. The glacier can also move when it is too cold for basal flow by a process called internal deformation, when the ice moves like plastic."

AQA defines rotational slip as occurring "when the ice moves in a circular motion. This process can help to erode hollows in the landscape, and deepen hollows into bowl shapes" — which is why it belongs in every corrie answer. The 2024 MC used the phrase "glacial ice moves in a circular motion causing hollows to form in the landscape".

The 2025 paper asked for the term describing "the process where a glacier moves forward and pushes material ahead of it" — bulldozing. The 2023 paper asked, in 1 mark, "give one way glaciers move material" — any of bulldozing, carrying it on the surface, carrying it within the ice, or dragging it at the base will do.

Why north-facing matters. In the northern hemisphere, north-facing slopes receive the least direct insolation, so snow there survives the summer. That is a tiny detail that explains a big one: corries in the Lake District and Snowdonia are overwhelmingly on the north and north-east sides of the mountains, which is why a question asking you to "suggest one reason for the shape of the land" on a north-facing hollow has a ready answer.

  • Ice forms by compression — snow accumulates in shady north-facing hollows and is compressed into ice.
  • Internal deformation — where it is too cold for basal flow, the ice moves like plastic.
  • Bulldozing — the snout pushes material of all shapes and sizes ahead of it by the sheer weight of the ice.

Transport — the three positions, from the mat

The 2024 6-marker was "explain the different ways that glacial material is transported and deposited", so these three need to be distinguishable, with the source of the material in each case.

  • Pushed in front — bulldozing. "The snout of the glacier bulldozes material which is moved forward by the sheer weight of the ice." AQA: "ice pushes material of all shapes and sizes as it moves slowly forward."
  • Carried on the surface — supraglacial. "Material is also carried on the surface of the glacier as the result of weathering on the mountainsides above the glacier" — that is, freeze-thaw shatters rock off the valley sides and it falls onto the ice.
  • Carried inside and at the base — englacial and subglacial. "Material is also carried inside the glacier, on the base where plucking has occurred. It is also found inside where rocks fall down crevasses."

Why deposited material is mixed in size and shape — the 2022 1-marker. Because the glacier carries everything, regardless of size, in all three positions at once, and ice has no sorting mechanism: unlike water, it does not drop the heaviest material first. So when the ice melts, boulders, sand and clay are all dumped together — which is exactly what till is, "an unsorted mixture of sand, clay and boulders".

subsections.heading: Glacial deposition — till and outwash
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · AQA List of Key Terms; 2019 Q5.2–5.3; 2022 Q5.5

  • Till — an unsorted mixture of sand, clay and boulders, dropped directly by the ice as ground moraine.
  • Outwash — sand and gravel deposited by meltwater streams in front of and beneath the glacier.
  • Outwash is sorted and rounded — water sorts by size and rounds material by attrition.
More detail

AQA's definitions: till is "an unsorted mixture of sand, clay and boulders carried by a glacier and deposited as ground moraine over a large area." Outwash is "material, chiefly sand or gravel, deposited by meltwater streams in front of, and underneath, a glacier. The material is sorted and rounded by water action."

The 2019 question is the clearest test of the contrast. The figure showed a till plain and an outwash plain either side of a moraine, with sediment sizes at location A (on the till plain) ranging from 1.4 cm to 26.7 cm — a range of 25.3 cm — and at location B (on the outwash plain) from 3.8 cm to 10.4 cm, a range of 6.6 cm. The explanation for the difference: the till at A was deposited directly by the ice, which carries material of every size together and has no means of sorting it, so the range is wide; the outwash at B was deposited by meltwater, which sorts material by size — dropping the heaviest first and carrying the finest furthest — so at any one point the material is of similar size and the range is narrow.

That same logic answers the 2022 1-marker — "suggest one reason why the material deposited by a glacier is mixed in size and shape": ice carries material on its surface, within itself and at its base simultaneously and, being solid, cannot sort by size or round the fragments by attrition, so everything from clay to boulders is dumped together and stays angular.

  • Glaciers deposit when they lose energy — chiefly as they melt, at the snout and during retreat.
  • Till is unsorted and angular — ice carries everything together and does not round the fragments.
  • That contrast is examined directly — the 2019 paper compared sediment range on a till plain with an outwash plain.

✗ "Glaciers deposit material when they stop." — glaciers deposit mainly as they melt; the ice keeps advancing while the snout retreats.
✓ "As the glacier melts it can no longer carry its load, so material is deposited — directly by the ice as unsorted till, and by meltwater streams as sorted, rounded outwash beyond the snout."

subsections.heading: Corries, arêtes and pyramidal peaks
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · Glacial Landscapes Revision Mat; Y10 feedback model answer; 2023 Q5.5 and 2025 Q5.5 (4 marks each)

  • Corrie defined — an armchair-shaped hollow in the mountainside, formed by glacial erosion, rotational slip and freeze-thaw.
  • Three processes shape it — freeze-thaw loosens, plucking removes, abrasion deepens.
  • The lip forms because erosion is weaker at the front — thinner, slower ice, plus deposited frost-shattered rock.
  • Arête and pyramidal peak — two corries back to back give a knife-edge ridge; three or more a peak.
More detail

AQA's definitions: a corrie (also called a cirque) is an "armchair-shaped hollow in the mountainside formed by glacial erosion, rotational slip and freeze-thaw weathering. This is where the valley glacier begins. When the ice melts, it can leave a small circular lake called a tarn." An arête is "a sharp, knife-like ridge formed between two corries cutting back by processes of erosion and freeze thaw." A pyramidal peak is formed "where several corries cut back to meet at a central point, [and] the mountain takes the form of a steep pyramid."

The arête and pyramidal peak sequence follows directly from the corrie one, which is why the 2020 6-marker could ask about all three at once. Two corries developing on adjacent sides of the same mountain each retreat their back wall by freeze-thaw and plucking. As both back walls move towards each other, the rock between them is reduced to a narrow, steep-sided, knife-edge ridge — an arête, such as Striding Edge on Helvellyn. Where three or more corries cut back towards the same point, what is left between them is a steep-sided, sharp-topped pyramidal peak.

Where to point in the Lake District: the corrie is Blea Water; the arête is Striding Edge. The school's own mock set OS map questions on Grisedale and a tarn in grid square 3415, and asked candidates to "suggest one reason for the shape of the land" in a photograph — the mark scheme accepts "it is a tarn", "a corrie formed here", "it represents a hollow enlarged during the ice age", and "erosive processes including plucking and abrasion created the landform".

  • It starts as snow in a hollow — on a shady, often north-facing slope where the snow survives the summer.
  • A tarn is the small circular lake left in the hollow when the ice melts.
  • Arête and pyramidal peak follow — two corries back to back give a knife-edge ridge; three or more give a peak.

Corrie formation — the school's own 4/4 model answer

This has been asked three times in five years. The school's feedback lesson explains the marking rule in one line: "you should link the cause (process) to the effect (a verb) to the result (characteristic of the landform) — e.g. freeze-thaw weathering loosens the rocks and plucking removes them creating a steep back wall." And it notes that at 4 marks you are not strictly required to define each process, though the best answers do; at 6 marks you would be.

"Snow collects in a sheltered hollow, often on a north-facing slope where there is less melting. Over time, the snow is compressed into ice.

Freeze-thaw weathering enlarges the hollow by loosening sediment. Due to pressure, meltwater forms beneath the ice and the glacier begins to move downhill by rotational slip. Meltwater freezes in cracks in the rock, causing pieces of rock to be plucked away and become trapped in the ice. The suspended scree within the ice causes abrasion, which occurs because rocks frozen into the bottom of the glacier scrape against the bedrock, making the hollow deeper. This makes the back wall steeper and creates the armchair shape.

A corrie lip forms at the front because erosion is weaker there as the ice is thinner so moves more slowly. Frost-shattered rock may also be deposited at the front of the corrie, helping to create the lip. After the glacier melts, water often fills the hollow to form a tarn."

The mat's version adds one further detail worth using: "freeze-thaw weathering supports the formation of ice by removing air", and "on the back wall of the corrie, above the ice, freeze-thaw weathering causes the top of the ice to be covered in rock debris. Over time, the back wall retreats backwards, cutting deep into the side of the mountain."

subsections.heading: Glacial troughs, truncated spurs, hanging valleys and ribbon lakes
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · AQA List of Key Terms; 2022 Q5.6 (4 marks); 2023 Q5.4; 2024 Q5.2–5.4

  • Glacial trough — a river valley widened and deepened by ice, so it becomes U-shaped not V-shaped.
  • Truncated spurs — former river valley spurs sliced off by the glacier, leaving cliff-like edges.
  • Hanging valleys — tributary valleys eroded less, left high above the main floor, often with a waterfall.
  • Ribbon lakes — long, narrow lakes where the glacier had more erosive power, so the floor was over-deepened.
More detail

AQA's definitions: a glacial trough is "a river valley widened and deepened by the erosive action of glaciers; it becomes 'U'-shaped instead of the normal 'V'-shape of a river valley." A truncated spur is "a former river valley spur which has been sliced off by a valley glacier, forming cliff-like edges." A hanging valley is "a tributary valley to the main glacier, too cold and high up for ice to be able to easily move. It therefore was not eroded as much as the lower main valley, and today is often the site for a waterfall crashing several hundred metres to the main valley floor." A ribbon lake is "a long, narrow lake found in glaciated valleys formed in locations where the glacier had more erosive power, eg in areas of softer rock, where the valley gradient temporarily steepened or a tributary glacier joined the main valley."

Ribbon lakes are the most examined of these, because they are easy to see on an OS map. The 2023 paper gave both a map extract and a photograph of Llyn Ogwen in Snowdonia and asked for two characteristics for 2 marks: it is long and narrow, it lies on the flat floor of a U-shaped valley with steep sides rising on either side, and it is aligned along the direction the valley runs. The 2024 paper asked which grid square showed part of a ribbon lake. Learn what one looks like in plan — a long thin blue shape running along a valley floor, with contours bunched tightly on both sides.

The 2024 2-marker asked candidates to "describe the shape of the valley and measure the width of the valley floor between points X and Y" on a Snowdonia map — so one mark is a description (U-shaped, flat-floored, with steep sides) and one is a measurement in metres, using the scale bar.

Where to point in the Lake District: the U-shaped valley is the Langdale Valley; the ribbon lake is Ullswater.

  • Glacial trough defined — a river valley widened and deepened by glacial erosion, so it becomes U-shaped not V-shaped.
  • The mechanism — a huge, rigid mass of ice erodes the sides as well as the floor, by abrasion and plucking.
  • Why there — softer rock, a temporarily steeper gradient, or a tributary glacier joining the main valley.

Glacial trough (U-shaped valley) — the sequence for the 4-marker

  1. Before glaciation the valley was a V-shaped river valley with interlocking spurs.
  2. During the ice age, ice accumulated in the corries at the head of the valley and flowed down it as a valley glacier. Unlike a river, the ice filled the whole valley and was rigid, so it could not flow around obstacles.
  3. Abrasion — rock frozen into the base and sides of the glacier acted like sandpaper, scratching and scraping both the floor and the valley sides.
  4. Plucking — meltwater froze around loose rock on the valley sides and floor, and as the ice moved forward it pulled the rock away along its joints.
  5. Freeze-thaw weathering above the ice shattered rock off the valley sides, supplying more abrasive material.
  6. Because the ice eroded laterally as well as vertically, the valley was widened, deepened and straightened into a U-shape with a flat floor and steep sides.
  7. The interlocking spurs that projected into the valley were sliced off, leaving truncated spurs.
  8. Tributary valleys, with far less ice, were eroded much less, so after the ice melted they were left hanging high above the main valley floor, often with a waterfall.
  9. Where the main glacier had more erosive power — softer rock, a steeper gradient, or a tributary glacier joining and adding ice — the floor was over-deepened, and after the ice melted that hollow filled with water to form a ribbon lake.

subsections.heading: Moraine — lateral, medial, terminal and ground
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · Glacial Landscapes Revision Mat; AQA List of Key Terms; 2019 Q5.6 (6 marks)

  • Lateral moraine — along the sides of the glacier, from freeze-thaw debris falling off the valley walls.
  • Medial moraine — a ridge down the middle, where two glaciers merge and their lateral moraines join.
  • Terminal moraine — a ridge across the valley at the furthest point the snout reached, bulldozed and dumped there.
  • Ground moraine — till spread over the valley floor as the ice melted, giving an uneven hummocky surface.
More detail

AQA: moraine is "frost-shattered rock debris and material eroded from the valley floor and sides, transported and deposited by glaciers."

The four types, each with the mechanism that produces it:

  • Lateral moraine. Freeze-thaw weathering shatters rock off the valley sides above the ice; the debris falls onto the edges of the glacier and is carried along as a ridge at the margin. When the ice melts, it is left as an embankment along each side of the valley.
  • Medial moraine. Where a tributary glacier joins the main glacier, the two lateral moraines on their adjoining sides meet and continue down the middle of the combined glacier as a single ridge.
  • Terminal moraine. At the snout, the glacier bulldozes material forward by the sheer weight of the ice, and melting releases the load it is carrying. The result is a ridge of unsorted till running across the valley, marking the furthest point the ice reached.
  • Ground moraine. Material carried at the base of the glacier, released as the ice melts, spread across the valley floor as a sheet of till — AQA's definition of till is "deposited as ground moraine over a large area".

The 2019 6-marker gave a diagram of drumlins and a terminal moraine in front of a retreating glacier and asked candidates to "explain the formation of different landforms of glacial deposition" — so the answer needs at least two, with their own sequences, and that is why the moraine types and drumlins should be learned together.

Beyond the terminal moraine lies the outwash plain: meltwater streams emerging from the snout carry sand and gravel out and deposit it in sorted, rounded layers, which is the contrast the 2019 sediment-range question tested.

  • Moraine defined — frost-shattered rock debris and material eroded from the valley floor and sides, transported and deposited by glaciers.
  • All of it is unsorted till — angular, mixed in size, because ice does not sort or round its load.

subsections.heading: Drumlins and erratics
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · AQA List of Key Terms; 2023 Q5.1; 2025 Q5.2–5.3

  • Drumlin — a hill of glacial till, elongated with its long axis parallel to former ice flow.
  • The shape — blunt and steep at the stoss (up-ice) end, tapering gently to a lee (down-ice) tail.
  • Why they form — the ice became overloaded with till and deposited it around an obstruction, then moulded it.
More detail

AQA: a drumlin is "a hill made of glacial till deposited by a moving glacier, usually elongated or oval in shape, with the longer axis parallel to the former direction of ice." Erratics are "rocks which have been transported and deposited by a glacier some distance from their source region."

Formation of a drumlin. As the glacier moved forward it became overloaded with till, either because it was melting or because it had picked up more material than it could carry. It deposited some of that till, often around an obstruction such as a resistant outcrop of bedrock. The ice continued to move over the deposit and moulded it, smoothing and streamlining it into the classic shape: steep and blunt on the up-ice (stoss) side where the ice pressed against it, and tapered into a long gentle lee slope on the down-ice side. Because the ice flowed in one direction, every drumlin in an area is aligned the same way, which is why they occur in swarms that look like a "basket of eggs".

The 2025 paper gave a contour map of a drumlin and asked for its length from point A to point B using the scale, and then to describe its shape — which is where the "hill or bump" warning applies. The 2023 paper tested erratic as a 1-mark multiple choice, with moraine, outwash and till as the distractors; the giveaway in the stem was "in areas with a different rock type".

Where to point in the Lake District: the drumlins are in Swindale.

  • Drumlin defined — a hill of glacial till, elongated or oval, with its long axis parallel to the former direction of ice flow.
  • They occur in swarms — "basket of eggs" topography, which is how you recognise them on a map.
  • Erratic defined — a rock transported and deposited by a glacier some distance from its source region.
  • Erratics prove ice direction — a boulder of a rock type foreign to the area shows where the ice came from.

✗ Describing a drumlin as "a hill" or "a bump". The school's feedback lesson states flatly: "a 'hill' or 'bump' does not refer to the correct shape."
✓ "Elongated or oval, with a steep, blunt end facing the direction the ice came from and a long, gently tapering tail pointing the way it was going — like an upturned spoon."

subsections.heading: The Lake District — landforms of erosion and deposition
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, section 10

  • Erosion — corrie Blea Water, arête Striding Edge, ribbon lake Ullswater, U-shaped valley Langdale.
  • Drumlins — in Swindale (deposition).
  • Four erosional, one depositional — so for depositional landforms, lead with Swindale's drumlins.
More detail

Why the Lake District looks the way it does. It lay under the last ice sheet, and its radial pattern of valleys meant ice flowed outwards from a central upland dome. Corries formed in the shady north- and east-facing hollows high on the fells; where their back walls retreated towards one another they left arêtes such as Striding Edge on Helvellyn; the valley glaciers that flowed out of those corries widened and deepened the pre-existing V-shaped river valleys into U-shaped troughs such as Langdale, truncating the spurs and leaving tributary valleys hanging; and where the ice had most erosive power the troughs were over-deepened into the long, narrow ribbon lakes — Ullswater, Windermere, Thirlmere — that the National Park is named for. As the ice melted it left till on the valley floors, moulded in places into the drumlin swarm at Swindale.

That single paragraph is also the answer to "explain why this area attracts tourists" (2024, 4 marks) in its physical half: the scenery is the glacial landscape.

The school's own Glaciers mock used OS maps of this area — Grisedale Beck, a tarn in grid square 3415, an arête at grid reference 347149 — so practising grid references on a Lake District map extract is directly useful.

  • Arête — Striding Edge (erosion).
  • Ribbon lake — Ullswater (erosion).
  • Corrie — Blea Water (erosion).
  • U-shaped valley — the Langdale Valley (erosion).

The Lake District — the UK upland example

The school's named example for "an example of an upland area in the UK affected by glaciation to identify its major landforms of erosion and deposition". Five landform–place pairs, each labelled erosion or deposition.

LandformExampleErosion or deposition
ArêteStriding EdgeErosion
Ribbon lakeUllswaterErosion
CorrieBlea WaterErosion
U-shaped valleyLangdale ValleyErosion
DrumlinsSwindaleDeposition

How to use it. The question "name one landform of glacial erosion shown in grid square 7112" (2024) is answered from an OS map, not from this list — but any question that says "an upland area you have studied" wants these names. Lead with the corrie at Blea Water and the arête at Striding Edge, because they are the two landforms whose formation is most often examined, and because Striding Edge is also a tourist attraction, which links the physical half of the module to the human half.

subsections.heading: Economic activities in glaciated upland areas
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · Glacial Landscapes Revision Mat; Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, section 11; 2019 Q5.5

  • Four spec-named activities — tourism, farming, forestry and quarrying.
  • Tourism dominates — worth £2.3bn and 75,000 jobs in the Lake District.
  • Farming and forestry — extensive sheep farming on thin upland soils; coniferous plantations worth £30m.
  • Quarrying — the Honister Slate Mine, which is both a working mine and a tourist attraction.
More detail

The mat names the four activities exactly as the spec does: "Farming (extensive agriculture), forestry, tourism and quarrying." The Case Study Summary Booklet attaches the figures:

  • Tourism — £2.3bn and 75,000 jobs.
  • Farming — sheep farming. Upland soils are thin and the climate is wet and cool, so arable farming is not viable; sheep can graze rough fell pasture, which is why extensive is the right word.
  • Forestry — coniferous forests, £30m. Conifers are planted because they tolerate thin, acidic soils and exposure.
  • Quarrying — the Honister Slate Mine, which combines mining with tourism: climbing and a 1 km zip-wire.

Why the glaciation explains the economy. Each activity exists because of the landscape the ice left. Tourism exists because the corries, arêtes, troughs and ribbon lakes are spectacular. Sheep farming exists because glacial erosion stripped the soil and left steep, thin-soiled fells where nothing else will grow. Forestry occupies the same marginal land. And quarrying exists because the ice exposed the hard volcanic rock and slate that is worth extracting. Saying that is the difference between listing the activities and explaining them.

The 2019 4-marker gave a figure listing tourism, quarrying, farming and forestry and asked candidates to "explain why there may be land use conflicts in glaciated upland areas" — so the four activities and the conflicts between them need to be learned as a single block.

  • Farming — extensive agriculture, overwhelmingly sheep farming on thin upland soils.
  • Forestry — coniferous plantations, worth £30m.
  • Honister doubles up — climbing and a 1 km zip-wire, so quarrying and tourism are not always opposed.

subsections.heading: Land use conflicts, and development versus conservation
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · Glacial Landscapes Revision Mat; 2019 Q5.5; 2023 Q5.6; 2025 Q5.4

  • Land use conflict — when different users of the land do not agree on how it should be used.
  • Tourists versus farmers — walkers with dogs disturb sheep, and footpaths cross working farmland.
  • Tourists versus developers — walkers object to wind turbines and zip wires spoiling the landscape.
  • Second homes versus locals — 20% of houses are second homes, pricing out local people.
More detail

AQA's definitions: land use conflicts are "disagreements which arise when different users of the land do not agree on how it should be used." Conservation is "managing the environment in order to preserve, protect or restore it."

Why conflict is structural here, not accidental. A glaciated upland is a small area of land that four economic activities all want, and three of them are incompatible with the fourth. Tourism needs the landscape to look untouched; quarrying removes it; forestry replaces open fell with dense conifer; farming needs stock left undisturbed. On top of that the land is inside a National Park, whose statutory purpose is conservation, while the local economy depends on development. So any proposal — a zip wire, a wind turbine, a reservoir, a new car park — pits the two purposes of the Park against each other.

The balancing strategies the mat lists, which answer "give three ways development and conservation can be balanced": set maximum visitor numbers; use signs to identify areas that are out of bounds; seasonal closure, which can involve closing visitor attractions in winter to allow the environment to recover; and restrict activities such as the use of motorbikes and horse riding.

  • Land use conflict defined — disagreements arising when different users of the land do not agree on how it should be used.
  • Tourists versus developers — walkers object to wind turbines ruining the landscape, and to zip wires spoiling the view.
  • Conservation versus forestry — environmentalists object to conifer plantations because they destroy habitats.
  • Reservoirs versus residents — constructing dams and reservoirs can cause locals to be relocated.

The conflicts, from the school mat

Learn these as pairs — who against whom, over what. The 2025 2-marker was "outline one possible conflict between tourists and farmers", and the feedback lesson's rule was strict: "you must refer to the activity of the tourist, and the development of the point must link to that. Be specific. Only one possible conflict is counted for the mark. Conflicts discussed must link to the landscape in the picture."

  • Walkers objecting to military training.
  • Constructing dams and reservoirs can cause locals to be relocated.
  • Tourists and walkers may object to wind turbines ruining the landscape.
  • Conservationists are against hunting.
  • Environmentalists object to conifer plantations as they destroy habitats.
  • Local people object to commercial logging as it can cause localised flooding.
  • Walkers with dogs disturb sheep (Case Study Summary Booklet) — the classic tourist–farmer conflict.
  • Second homeowners price out locals — 20% of houses in the Lake District are second homes.
  • Traffic. 89% of visitors arrive by road, causing congestion and air pollution in Ambleside on roads farmers need to work their land.

Development versus conservation — the 2023 question. The figure described concerns about plans to build a zip wire across the Thirlmere Valley in the Lake District: "some people think it will spoil the view. Others are concerned about the extra traffic it will bring to the narrow roads." That is the perfect worked example, because the Honister Slate Mine already runs a 1 km zip-wire — so the same development is an economic opportunity in one valley and a conservation threat in another.

✗ "Tourists and farmers don't get on." — no activity, no mechanism, no mark.
✓ "Tourists walking their dogs on footpaths crossing fell pasture may let them off the lead (1), which disturbs the sheep, and can cause ewes to abort or flocks to scatter, costing the farmer money and time rounding them up (1)."

subsections.heading: The Lake District — tourism, its impacts, and managing them
subsections.html:
Spec 3.1.3.4 · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, section 11; Y10 feedback model answer; 2022 and 2025 6-markers

  • The scale — 18 million tourists a year, against 40,000 local people.
  • Environmental impacts — footpath erosion at honeypot sites, boat pollution in Windermere, air pollution in Ambleside.
  • Economic impacts — tourism is worth £2.3bn and 75,000 jobs.
  • Four named strategies — Fix the Fells, Friends of the Lake District, the 10 knot speed limit, and park and ride.

The Lake District — the figures that win marks

  • 18 million tourists a year against 40,000 local people, and 89% arrive by road.
  • Tourism is worth £2.3bn and supports 75,000 jobs; coniferous forestry adds £30m.
  • 20% of houses are second homes, which prices out locals and closes services out of season.
  • Footpath erosion at honeypot sites, boat and noise pollution on Windermere, air pollution in Ambleside.
  • Fix the Fells — repairs 410 miles of footpath with a permanent surface of resistant rock.
  • A 10 knot speed limit on Lake Windermere, to cut noise, wash and pollution.
  • Park and Sail and the Honister Rambler park and ride, plus by-pass dual carriageways.
  • Friends of the Lake District — conserves the area by restricting planning development.
  • Honister Slate Mine — climbing and a 1 km zip-wire: quarrying and tourism together.
More detail

The school's 6/6 model answer for "Discuss how different strategies are used to manage the impacts of tourism in glaciated areas in the UK. Use Figure 18 and your own understanding" is the template to copy. Two strategies, each with mechanism, figure, and an honest limitation:

"Repairing paths (as shown in Figure 18) can help to reduce environmental impact of footpath erosion in the Lake District. 18.4 million tourists visit the area each year, and when tourists stray from the path, it can damage the grass and take a long time to recover. The 'Fix the Fells' organisation is aiming to repair 410 miles of footpaths by laying a more permanent pathway made of resistant rocks. However, this will take a long time to achieve and is reliant on volunteers. Some visitors will also still not necessarily use these paths."

"The 'park and sail' strategy helps to reduce the impact of traffic congestion by encouraging visitors to travel by boat instead. This is important because 80% of people travel by car to the Lake District, and therefore the scheme will reduce the likelihood of traffic jams on the narrow roads, improving accessibility for local farmers who use the roads to manage their farmland. In addition, it will reduce the air pollution caused by the emissions of idling cars and encourage the visitors to leave them outside the National Park. However, the water turbulence caused by the boat engines can still harm aquatic life, and the visitors may not be staying near to the lakes and need onward transport on the other side."

The feedback lesson's checklist for that question: refer to the figure; there are two strategies you could discuss — repairing paths and the Park and Sail scheme; the command word is discuss, so discuss how each scheme is used and how well it manages the impacts; and "Level 3 (5–6 marks) requires 'use of the figure and your own example'. Therefore, you should be including facts in your answer e.g. the number of tourists."

A note on figures. The Case Study Summary Booklet gives 18 million tourists and 89% arriving by road; the model answer says 18.4 million and 80% travel by car. Both are the school's own documents and either will be credited; the Case Study Summary Booklet is the revision document, so use 18 million and 89% if you need to pick.

The 2022 question — "assess the economic and environmental impacts of tourism in a glaciated upland area" — was set on a figure of Snowdonia tourism statistics, including 595 000 visitors to Snowdon annually. The Lake District material answers it directly: the economic impacts are £2.3bn and 75,000 jobs set against congestion costs and the second-home effect on house prices; the environmental impacts are footpath erosion, boat pollution in Windermere and air pollution in Ambleside.

  • Why they come — the glacial scenery, walking, boating, and attractions such as the Honister zip-wire.
  • Social impacts — 20% of houses are second homes, which prices out locals; walkers with dogs disturb sheep.

The Lake District — attractions, impacts and management

The school's named example for "an example of a glaciated upland area in the UK used for tourism". The spec asks for three things, so learn it in three blocks.

Attractions. Walking — 18 million tourists per year come to the Lake District to walk and enjoy the beautiful scenery, compared with just 40,000 local people. Boating on the lakes, especially Windermere. Driving through the scenery. Plus the Honister Slate Mine, which offers climbing and a 1 km zip-wire.

Impacts.

  • Environmental — footpath erosion at honeypot sites. Pollution from boat engines and oil in Lake Windermere, plus noise pollution from boats. Air pollution due to traffic congestion in Ambleside, because 89% of visitors arrive by road.
  • Social — walkers with dogs disturb sheep. Second homeowners can price out locals, and 20% of houses are second homes, which hollows out villages and closes local services out of season.
  • Economic — tourism is worth £2.3bn and supports 75,000 jobs, alongside sheep farming, £30m of coniferous forestry and quarrying at Honister.

Strategies to manage the impacts.

  • Fix the Fells — a scheme set up to repair damaged footpaths. The school's model answer adds that it aims to repair 410 miles of footpaths by laying a more permanent pathway made of resistant rocks.
  • Friends of the Lake District — try to conserve the environment by restricting planning development.
  • A 10 knot speed limit imposed on boats on Lake Windermere, to reduce noise, wash and pollution.
  • Dual carriageways built to by-pass congested towns, and park and ride services like the Honister Rambler — plus the Park and Sail scheme, which encourages tourists to travel by boat rather than by car.

The facts you cannot sit the paper without

Ice extent. All of Scotland and Ireland, Wales and northern England as far south as the Midlands; southern England ice-free. Ice was deeper over Scandinavia than over the British Isles.

Keep the four process lists separate. Weathering — freeze-thaw (water expands 9%; gives scree slopes and block-fields). Erosion — abrasion and plucking. Movement and transport — rotational slip, bulldozing, basal flow, internal deformation. Deposition — till (unsorted) and outwash (sorted and rounded).

Erosional landforms. Corrie (armchair hollow; freeze-thaw + rotational slip + plucking + abrasion; lip; tarn) → arête (two corries back to back) → pyramidal peak (three or more). Glacial trough (V → U, widened, deepened, straightened) with truncated spurs, hanging valleys and ribbon lakes.

Depositional landforms. Moraine — lateral (valley sides), medial (two glaciers merge), terminal (the snout's furthest point), ground (valley floor). Drumlins — elongated till hills, steep blunt stoss end up-ice, tapering lee tail down-ice, in swarms. Erratics — boulders of foreign rock carried far from source.

Lake District landforms. Arête Striding Edge · ribbon lake Ullswater · corrie Blea Water · U-shaped valley Langdale · drumlins Swindale.

Lake District economy. Tourism £2.3bn, 75,000 jobs · sheep farming · coniferous forestry £30m · quarrying at the Honister Slate Mine (climbing and a 1 km zip-wire).

Lake District tourism. 18 million tourists a year vs 40,000 locals · 89% arrive by road · 20% of houses are second homes · footpath erosion at honeypot sites · boat engine and oil pollution plus noise in Windermere · air pollution in Ambleside.

Management. Fix the Fells (410 miles of footpath) · Friends of the Lake District (restricting planning development) · 10 knot speed limit on Windermere · dual carriageways bypassing congested towns · park and ride (the Honister Rambler) and Park and Sail · maximum visitor numbers · out-of-bounds signs · seasonal closure · restricting motorbikes and horse riding.

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
Freeze-thaw weatheringAlso called frost-shattering: in cold climates, water enters cracks during the warmer day and freezes at night, expanding and exerting pressure on the rock, causing pieces to break off
AbrasionErosion caused by rocks and boulders in the base of the glacier acting like a giant file, scratching and scraping the rocks below
PluckingErosion where meltwater in the glacier freezes onto rocks and, as the ice moves forward, plucks or pulls out large pieces along the rock joints
Rotational slipOccurs when the ice moves in a circular motion; it erodes hollows in the landscape and deepens them into bowl shapes
BulldozingIce pushes material of all shapes and sizes as it moves slowly forward
Basal flowThe glacier slides over the bedrock on a film of meltwater
Internal deformationMovement where it is too cold for basal flow: the ice moves like plastic
TillAn unsorted mixture of sand, clay and boulders carried by a glacier and deposited as ground moraine over a large area
OutwashMaterial, chiefly sand or gravel, deposited by meltwater streams in front of and underneath a glacier; sorted and rounded by water action
CorrieAlso called a cirque: an armchair-shaped hollow in the mountainside formed by glacial erosion, rotational slip and freeze-thaw weathering; where the valley glacier begins, and when the ice melts it can leave a tarn
TarnThe small circular lake left in a corrie after the ice has melted
ArêteA sharp, knife-like ridge formed between two corries cutting back by erosion and freeze-thaw
Pyramidal peakWhere several corries cut back to meet at a central point, so the mountain takes the form of a steep pyramid
Glacial troughA river valley widened and deepened by the erosive action of glaciers; it becomes U-shaped instead of the normal V-shape of a river valley
Truncated spurA former river valley spur sliced off by a valley glacier, forming cliff-like edges
Hanging valleyA tributary valley to the main glacier, too cold and high up for ice to move easily, so it was not eroded as much as the main valley and is often the site of a waterfall
Ribbon lakeA long, narrow lake in a glaciated valley, formed where the glacier had more erosive power — softer rock, a temporarily steeper gradient, or a tributary glacier joining
MoraineFrost-shattered rock debris and material eroded from the valley floor and sides, transported and deposited by glaciers
DrumlinA hill made of glacial till deposited by a moving glacier, usually elongated or oval, with the longer axis parallel to the former direction of ice
ErraticsRocks transported and deposited by a glacier some distance from their source region
ConservationManaging the environment in order to preserve, protect or restore it
Land use conflictsDisagreements which arise when different users of the land do not agree on how it should be used
Honeypot siteA place of particular attraction to tourists, which therefore receives concentrated visitor pressure and damage
LandscapeAn extensive area of land regarded as being visually and physically distinct

The 6-mark frame — Section C's biggest question

Section C has no 9-markers, so the 6-mark discuss decides your grade here. Level marked: Basic 1–2, Clear 3–4, Detailed 5–6, with AO2 and AO3 split evenly. The school's feedback lesson states the Level 3 requirement outright: "Level 3 (5–6 marks) requires 'use of the figure and your own example'. Therefore, you should be including facts in your answer e.g. the number of tourists."

  • Name a strategy or impact visible in the figure. "Repairing paths, as shown in Figure 18, can help to reduce the environmental impact of footpath erosion in the Lake District." You must write "in Figure…".
  • Give the scale of the problem with a figure. "18 million tourists visit each year against 40,000 local people, and when tourists stray from the path it damages the grass, which takes a long time to recover."
  • Name the scheme and what it actually does. "Fix the Fells is repairing 410 miles of footpath by laying a permanent pathway made of resistant rocks."
  • Concede a limitation — this is the AO3 mark. "However, this will take a long time to achieve and relies on volunteers, and some visitors will still not use the paths."
  • Do the same for a second strategy. Park and Sail, or the 10 knot limit on Windermere, or Friends of the Lake District restricting planning development — each with mechanism, figure and limitation.
  • Finish with a comparative judgement. "Overall, managing transport is the more effective strategy, because 89% of visitors arrive by road, so reducing car use addresses congestion, air pollution and the pressure on honeypot sites at once — whereas footpath repair treats the damage after it has happened."

Starters: "This is largely / somewhat / fully effective because…" · "This is important because 89% of visitors…" · "However, this relies on…" · "In addition, it will…" · "This strategy is more effective than… because it tackles the cause rather than the symptom" · "Overall, tourism brings mostly advantages, because…"
