drill.intro:
What each command word actually wants

Paper 1 is 1 hour 30 minutes, 88 marks, 35%. In Section C you answer two questions from Coasts, Rivers and Glacial — the class did Coasts and Glacial — and each is worth 15 marks. The guide's first rule: "Don't answer the wrong questions."

  • 1 mark — process definition, landform identification, OS map or data. Shade one circle only. Four-figure grid reference for a square, six-figure for a point; distance with the scale bar; direction of view by comparing map and photograph; range, mean, median and mode. Keep the four process lists separate — weathering, erosion, movement, deposition — because the multiple choice swaps them deliberately.
  • 2 marks — describe / outline / suggest. Point plus development, or two linked points, using the figure. For a conflict question the school's feedback is strict: refer to the activity, develop the point so it links to the question, be specific, and link it to the landscape shown.
  • 4 marks — explain the formation of a landform. Level marked: Basic 1–2, Clear 3–4. The rule from the feedback lesson: link the cause (process) to the effect (a verb) to the result (characteristic of the landform) — "freeze-thaw weathering loosens the rocks and plucking removes them creating a steep back wall." At 4 marks you need not define each process, though the best answers do; at 6 marks you must. If it says "use one or more diagrams", annotate rather than label.
  • 4 marks — explain why the area attracts tourists / why there are conflicts. Same level marking, needs the named upland area and its figures.
  • 6 marks — explain / assess / discuss. Level marked: Basic 1–2, Clear 3–4, Detailed 5–6. Refer to the figure and write "in Figure…". Discuss at least two strategies or landforms. Make a judgement with a degree word. Level 3 requires the figure and your own example, with facts such as visitor numbers.
  • 9 marks — not in Section C. The school's booklet confirms: "only 6 markers on this topic, no 9 markers". D11 and D12 below are marked stretch — they drill the same material in the 9-mark evaluate shape, which is how Section B and Paper 3 use it, and they are the best practice for the 6-mark judgement.

Twelve questions. The 6s and 9s are written as plans — AQA marks them in levels, so the mark points are a coverage target, not a tick list.

modules.title: Urban Issues and Challenges
modules.standfirst: Section A of Paper 2 Challenges in the Human Environment — global urbanisation, megacities, the growth of a major city in an NEE (Rio de Janeiro, with the Favela-Bairro Project), urban change in a major UK city (London, with regeneration at Stratford and the Olympic Park), and sustainable urban living (East Village) plus sustainable transport. Every year the section runs the same shape: a few map and graph marks, a 4-marker, a 6-marker on a figure, and one 9-marker (+3 SPaG). The marks live in Rio and London figures, not in general statements about cities.

subsections.html:
What they actually ask

Every Section A question from the June 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 papers, with marks. Note the pattern: the 9-marker alternates between LIC/NEE opportunities or challenges and UK urban change, and 2024 broke the pattern by giving the 9-marker to sustainability.

  • The 9-marker (+3 SPaG) — UK urban change in 2019 and 2022, LIC/NEE opportunities or challenges in 2021 (school list) and 2025, sustainability in 2024.
  • Map, graph and calculation skills — every single year, worth 4–6 marks a paper: area, distance, grid references, direction, graph completion.
  • LIC/NEE opportunities and challenges — 6- or 9-mark answers in 2019, 2023, 2024 and 2025, plus the school's 2021. This is Rio.
  • UK urban change — 2019, 2022, 2024, 2025: regeneration, dereliction, urban greening, national migration. This is London and Stratford.
  • The short openers — what urbanisation is, its causes, and a city's importance: 1–4 marks in all five papers.
  • Overdue — urban planning for the urban poor (Favela-Bairro) last asked in 2022; the rural–urban fringe appeared for the first time in 2025.

Examiners' refrain: develop the figure instead of repeating it, and answer the "to what extent".

Every Section A question from 2019–2025, with the exact wordings

Every Section A question from the June 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 papers, with marks. Note the pattern: the 9-marker alternates between LIC/NEE opportunities or challenges and UK urban change, and 2024 broke the pattern by giving the 9-marker to sustainability.

  • Defining and measuring urbanisation — "Use the following data to complete Figure 1" on natural increase (2019, 2 marks); "Calculate the mean rate of growth per hour for the Asian cities shown" (2022, 2 marks); "Give one reason for the growth of megacities in LIC/NEEs" (2023, 1 mark); "Calculate the mean size of the cities shown… to one decimal place" (2023, 2 marks); "Which of the following statements is true?" (2024, 1 mark); "What is urbanisation?" (2025, 1 mark); "Which continent is expected to have the most new megacities in 2050?" and "What is the expected percentage growth of Nairobi 2022–2050?" (2025, 1 mark each).
  • Causes of urban growth — migration and natural increase — "Outline one reason why rates of natural increase are high in many cities in LIC/NEEs" (2019, 2 marks); "Outline one reason for the slower rates of growth in HIC cities" (2022, 2 marks); "Give two push factors that encourage people to leave rural areas in LICs/NEEs" (2024, 2 marks); "Suggest how natural increase and migration affect the growth of LIC/NEE cities. Use Figure 2 and your own understanding" (2025, 4 marks).
  • The importance of a city — "Give one way in which a major city in an LIC/NEE is regionally important" (2022, 1 mark); "Give one way a major city in a LIC/NEE is nationally important" (2024, 1 mark); "Complete the following factfile for a UK city you have studied" (2019, 2 marks); "Outline one way in which a UK city you have studied is important in the UK" (2023, 2 marks); "Describe the importance of a named UK city for the rest of the UK" (2025, 2 marks).
  • Opportunities of urban growth in an LIC/NEE — "Explain how urban industrial areas can help encourage development. Use Figure 2 and your own understanding" (2019, 6 marks); "To what extent has urban growth created social opportunities? Use Figure 3 and a LIC/NEE example you have studied" (2023, 6 marks); "Discuss how urban growth in LIC/NEE cities has created social and economic opportunities. Use Figure 6 and a case study" (2025, 9 marks + 3 SPaG).
  • Challenges of urban growth in an LIC/NEE — "Outline one reason why reducing crime is a challenge in some LIC/NEE cities" (2023, 2 marks); "To what extent is managing environmental issues, such as waste disposal, a challenge in cities in LICs/NEEs? Use Figure 2 and your own understanding" (2024, 6 marks). The school's own question list adds "Assess the extent of the challenges created by urban growth in LICs/NEEs. Use a case study of a city you have studied" (2021, 9 marks).
  • Urban planning for the urban poor — "Explain how urban planning is improving quality of life for the urban poor. Use Figure 2 and an LIC/NEE example you have studied" (2022, 6 marks). This is the Favela-Bairro question and it is overdue.
  • Urban change in the UK — opportunities and challenges — "Explain how regeneration can help to solve urban problems. Use Figure 4 and your own understanding" (2019, 4 marks); "To what extent has urban change created social and economic opportunities in a UK city you have studied?" (2019, 9 marks + 3 SPaG); "Assess the challenges created by urban change in a UK city you have studied" (2022, 9 marks + 3 SPaG); "Outline one problem caused by dereliction in cities" (2024, 2 marks); "Suggest how urban greening can create opportunities in UK cities" (2024, 4 marks); "Outline one impact of national migration on a named UK city" (2025, 2 marks).
  • Urban sprawl and the rural–urban fringe — "Suggest how the growth of a commuter settlement has impacts on the rural-urban fringe. Use Figure 4 and Figure 5 and your own understanding" (2025, 6 marks). First appearance of this spec bullet as an extended answer.
  • Sustainable urban living and transport — "Suggest how developments such as this can help urban areas to become more sustainable. Use Figure 3 and your own understanding" (2022, 4 marks); "Suggest how urban transport strategies can be used to reduce traffic congestion. Use Figure 4 and your own understanding" (2023, 4 marks); "To what extent can water and energy conservation make cities more sustainable?" (2024, 9 marks).
  • Map and graph skills, every single year — area of an enclosed feature (2019 Area Y, 2025 Saxilby village), straight-line distance (2019, 2024, 2025), six-figure grid references and "what is found at 298333?" (2024), direction the photographer was facing (2024), route choice and journey time (2023), and a graph or table completion (2022, 2023, 2025). These are 4–6 marks a paper for map work alone — practise them.

What the examiners keep saying. On the 6-markers (2022 01.4, 2023 01.6): "the majority spent their answer space repeating information from the figure with little or no development, just stating that quality of life was improved without saying how". On the 9-marker (2023 01.11): many "struggled to move beyond a generic 'geography of anywhere' as their answers lacked AO1", and "students frequently confused 'social opportunities' with 'socialising'". And "very few students considered the to what extent aspect of the question".

How Section A is built, in full

Section A is compulsory, worth about 33 marks, and always Question 01. It splits into four blocks that appear in the same order nearly every year: global urbanisation (1–4 marks), the NEE city (Rio — usually the 6-marker or the 9-marker), OS map and graph skills (3–5 easy marks), and the UK city (London — the other extended answer). Learn which of Rio and London is carrying the 9-marker in a given year by reading the last question first.

subsections.heading: Global urbanisation — the process, the pattern and the numbers
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.1 · Urban Issues and Challenges revision, slides 3–4; Urban Revision Mat

  • Urbanisation is a proportion, not a total — the rising percentage of a country's population living in towns and cities.
  • Over 55% of the world is now urban — and 90% of future growth is in Africa and Asia.
  • Growth is fastest in LICs and NEEs — India, China and Nigeria are 37% of urban growth to 2050.
  • Two factors only — migration and natural increase set the rate of urbanisation, and examiners want both named.
More detail

Urbanisation is the process by which an increasing percentage of a country's population comes to live in towns and cities. Rapid urbanisation is a feature of many LICs and NEEs. Keep it separate from urban growth, which is the absolute increase in the size of a city — examiners reward the precise term.

The global picture, in the figures the school's slides give: 55%+ of the world's population lives in urban areas (UN, 2023); there were 33 megacities worldwide in 2023 and 50 are expected by 2050; and 90% of the increase in the world's urban population will be in Africa and Asia.

Why urbanisation happened first in HICs. It began during the industrial revolution. People were pulled to urban areas from rural areas to work in factories, and they were pushed as developments in technology led to mechanisation on farms.

The pattern in HICs today. HICs such as the USA, most of Europe, Australia and Japan are highly urbanised, with at least 75% of the population living in urban areas. North America is the most urbanised region, with 82% of its population in urban areas. The rate of urbanisation in HICs is slowing down, and counter-urbanisation is occurring in some HICs as people move from overcrowded urban areas to more attractive rural environments.

Four reasons the school gives for the counter-urbanisation trend: (1) car ownership has risen over the last 40 years so people are more mobile, and information technology means more people can work from home; (2) urban areas are becoming increasingly unpleasant places to live, through pollution, crime and traffic congestion; (3) more people move when they retire; (4) new business parks on greenfield sites at the edge of cities mean people no longer have to travel to the city centre, so they prefer to live on the outskirts near where they work.

Why rates are higher in LICs and NEEs. As LICs develop, people are pushed from the countryside as mechanisation leads to fewer jobs. People are pulled to cities by the growth of jobs in urban industries, and are also attracted by higher living standards, education and better healthcare. India, China and Nigeria are expected to account for 37% of the growth in the world's urban population between 2014 and 2050.

  • Urbanisation is a proportion, not a total — the rising percentage of a country's population living in towns and cities.
  • Over 55% of the world now lives in urban areas — and 90% of the increase will be in Africa and Asia.
  • HICs urbanised first — during the Industrial Revolution; North America is now 82% urban, HICs at least 75%.
  • Growth is fastest in LICs and NEEs — India, China and Nigeria alone account for 37% of urban growth 2014–2050.
  • HIC rates are slowing — some are counter-urbanising, with people leaving crowded cities for the countryside.
  • Two factors only — the rate of urbanisation is set by migration and natural increase, and examiners want both named.

✗ "Urbanisation is when cities get bigger." — that is urban growth, and the 1-marker in 2025 was marked on the exact wording.
✓ "Urbanisation is the increase in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities." A rural population can still be rising while urbanisation happens.

subsections.heading: Why cities grow — push, pull and natural increase
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.1 · Urban Revision Mat (with answers); 2025 Q01.4 mark scheme

  • Two causes, always both — rural–urban migration, and natural increase (birth rate minus death rate).
  • Push factors — no well-paid work, poor sanitation, limited schooling, drought, soil erosion, machines replacing farm jobs.
  • Pull factors — better-paid jobs, better education and healthcare, water and sanitation, family already there.
  • Migration drives the natural increase — migrants are typically 18–35, so births are high and deaths low.
More detail

The two factors that affect the rate of urbanisation are migration, as people move from rural to urban areas, and natural increase, as birth rates are higher than death rates in urban areas. The link between them is the one that earns the top marks: migrants are typically aged 18–35, which produces a high birth rate and a low death rate, so the city grows twice over.

Push factors (rural areas): limited opportunities for well-paid employment; poor transport infrastructure; lack of sanitation; limited opportunities to get a good education; environmental issues such as drought, soil erosion and desertification; poor harvests resulting in limited food; agricultural jobs being replaced by machinery; limited services such as fresh water, health care and electricity.

Pull factors (urban areas): employment opportunities in better-paid jobs; a large market for goods and services; improved education and healthcare provision; better services such as fresh water and sanitation; family and friends who may have already moved; better public transport provision; a higher standard of living due to higher wages and higher quality housing with services.

The 2025 mark scheme for the 4-marker on exactly this shows what "application" means. From the figure: a low median age and a weekly growth figure of many thousands. From your own understanding: the low median age means young people of reproductive age, so larger numbers of children swelling the population; the weekly figure shows rapid growth — and manipulating that figure further (dividing it to give a daily total) is specifically credited as evidence you understand the scale. The scheme also credits consequences: a youthful population provides a supply of factory workers; rapid growth creates resource and housing pressure; urban sprawl and informal settlements grow.

For the HIC version, the 2022 examiner's report says 1 mark was widespread for access to contraception, with better answers developing this to lower birth rates, and the best answers showed understanding of earlier industrialisation, urbanisation and urban–rural migration.

  • Push factors — no well-paid work, poor transport, no sanitation, limited schooling, drought, soil erosion, poor harvests, machines replacing farm jobs.
  • Pull factors — better-paid jobs, a big market, better education and healthcare, fresh water and sanitation, family already there, better transport.
  • Migration causes the natural increase — migrants are typically 18–35, so the birth rate is high and the death rate low.
  • The exam link to make — a low median age means more people of reproductive age, so more children swell the population further.
  • HIC growth is slower — earlier industrialisation, earlier urbanisation, access to contraception, and lower birth rates.

✗ "People move to cities for a better life." — one undeveloped assertion; the 2-markers need point plus development.
✓ "People are pushed from rural areas by poor harvests (1); the lack of food and produce to sell forces them to the city, where food supply and jobs are more regular (1)."

subsections.heading: Megacities, world cities and primate cities
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.1 · Urban Revision Mat; Case Study Summary Booklet quiz facts

  • Megacity — an urban area of at least 10 million people. Learn the number, not "very big".
  • 33 in 2023, about 50 by 2050 — and the new ones will be overwhelmingly in Africa and Asia.
  • World city — global influence in finance, trade, culture or politics; London is an "Alpha++" world city.
  • Primate city — a city that dominates its country, usually more than twice the size of the next largest.
More detail

A megacity is a city with a population of at least 10 million people. The majority of the world's megacities are located in LICs and NEEs, particularly in Asia and Africa. The school's figures: 33 megacities in 2023, rising to around 50 by 2050, with 90% of the world's increased urban population in Africa and Asia.

The 2022 Paper 2 Figure 1 was a world map of growth rates per week for named cities, which is worth knowing as a reference list of megacities and their growth: Lagos +85, Dhaka +74, Kinshasa +63, Mumbai +51, Manila +29, Jakarta +27, Mexico City +22, São Paulo +18, Rio de Janeiro +10, New York +10, Berlin +1 — the HIC/LIC contrast in one figure.

The spec also names world cities and primate cities. A world city has influence over the whole globe through its financial, cultural and political reach — London and New York are the two standard examples. A primate city dominates its own country's urban hierarchy.

  • Megacity — an urban area with a population of at least 10 million. Learn the number, not "very big".
  • 33 in 2023, around 50 expected by 2050 — and the new ones will be overwhelmingly in Africa and Asia.
  • Most are in LICs/NEEs — in 2014, at least 21 megacities were in LICs/NEEs against just 7 in MICs.
  • World city — a city with global influence in finance, trade, culture or politics; London is an "Alpha++" world city.
  • Examples to name — Tokyo, Mumbai, São Paulo, Lagos, Dhaka, Kinshasa, Manila, Jakarta.

subsections.heading: Rio de Janeiro — location and importance
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.2, Case Study Three · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, pp. 12

  • Where — south-east Brazil, grown up around a large natural bay called Guanabara Bay; Brazil is an NEE.
  • Population — around 13 million in the Greater Rio metropolitan area; roughly 1.5 million live in favelas.
  • Regionally — a huge job market, especially construction and banking; Brazil's second most important industrial centre.

Rio de Janeiro — the figures that win marks

  • Where and how big — south-east Brazil (an NEE), around Guanabara Bay; about 13 million people, 1.5 million of them in favelas.
  • Why it matters — 5% of Brazil's GNI, the 3rd busiest port in Brazil, host of the 2016 Olympics.
  • Opportunity — health: free care and 3.44 doctors per 1,000 against 2.81 nationally.
  • Opportunity — education, water and energy: literacy 97% against 93%; the Guandu works, the world's largest; 99% of homes have electricity.
  • Challenge — housing: about 1,000 favelas on steep hillsides, so landslide and flood risk is high.
  • Challenge — health and water: favela residents live about 13 years less; 12% have no running water; 35% of sewage runs in open sewers.
  • Challenge — jobs and crime: 20% favela unemployment, 3.5 million in the informal economy, a murder rate of 20 per 1,000.
  • Challenge — environment: 5,000 traffic-pollution deaths a year and under 2% of waste recycled.
  • Favela-Bairro Project — 1995–2009, $1 billion, 250,000 people across 100+ favelas: legal land title, 12 sewage works, a 3.5 km cable car.
More detail

The spec bullet is "the location and importance of the city, regionally, nationally, and internationally", so answer in three tiers — the 1-markers in 2022 and 2024 asked specifically for regional and national importance, and the 2022 examiner's report notes that "few showed understanding of 'regional'". Regional means within south-east Brazil; national means to Brazil as a whole; international means to the world.

Why Rio and not Lagos. Your class studied Rio as the LIC/NEE city. Lagos appears in the published revision mat but is not your case study — do not mix them, and do not use Lagos figures in a Rio answer.

  • Nationally — 5% of Brazil's GNI and the 3rd busiest port in Brazil.
  • Internationally — 3 airports, 5 ports; exports coffee, sugar and iron ore; hosted the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics.
  • Demographics — mostly under 30, which is why natural increase keeps the growth going.

Rio de Janeiro — the facts and figures

  • Location. South-east Brazil, on the Atlantic coast, grown up around Guanabara Bay, a large natural bay. Brazil is a Newly Emerging Economy and the world's 12th largest economy.
  • Population. Greater Rio de Janeiro area 13 million; around 1.5 million people live in favelas, which the school's booklet puts at 24% of the population across roughly 1,000 favelas. Population is mostly under 30.
  • Inequality. Gini coefficient around 0.53 — very high.
  • Regional importance. Many jobs, especially in construction and banking.
  • National importance. 5% of Brazil's GNI; the 3rd busiest port in Brazil; Brazil's second most important industrial centre.
  • International importance. 3 airports and 5 ports; main exports coffee, sugar and iron ore; hosted the World Cup in 2014 and the Olympics in 2016; Christ the Redeemer draws global tourism; tourism concentrates in the south zone around Copacabana Beach.
  • Causes of growth. Natural increase — high birth rate, low death rate. Internal migration — large-scale rural–urban migration within Brazil, especially from the drought-stricken Caatinga. International migration from HICs including the USA, UK and Portugal.

subsections.heading: Rio — the opportunities urban growth created
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.2 · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026; Urban revision slides

  • Health — free Unified Health care, more doctors per 1,000 than Brazil as a whole (3.44 v 2.81).
  • Education — over 400 secondary schools and 6 universities; literacy 97% against a national 93%.
  • Energy — 99% of homes have electricity; the Simplício HEP scheme added 30% of Rio's supply in 2013.
  • Formal jobs — tertiary work in retail and public services raises disposable income and tax revenue, driving the multiplier effect.
More detail
  • Water — the Guandu plant is the largest water treatment works in the world and supplies most of Rio's water.
  • Industry and port — Ternium Steelworks employs favela residents; the port exports coffee, sugar and iron ore.

Rio de Janeiro — opportunities, with the figures

  • Healthcare. Unified Health provides free health care across the city, with 3 public and 6 private hospitals. Rio has 3.44 doctors per 1,000 people against Brazil's 2.81. Travelling health care clinics in Santa Maria bring staff to people's homes; Family Health Teams reach around 3,000 people.
  • Education. Over 400 secondary schools and 6 universities; education compulsory to 14. Literacy is 97% in Rio against a national average of 93%. A private university has been set up in Rocinha; local government grants support families with children at school; the Schools of Tomorrow programme runs practical skills-based courses in poor, violent areas; the NGO Alfazendo prepares children in Cidade de Deus for college exams.
  • Water. The Guandu treatment plant is the largest in the world and supplies the great majority of Rio's fresh water. 7 new water treatment plants were built and over 300 km of water pipes laid between 1998 and 2014.
  • Energy. 99% of homes have electricity. 60 km of new power cables installed; 2 new nuclear reactors; the Simplício hydro plant, built at a cost of $2 billion and opened in 2013, supplies 30% of Rio's energy; 150 solar panels in the Santa Marta favela; the NGO Revolusolar has installed panels in Babilônia.
  • Economy. Growth in the formal economy, especially tertiary jobs in retail and public services, raises disposable income and tax revenue and triggers the multiplier effect. Oil has been discovered offshore. The Ternium Steelworks in the west of the city employs favela residents. The port is Brazil's third largest, handling coffee, sugar and iron ore exports.
  • Transport. The metro has been expanded under Guanabara Bay; the Olympics brought metro Line 4 connecting Barra da Tijuca to the city centre and the VLT light rail through the regenerated Porto Maravilha district.

✗ "Rio has schools and hospitals so quality of life is better." — generic, and the 2023 examiner's report calls this out: social opportunities "were often simply seen as socialising".
✓ "Rio has over 400 secondary schools and 6 universities, which is why its literacy rate of 97% exceeds Brazil's 93% — but only half of children continue beyond 14, so the opportunity is unequally distributed. To what extent is answered by that contrast, not by the list."

subsections.heading: Rio — the challenges urban growth created
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.2 · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026; Urban revision slides

  • Housing — around 1,000 favelas, built on steep hillsides, so landslide and flood risk is high.
  • Health gap — favela residents live about 13 years less; infant mortality 21/1000 in Cidade de Deus against 9/1000 in Barra.
  • Crime and unemployment — murder rate 20 per 1,000 in favelas; 20% favela unemployment; 3.5 million in the informal economy.
  • Environment — the most congested city in South America, 5,000 traffic-pollution deaths a year, Guanabara Bay polluted.
More detail
  • Education gap — only 50% continue beyond 14; Rio das Pedras has 50,000 people and 2 schools.
  • Water and sanitation — 12% of favela homes lack running water; 35% of sewage runs in open sewers.
  • Environment — most congested city in South America, 5,000 traffic-pollution deaths a year; Guanabara Bay severely polluted; under 2% of waste recycled.

Rio de Janeiro — challenges, with the figures

  • Managing growth. Around 1,000 favelas in the Greater Rio area, holding roughly 1.5 million people — the booklet puts it at 24% of Rio's population. Many are built on steep hillsides, so landslide risk is high in the heavy rains of April–October.
  • Health. Only 70% of slums have access to health cover, and the city has only 6 hospitals, mainly in affluent areas. Infant mortality is 21 per 1,000 in Cidade de Deus against 9 per 1,000 in Barra. In Rocinha, 6,000 people have at least one serious health problem, and there are two health clinics for about 100,000 people. Favela residents live on average 13 years less than people in wealthier parts of Rio.
  • Education. Only 50% of children continue education beyond 14. Rio das Pedras has a population of 50,000 and only 2 schools.
  • Water and sanitation. 12% of Rio's slums have no access to running water; a third of the supply is lost through leaky pipes, fraud and illegal access; about 35% of the city's sewage is carried in open sewers, often through the favelas, into Guanabara Bay.
  • Energy. Large numbers of favela dwellers illegally tap the grid, which is dangerous, and blackouts still occur.
  • Crime. Favelas are controlled by armed gangs — the Red Command in Jacarezinho. The murder rate is 20 per 1,000 in the favelas. Pacifying Police Units (UPPs) were established from 2013 to reclaim favelas from drug dealers, but have been criticised for focusing on favelas near Olympic sites, and pacification collapsed in many favelas after 2016.
  • Unemployment and the informal economy. 20% unemployment in the favelas. 3.5 million people work in the informal economy on about £75 a month — unregulated, often dangerous, no sick pay, and no tax paid, which starves the city of the revenue it needs for infrastructure.
  • Traffic and air pollution. Rio is the most congested city in South America; car ownership rose 40% in ten years; air pollution causes 5,000 deaths a year.
  • Water pollution. 150 tonnes of pollution pours into Guanabara Bay per day; 55 rivers flowing into the bay are classed as heavily polluted; over 50 tonnes of industrial waste is discharged daily; the Petrobras oil refinery has regular oil spills. 12 new sewage works have been built and ships are fined for discharging fuel.
  • Waste disposal. Rio produces around 3.5 million tonnes of waste a year and less than 2% is recycled. Most goes to the Seropédica landfill, 70 km from the city, where landfill gas is used to generate electricity or converted into fuel for waste collection vehicles. Collection is hardest in the favelas because the streets are too narrow for lorries.
  • Note — the Case Study Summary Booklet prints 79m tonnes/year in Rio's waste row. That is Brazil's national total; for Rio city it would mean about 32 kg of waste per person per day, which cannot be right. Rio city produces around 3.5 million tonnes a year. If the class wants the booklet's number, label it Brazil.
  • The Olympic cost. The 2016 Games cost $13.1 billion and displaced around 77,000 residents, many forcibly evicted from Vila Autódromo; gentrification in Porto Maravilha drove up rents; several venues fell into disrepair.

✗ "There is lots of pollution in Rio." — the slides are blunt: "Examiners don't reward 'pollution' unless classified".
✓ Name the type and give the figure: air pollution (5,000 deaths a year from congestion), water pollution (150 tonnes a day into Guanabara Bay, 55 heavily polluted rivers), waste (under 2% recycled, Seropédica landfill 70 km away).

subsections.heading: Urban planning for the urban poor — the Favela-Bairro Project
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.2, named example · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 13

  • A site-and-service scheme — upgrade the favelas where they stand rather than demolish them.
  • 1995–2009 — cost the city government $1 billion and helped 250,000 people across 100+ favelas.
  • Legal land ownership — the key move: with title and low-interest loans, residents invest in their own homes.
  • Infrastructure — 12 new sewage works, 60 km of new power cables, paved roads, drainage, and postcodes.
More detail
  • Legal land ownership — the key move: with title, 100% mortgages and low-interest loans, residents invest in their own homes.
  • Self-help — people were given tools and training to rebuild in brick; education programmes fought unemployment.
  • The cable car — a 3.5 km cable car across Complexo do Alemão, so the hillside is connected to the city.

The Favela-Bairro Project, Rio de Janeiro

  • The problem. 1,000 favelas in the Greater Rio area. In non-improved favelas, 30% had no electricity and 50% no sewage connections. No legitimate housing, so no incentive to build properly; poor employment prospects and a lack of education; many houses poorly constructed from scrap.
  • What it was. A site and service scheme running 1995–2009, costing the government $1 billion and helping 250,000 people. It covered over 100 favelas by 2005. The principle was to upgrade existing favelas rather than demolish them.
  • Services installed. 12 new sewage works; 60 km of new power cables; houses built with electricity and sanitation; new roads, drainage and elevated pavements; the Simplício hydro plant ($2 billion, 30% of Rio's energy) came in the same period.
  • Legal rights. People were given legal ownership of the land they live on, 100% mortgages, low-interest loans to improve their homes, and postcodes — some were allowed to buy their homes outright. This is the mechanism that matters: with legal title, residents invest.
  • Social provision. Community centres, nurseries and health clinics; job training and skills programmes; "fighting unemployment with education"; free childcare for teenage parents so they can return to education.
  • Self-help schemes. People were given tools and training to improve their own homes and rebuild in brick.
  • Transport. A 3.5 km cable car across Complexo do Alemão, linking a hillside favela to the rest of the city.
  • Outcomes — the good. Quality of life improved for about 250,000 residents; infant mortality fell; access to clean water improved; residents invested in their homes once they had legal rights.
  • Outcomes — the limits. Improvements were uneven and some favelas were left out; funding was cut after 2008 so the long-term sustainability is questioned; pacification displaced some residents; and some of the new pavements actually increased flood risk on the steep slopes.

✗ "The Favela-Bairro Project improved quality of life for the urban poor." — the 2022 examiner's report says the majority "just stat[ed] that quality of life was improved without saying how".
✓ Give the mechanism: "Residents were given legal ownership of their land, which meant they could get a 100% mortgage and a low-interest loan; because the house was now theirs, they invested in rebuilding it in brick, which made it safer on the steep slope and raised its value."

subsections.heading: London — location, importance and the impact of migration
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.3, Case Study Four · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 14; HIC City Revision Mat

  • Where — south-east England on the River Thames; 32 boroughs plus the City of London; around 9 million people.
  • Nationally — capital city, the UK's biggest city and biggest financial centre; 22% of UK GNI.
  • Migration since WWII — the former British Empire (India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Kenya, Jamaica), then Eastern Europe after 2007.
  • The result — 37% of Londoners were born outside the UK, and a population spike aged 20–40.

London — the figures that win marks

  • Where and how big — south-east England on the River Thames; 32 boroughs plus the City; about 9 million people.
  • Why it matters — 22% of UK GNI, a leading world financial centre, 30 million tourists a year, earnings about £6,000 above the UK average.
  • Migration — 37% of Londoners were born outside the UK: Empire arrivals after the war, then Eastern Europe after 2007.
  • Opportunity — the Docklands: the LDDC drew £7.7 billion, 2,700 companies and 120,000 jobs; Canary Wharf holds about 100,000 finance jobs.
  • Opportunity — transport and greening: the Elizabeth Line halved journeys to Heathrow and raised property values 25%; 47% of London is green space.
  • Challenge — deprivation: 2 million (27%) in poverty, 56% in Tower Hamlets; life expectancy 88 in Chelsea against 80 in Tower Hamlets.
  • Challenge — housing: 170,000 homeless, half the UK total, and an average house price over £500,000.
  • Challenge — dereliction and waste: almost 3,000 brownfield sites over 2,600 hectares; 970 kg of waste per household, 66% incinerated.
More detail

The 2025 mark scheme for "Describe the importance of a named UK city for the rest of the UK" shows the shape of the 2-marker: one mark for an initial statement, a second for developing it or adding a separate statement — "London is the UK capital (1)"; "Liverpool is an important city in the North West (1), the largest port for [trade with Ireland] (1)". The 2023 report notes that "many students struggled to access both marks with largely generic answers that could have applied to any UK city". So the second mark comes from the figure, not from a second vague adjective.

The wider UK population distribution is worth a line because the examiners sometimes set it up: upland areas such as northern Scotland are sparsely populated because they are difficult to build on, the climate is cold and wet, the land is hard to farm and natural resources are lacking. Coastal locations near estuaries have high density because harbours could be built, allowing fishing and trade. Urban areas also grew where there were reserves of iron ore and coal — Newcastle and Leeds. Density is highest in the south-east because of the favourable climate and proximity to London.

  • Locally — average earnings about £6,000 a year higher than the UK average.
  • Internationally — one of the world's two leading financial centres; 6 major airports; 30 million tourists a year.
  • The result — 37% of Londoners were born outside the UK, and a population spike in the 20–40 age bands.

London — the facts and figures

  • Location and size. South-east England on the River Thames; 32 boroughs plus the City of London; around 9 million people in Greater London; an Alpha++ world city.
  • Local importance. Average earnings are about £6,000 a year higher in London.
  • National importance. Capital city of the UK; biggest city; biggest financial centre; 22% of UK GNI is generated in London; housing in London's top 10 boroughs is worth more than all the housing in Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales combined; over 200,000 start-up companies were established in 2015.
  • International importance. With New York, one of the two most important financial centres in the world; headquarters of many large international companies; an international centre for media and communications, education (world-renowned universities), legal and medical facilities, and entertainment and tourism; 6 major airports, all connected by public transport; 30 million tourists per year.
  • Migration. Post-WWII streams were dominated by migrants from the former British Empire — India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Kenya, Jamaica — and from Eastern Europe since EU free movement in 2007. Result: 37% of London's population was born outside the UK, and there is a population spike in the 20–40 age bands.
  • Positive effects of migration. More skilled workers competing for jobs, which benefits companies recruiting; migrants contributed £20 billion to UK public finances between 2000 and 2011; London is one of the most culturally diverse cities in the UK, with migrants bringing different entertainment, clothing and foods — areas such as Chinatown in Soho were created by the Chinese diaspora.
  • Negative effects of migration. Population growth has led to housing shortages; there are social and racial tensions in some areas; pressure on schools, with a shortage of places; increased competition for jobs.

subsections.heading: London — the opportunities of urban change
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.3 · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 14; Urban London Model Answers

  • Cultural mix and recreation — the West End, Oxford Street, Battersea Power Station, Shoreditch's "Silicon Roundabout".
  • The Docklands — containerisation killed the docks in 1981; the LDDC rebuilt them as Canary Wharf.
  • Integrated transport — the Elizabeth Line halved journey times to Heathrow and raised property values 25% around stations.
  • Urban greening — 47% of London's area is green space, 8.3 million trees, 30,000 allotments.
More detail

The school's model 9-mark answer on the Docklands makes the link that pushes an answer into Level 3, and it is worth copying: investment → companies move in → jobs → income tax and corporation tax → government revenue → spending on healthcare, hospitals and education. In other words, the economic opportunity produces a social opportunity, which is exactly the kind of connected reasoning the mark scheme calls AO2.

The counter-argument in the same model answer is equally important: the dock workers were lower-skilled and could not apply for the new finance jobs in Canary Wharf, and the low-income neighbourhoods right next door — Poplar and the Isle of Dogs — have continued to suffer poverty and unemployment. "Success for some, not all" is the conclusion the examiners reward.

  • The Docklands — containerisation killed the docks in 1981; the LDDC rebuilt them as Canary Wharf, around 100,000 finance jobs by 2025.
  • Private investment followed — the LDDC attracted £7.7 billion, about 2,700 companies and 120,000 jobs.
  • Tax multiplier — the exam point: jobs → higher wages → higher tax → more public spending on health and schools.

London — opportunities, with the figures

  • Cultural change, recreation and entertainment. Shoreditch — old industrial buildings reused for circus training; Old Street Roundabout became "Silicon Roundabout" for tech firms; low-income Bangladeshi families moving out as the area gentrified. The West End is famous for its shows; shopping on Oxford Street; major new developments such as Battersea Power Station. London has a huge range of recreational opportunities and regularly hosts world-class sporting events, and entertainment has created many jobs.
  • The Docklands. Containerisation in 1981 ended dock work, and the London Docklands Development Corporation was set up the same year to regenerate the derelict area. The result was Canary Wharf: by 2025, around 100,000 finance workers. The LDDC attracted £7.7 billion in private sector investment, with roughly 2,700 companies now operating in the area providing about 120,000 jobs in finance, retail and services.
  • Integrated transport. Demand for travel is predicted to grow 60% by 2050. The Elizabeth Line (Crossrail) halves journey times to Heathrow, raises property values by 25% around its stations, and brings 1.5 million more people within 45 minutes of central London. London has 6 main airports, all connected by public transport, plus the Underground, buses, Tramlink and the DLR.
  • Urban greening. 47% of London's area is green space; 30,000 allotments; 8.3 million trees; 223 of London's parks and green spaces hold Green Flag awards.
  • Economic. London generates 22% of UK GNI; its transport network allows the free flow of goods and services; it attracts educated graduates from around the world into research and development, finance and education, who pay taxes to the UK government.

subsections.heading: London — the challenges of urban change
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.3 · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 14; Urban revision slides

  • Deprivation — 2 million Londoners (27%) live in poverty; Tower Hamlets has the highest rate at 56%.
  • Housing — 170,000 homeless, half the UK total; average house price over £500,000.
  • Dereliction and brownfield — almost 3,000 brownfield sites covering 2,600 hectares; enough for over a million homes.
  • Waste — 970 kg per household a year; 66% incinerated in 2021; only 20% composted.
More detail
  • Life expectancy gap — 88 years in Chelsea against 80 in Tower Hamlets; infant mortality in Hackney is 3.4× Bromley's.
  • Education and jobs — GCSE attainment 74% in Kensington and Chelsea against 51% in Lewisham; unemployment 4% v 10%.
  • Waste — 970 kg per household a year; 66% incinerated in 2021; 750,000 tonnes to landfill; only 20% composted.

London — challenges, with the figures

  • Urban deprivation. 2 million people (27%) live in poverty, against about 20% for the rest of England. Tower Hamlets has the greatest poverty rate of any London borough at 56%. Newham has a 44% child poverty rate. Deprivation is increasing in the outer boroughs as affordable housing in inner London becomes harder to find.
  • Inequality in health. Life expectancy is 88 in Chelsea and 80 in Tower Hamlets — an 8-year gap. Infant mortality in Hackney is 3.4 times that of Bromley. Quality of healthcare is inconsistent across boroughs.
  • Inequality in education. GCSE attainment is 74% in Kensington and Chelsea, 1.5 times the 51% in Lewisham. The city is struggling to provide enough school places.
  • Inequality in employment. Unemployment is 4% in Chelsea and 10% in Tower Hamlets; London's unemployment rate is still higher than the UK average.
  • Housing. 170,000 homeless — about 50% of the UK total; average house price over £500,000 (2024); average central London rent over £2,000 a month; overcrowding in inner boroughs; rough sleeping up 23% since 2020. Rising housing costs are reducing living standards.
  • Dereliction, brownfield and greenfield. Areas such as Battersea Power Station were derelict until recently redeveloped; many East London buildings became derelict through de-industrialisation. In 2019 there were almost 3,000 brownfield sites in London covering 2,600 hectares — enough brownfield land remains for over a million homes. Merton has the most brownfield sites of any borough (6,809); Westminster has none. Brownfield development is expensive, which is why greenfield sites on the fringe come under pressure.
  • Waste disposal. The average London household produces 970 kg of waste per year. London sent the largest proportion of its waste to incineration of any UK region in 2021 (66%); 750,000 tonnes goes to landfill every year; only 20% is composted, and recycling rates are the lowest in the country.
  • Environment. NO₂ levels breach WHO limits in central London; the urban heat island makes the city up to 5°C warmer than its surroundings; the Thames Barrier has closed over 200 times; green space is unequally distributed between boroughs even though 47% of London is green.
  • Urban sprawl. A rising population puts pressure on the rural–urban fringe for new homes and for cheap land for businesses.

subsections.heading: Urban sprawl, the rural–urban fringe and commuter settlements
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.3 · HIC City Revision Mat; 2025 Q01.10 mark scheme

  • Rural–urban fringe — the zone of transition between built-up area and countryside, where land uses compete.
  • Positives — rising house prices for existing residents, more services, greater cultural diversity, better transport.
  • Negatives — loss of farmland and habitats, urban sprawl, worse public transport so more cars, land never returns to countryside.
  • Commuter settlements — villages within rail or motorway reach of a city, which fill with estates of identikit housing.
More detail

The rural–urban fringe is a zone of transition between the built-up area and the countryside, where there is often competition for land use — out-of-town shopping centres and golf courses alongside farmland and motorways. Urban sprawl is the unplanned growth of urban areas into the surrounding countryside.

Positive impacts of urban sprawl on the fringe: house prices can increase for those already living there; services such as schools and healthcare increase to meet the needs of the growing population; cultural diversity could increase; transport infrastructure could be improved.

Negative impacts: public transport is worse in rural areas, so there are more cars on the road; urban sprawl itself; land is unlikely ever to return to countryside once built on; valuable farmland or recreational land is lost; natural habitats may be destroyed.

The 2025 mark scheme for the 6-marker is a model of what "suggest" allows: loss of habitats, greenfield land and farmland; loss of rural or unique character; increased air pollution and congestion from the extra cars; increasingly busy branch-line train services; and impacts on drainage from the additional tarmac — with credit specifically given to students who spotted the swales in the photograph as evidence that drainage is already a problem.

  • The figure evidence in 2025 — cul-de-sac estates eating greenfield land, surrounded by farmland, station and A-road nearby, lots of cars, swales for drainage.
  • Loss of character — the "identikit" point: the settlement stops being rural without becoming urban.

subsections.heading: Urban regeneration — Stratford and the Olympic Park
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.3, named example · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 15; Urban revision slides

  • Why it needed regeneration — one of the country's most deprived areas and the most polluted site in Western Europe.
  • Scale — the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park covers 250 hectares, including 100 hectares of green space.
  • Jobs — International Quarter for 25,000 workers, Westfield over 10,000, and £5 billion of investment.
  • The cost — gentrification: house prices up 50%+ since 2012, and original low-income residents priced out.
More detail
  • Why it needed regeneration — one of the most deprived communities in the country, high unemployment, poor health.
  • The environment was the worst in Europe — Stratford was the most polluted site in Western Europe, with derelict industry and no transport links.
  • Homes and schools — East Village, the converted athletes' village, and Mossbourne Riverside Academy for about 2,000 pupils.
  • Jobs — International Quarter for 25,000 workers; Westfield Stratford employs over 10,000; 20,000 jobs by 2030 and £5 billion.

Stratford and the Olympic Park, east London

  • Reasons for regeneration. Stratford had one of the most deprived communities in the country, with high unemployment and poor levels of health. Infrastructure was lacking and environmental quality was poor: it was the most polluted site in Western Europe, with derelict industries and few transport connections — the legacy of de-industrialisation in the Lower Lea Valley.
  • Social features. East Village — the converted athletes' village. The Case Study Summary Booklet gives 3,000 affordable homes for local people; the development is about 2,800 homes in total, roughly half of them affordable, so write the booklet's figure and call them affordable homes. Here East, an events space in the former media centre. V&A East and Sadler's Wells East as culture and arts centres. Mossbourne Riverside Academy, educating around 2,000 pupils aged 3 to 18.
  • Economic features. Stratford is now well connected, letting commuters travel to work easily; new jobs in construction and tourism created a multiplier effect. The International Quarter is a commercial district for 25,000 people. Westfield Stratford, the largest urban shopping centre in Europe, employs over 10,000. It is estimated that over 20,000 jobs could be created by 2030, bringing more than £5 billion into the area.
  • Environmental features. Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park — 100 hectares of green space within a 250-hectare park, with parklands, canals and walking routes. New transport: DLR extension, Stratford International, Overground upgrades.
  • Evaluation — has it worked? For: employment rose; house prices in Stratford rose over 50% since 2012; green space improved. Against: gentrification priced out original low-income residents; benefits concentrated near the Park rather than across the whole borough; some facilities went unused after the Games.

✗ "Regeneration improved the area." — no place detail, no figure, no evaluation, so Level 1 at best.
✓ "Stratford was the most polluted site in Western Europe before 2005; the 250-hectare Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park and Westfield's 10,000 jobs transformed it, and over 20,000 jobs are expected by 2030 bringing £5 billion. However, house prices rose over 50% since 2012, so many of the original residents were priced out — the regeneration succeeded for some."

subsections.heading: Sustainable urban living — East Village, and sustainable transport
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.1.4, named examples · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 16; Urban revision slides

  • East Village water — recycling and grey water cut consumption to 50% less than average.
  • East Village energy — 30% less than average, from biomass through a Combined Heat and Power (CHP) system.
  • Waste and green space — 99% of parkland waste recycled; 10 hectares of green space in 27 hectares.
  • City-wide transport — the Elizabeth Line, the Congestion Charge (traffic down 30%) and ULEZ (NO₂ down 44%).
More detail
  • Four features to cover — water and energy conservation, waste recycling, creating green space, and urban transport strategies.
  • Waste and green space — 99% of parkland waste recycled; 10 hectares of green space in a 27-hectare development, with green roofs and wetlands.
  • Transport on site — 37 EV charging points, designated cycle lanes, 6 bus routes plus an international station.

East Village, Stratford — sustainable urban living

  • What it is. The former Olympic Athletes' Village (2012), converted into around 2,800 homes in Stratford and designed as a model of sustainable urban living.
  • Water conservation. Water recycling cuts use to 50% less than average — rainwater harvesting, grey water recycling (wastewater from sinks and showers reused for toilet flushing), and water-efficient appliances in every home.
  • Energy conservation. 30% less energy than average, from biomass energy produced by a Combined Heat and Power (CHP) system on site, plus high insulation standards and integrated renewables, aiming at carbon neutrality.
  • Waste recycling. 99% of parkland waste is recycled; automated waste collection means no bin lorries; food waste composting; recycling rates well above the London average, with a zero-landfill ambition.
  • Green space. 10 hectares of green space within a 27-hectare development; ponds and wetland areas; green roofs; community gardens; biodiversity corridors along the waterways; linked to the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park.
  • Transport strategies. 37 EV charging points; designated cycle lanes; 6 bus routes plus Stratford International station; and the site sits inside the Congestion Zone and ULEZ.

London's integrated transport strategies

  • Elizabeth Line (Crossrail). £18.9 billion, 118 km, 41 stations, opened 2022, over 200 million journeys a year. Paddington to Canary Wharf in 17 minutes; it cuts crowding on the Central, District and Jubilee lines; connects deprived east London to the City's jobs; all stations step-free; estimated to boost London's economy by £42 billion. Limits: cost overran by over £4 billion and it opened in 2022 rather than 2018; property prices along the route rose up to 50%, displacing lower-income residents; it runs west–east, so it does nothing for south London congestion.
  • Congestion Charge. £15 a day to drive in central London; traffic in the zone is down 30% since 2003; the revenue funds public transport. Criticised as a "tax on the poor".
  • ULEZ. The Ultra Low Emission Zone, expanded to the whole of Greater London in August 2023, charges drivers of older, more polluting vehicles. NO₂ fell 44% in the original zone. Controversial because of the cost burden on low-income drivers.
  • Cycle hire. Santander Cycles have over 800 docking stations, alongside Lime, Forest and HumanForest e-bikes; these cut car journeys for short trips and promote active travel.

✗ "Public transport is better for the environment." — the 2023 report: marks were lost "where the congestion reduction was implicit only".
✓ Chain it explicitly: "The Elizabeth Line cut the Paddington–Canary Wharf journey to 17 minutes, which makes the train faster than driving; therefore commuters switch from cars to rail, so there are fewer vehicles on the road and congestion falls."

The facts you cannot sit Section A without

Global: urbanisation = rising proportion in towns and cities · 55%+ of the world urban (UN 2023) · 90% of future urban growth in Africa and Asia · 33 megacities (2023) → ~50 by 2050 · megacity = 10 million+ · North America 82% urban, HICs 75%+ · India, China and Nigeria = 37% of urban growth 2014–2050 · two causes only: migration + natural increase · migrants aged 18–35.

Rio — scale: Greater Rio 13 million · ~1,000 favelas · ~1.5 million favela residents (24%) · Gini ~0.53 · population mostly under 30 · grew around Guanabara Bay.

Rio — importance: 5% of Brazil's GNI · 3rd busiest port in Brazil · Brazil's 2nd industrial centre · 3 airports, 5 ports · coffee, sugar, iron ore · World Cup 2014, Olympics 2016 · Christ the Redeemer · Copacabana.

Rio — opportunities: 3.44 doctors/1000 v Brazil 2.81 · 400+ secondary schools, 6 universities · literacy 97% v 93% · Guandu = world's largest water treatment plant · 7 new plants + 300 km of pipes 1998–2014 · 99% of homes have electricity · Simplício HEP $2bn = 30% of energy (2013) · 150 solar panels Santa Marta · Ternium Steelworks · metro Line 4 and VLT light rail.

Rio — challenges: favela life expectancy 13 years lower · infant mortality 21/1000 Cidade de Deus v 9/1000 Barra · only 70% of slums have health cover · 6 hospitals · Rocinha 2 clinics for ~100,000 · only 50% stay in school past 14 · Rio das Pedras 50,000 people, 2 schools · 12% of slums no running water · a third of water lost to leaks and theft · 35% of sewage in open sewers · murder rate 20/1000 · UPPs from 2013 · Red Command in Jacarezinho · 20% favela unemployment · 3.5 million informal workers on ~£75/month · most congested city in South America, cars +40% in 10 years, 5,000 deaths/yr · 150 tonnes/day into Guanabara Bay · 55 heavily polluted rivers · ~3.5 million tonnes of waste, under 2% recycled · Seropédica landfill 70 km away · Olympics cost $13.1bn and displaced 77,000.

Favela-Bairro: site and service scheme, 1995–2009, $1 billion, 250,000 people, 100+ favelas · before: 30% no electricity, 50% no sewage · legal land title, 100% mortgages, low-interest loans, postcodes · 12 new sewage works, 60 km of power cables · self-help: tools and training, brick houses · Complexo do Alemão 3.5 km cable car · limits: uneven, funding cut after 2008, pacification displacement, some pavements raised flood risk.

London — importance: ~9 million · 32 boroughs + City · Alpha++ world city · earnings £6,000/yr above average · 22% of UK GNI · 6 major airports · 30 million tourists/yr · 200,000 start-ups in 2015 · 37% born outside the UK · migrant streams: Empire (India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Kenya, Jamaica) then Eastern Europe from 2007 · migrants contributed £20bn to public finances 2000–2011 · Chinatown, Soho.

London — opportunities: Docklands: containerisation 1981 → LDDC → Canary Wharf, 100,000 finance workers by 2025, £7.7bn private investment, ~2,700 companies, 120,000 jobs · Shoreditch / Silicon Roundabout · Battersea Power Station · Elizabeth Line halves Heathrow times, +25% property values, 1.5m more people within 45 mins · travel demand +60% by 2050 · greening: 47% green space, 8.3 million trees, 30,000 allotments, 223 Green Flag parks.

London — challenges: 2 million in poverty (27%) · Tower Hamlets 56% poverty, Newham 44% child poverty · life expectancy Chelsea 88 v Tower Hamlets 80 · infant mortality Hackney 3.4× Bromley · GCSE 74% K&C v 51% Lewisham · unemployment 4% v 10% · 170,000 homeless (50% of UK) · average house >£500,000 · rough sleeping +23% since 2020 · ~3,000 brownfield sites, 2,600 hectares, room for 1m+ homes · Merton 6,809 brownfield sites, Westminster 0 · 970 kg waste per household · 66% incinerated (2021) · 750,000 tonnes to landfill · 20% composted · NO₂ breaches WHO limits · heat island +5°C · Thames Barrier closed 200+ times.

Stratford: most polluted site in Western Europe · Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park 250 ha, 100 ha green · East Village 3,000 affordable homes (~2,800 in total) · Mossbourne Riverside Academy ~2,000 pupils · International Quarter 25,000 workers · Westfield 10,000+ jobs, largest urban mall in Europe · 20,000 jobs by 2030, £5bn · Here East, V&A East, Sadler's Wells East · house prices +50% since 2012 · gentrification.

East Village: water −50%, energy −30% via biomass CHP · 99% of parkland waste recycled · 10 ha green in 27 ha · green roofs, ponds, wetlands · 37 EV points · 6 bus routes + International station · inside Congestion Zone and ULEZ.

Transport: Elizabeth Line £18.9bn, 118 km, 41 stations, 2022, 200m+ journeys/yr, Paddington–Canary Wharf 17 mins, £42bn economic boost, overran £4bn+ · Congestion Charge £15/day, traffic −30% since 2003 · ULEZ expanded Aug 2023, NO₂ −44% · 800+ Santander docking stations.

subsections.heading: Quotes and figures to learn
subsections.html:
Geography's marks live in the figures. The front of each card names the case study and what the figure measures, so you can test whether you can produce the number from the prompt alone — and the back says what argument it is for, because a figure with no argument attached earns nothing.

Rio — population and favelasGreater Rio de Janeiro 13 million; around 1,000 favelas holding roughly 1.5 million people — about 24% of the cityUsed to argue: the scale of the housing challenge — one in four Rio residents lives in an informal settlement, so "managing urban growth" is not a side issue but the central one
Rio — national and international importance5% of Brazil's GNI; 3rd busiest port in Brazil; 3 airports and 5 ports; hosted the World Cup (2014) and Olympics (2016)Used to argue: Rio matters nationally through its economy and port and internationally through its global events — the three-tier answer the 1- and 2-markers want
Rio — the health gapFavela residents live on average 13 years less; infant mortality is 21 per 1,000 in Cidade de Deus against 9 per 1,000 in BarraUsed to argue: urban growth created opportunity and inequality at once — the single best pair of figures for a "to what extent" answer on social opportunities
Rio — education, both sidesOver 400 secondary schools and 6 universities, literacy 97% against Brazil's 93% — but only 50% of children continue beyond 14, and Rio das Pedras has 50,000 people and 2 schoolsUsed to argue: the opportunity is real but unevenly distributed, which is how you answer "to what extent has urban growth created social opportunities?" rather than listing facilities
Rio — water and sanitationThe Guandu plant is the world's largest water treatment works, yet 12% of favela homes lack running water, a third of supply is lost to leaks and theft, and 35% of sewage runs in open sewersUsed to argue: supply is not the same as access — infrastructure exists but does not reach the poorest, which is the real challenge of rapid growth
Rio — the informal economy3.5 million people work informally for about £75 a month; favela unemployment is 20%Used to argue: informal work is an opportunity (it is employment, and it exists) and a challenge (unregulated, no sick pay, no tax revenue for the city) — a ready-made evaluation
Rio — traffic and air pollutionThe most congested city in South America; car ownership up 40% in ten years; air pollution causes 5,000 deaths a yearUsed to argue: environmental challenges in an NEE city affect everyone, not just the poor — the point that lifts a waste-disposal or pollution answer above the favelas
Rio — water pollution150 tonnes of pollution enters Guanabara Bay every day; 55 rivers feeding the bay are classed as heavily polluted; over 50 tonnes of industrial waste discharged dailyUsed to argue: the environmental cost of growth is measurable — and it threatens the tourist beaches that the economy depends on, so the challenge is economic too
Rio — waste disposalAround 3.5 million tonnes of waste a year, under 2% recycled; most to the Seropédica landfill 70 km from the city, where landfill gas generates electricityUsed to argue: the 2024 6-marker exactly — waste is a serious challenge, but the landfill gas scheme shows it is being managed, so "to what extent" has a genuine answer
Favela-Bairro — scale and costA site and service scheme, 1995–2009, costing the government $1 billion and improving life for 250,000 people across more than 100 favelasUsed to argue: urban planning for the urban poor at genuine scale — the figures that turn "it helped people" into a Level 3 answer
Favela-Bairro — the mechanismLegal ownership of the land, 100% mortgages, low-interest loans and postcodes, plus tools and training so residents rebuilt in brickUsed to argue: how quality of life improved, not just that it did — legal title creates the incentive to invest, which is the causal chain the examiners say is missing from most answers
Favela-Bairro — the limitsImprovements were uneven and some favelas were left out; funding was reduced after 2008; pacification displaced residents; some new pavements increased flood risk on steep slopesUsed to argue: the counter-case in an "evaluate the success" answer — needed for the top level, since a one-sided answer caps at Level 2
London — importance22% of UK GNI; average earnings £6,000 a year above the UK average; 6 major airports; 30 million tourists a year; 37% of Londoners born outside the UKUsed to argue: the three tiers of importance — local earnings, national GNI, international connections — which is what the 2-mark "describe the importance" question wants
London Docklands — the regeneration figuresContainerisation closed the docks in 1981; the LDDC attracted £7.7 billion of private investment, about 2,700 companies and 120,000 jobs; Canary Wharf holds roughly 100,000 finance workers by 2025Used to argue: urban change created enormous economic opportunity — and the tax it generates funds the social opportunities, which is the link that reaches Level 3
London — the inequality figures2 million Londoners (27%) in poverty; Tower Hamlets 56%; life expectancy 88 in Chelsea against 80 in Tower Hamlets; GCSE attainment 74% in Kensington and Chelsea against 51% in Lewisham; unemployment 4% against 10%Used to argue: urban change in a UK city created challenges as sharp as its opportunities — the set of paired figures that makes an "assess the challenges" answer place-specific
London — housing and homelessness170,000 homeless, about half the UK total; average house price over £500,000; rough sleeping up 23% since 2020Used to argue: the housing crisis is the challenge that connects to every other — deprivation, health inequality and pressure on the rural–urban fringe all follow from it
London — brownfield and derelictionAlmost 3,000 brownfield sites covering 2,600 hectares (2019), with enough brownfield land for over a million homes; Merton has 6,809 sites, Westminster noneUsed to argue: dereliction is a challenge but also the solution to urban sprawl — building on brownfield protects the rural–urban fringe, though it costs more than greenfield
London — waste970 kg of waste per household per year; 66% sent to incineration in 2021, the highest share of any UK region; 750,000 tonnes to landfill; only 20% compostedUsed to argue: waste disposal is a challenge of urban change in an HIC as well as an NEE — and the comparison with Rio's under-2% recycling rate is a ready evaluation
Stratford — before and afterThe most polluted site in Western Europe and one of the country's most deprived communities; now a 250-hectare park with 100 hectares of green space, Westfield's 10,000+ jobs, and over 20,000 jobs and £5 billion expected by 2030Used to argue: the scale of what regeneration achieved — the before-and-after contrast is the structure of the answer, not just decoration
Stratford — the cost of successHouse prices in Stratford rose over 50% since 2012, and benefits concentrated near the Park rather than across the boroughUsed to argue: gentrification — regeneration succeeded for some and not for others, which is the judgement the 9-marker is really asking for
East Village — sustainability figuresWater use 50% below average and energy use 30% below average, from biomass through a Combined Heat and Power system; 99% of parkland waste recycled; 10 hectares of green space in a 27-hectare developmentUsed to argue: sustainable urban living is achievable and measurable — the four named figures the 2024 9-marker on water and energy conservation needed
Elizabeth Line — the transport figures£18.9 billion, 118 km, 41 stations, opened 2022, over 200 million journeys a year; Paddington to Canary Wharf in 17 minutes; a £42 billion boost to London's economy; property values up 25% around stationsUsed to argue: an integrated transport system reduces congestion by making rail faster than driving — but it overran by £4 billion, opened four years late and does nothing for south London
ULEZ and the Congestion ChargeNO₂ fell 44% in the original ULEZ zone; ULEZ expanded to all of Greater London in August 2023; the £15-a-day Congestion Charge has cut central traffic 30% since 2003Used to argue: pricing strategies work on congestion and air quality — with the counter that both are criticised as a tax on low-income drivers

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
UrbanisationThe process by which an increasing percentage of a country's population comes to live in towns and cities
Urban growthThe absolute increase in the size of a city — not the same as urbanisation, which is a proportion
Mega-cityAn urban area with a total population in excess of ten million people
MigrationWhen people move from one area to another; in many LICs from rural to urban areas (rural–urban migration)
Natural increaseThe birth rate minus the death rate of a population
Counter-urbanisationPeople moving away from cities to rural areas
Squatter settlementAn area of poor-quality housing, lacking amenities such as water supply, sewerage and electricity, which develops spontaneously and illegally in a city in an LIC
FavelaThe Brazilian term for an informal settlement with self-built housing
Formal economyThe part of an economy of which the government is fully aware and that is regulated by government authorities
Informal economyActivities that have market value but are not formally registered — so untaxed and unregulated
Social opportunitiesChances for people to improve their quality of life, for instance access to education and health care
Economic opportunitiesChances for people to improve their standard of living through employment
InequalitiesDifferences between poverty and wealth, and in wellbeing and access to jobs, housing and education
Social deprivationThe degree to which an individual or area is deprived of services, decent housing, adequate income and local employment
SanitationMeasures designed to protect public health, including clean water and the disposal of sewage and waste
PollutionThe presence of chemicals, noise, dirt or other substances with harmful or poisonous effects on an environment — always classify it as air, water or land
Traffic congestionWhen there is too great a volume of traffic for roads to cope with, so jams form and traffic slows to a crawl
Urban regenerationThe revival of old parts of the built-up area by renewal (modern facilities in old buildings) or redevelopment (demolishing and starting afresh)
GentrificationWealthier people moving into poorer areas, raising prices and displacing the original residents
DerelictionAbandoned buildings and wasteland
Brownfield siteLand that has been used, abandoned and now awaits some new use — commonly found in the inner city
Greenfield siteA plot of land, often rural or on the edge of an urban area, that has not yet been subject to any building development
Urban sprawlThe unplanned growth of urban areas into the surrounding countryside
Rural–urban fringeA zone of transition between the built-up area and the countryside, where there is competition for land use
Urban greeningThe process of increasing and preserving open space such as public parks and gardens in urban areas
Integrated transport systemWhen different transport methods connect together, making journeys smoother so public transport becomes more appealing and car use falls
Waste recyclingThe process of extracting and reusing useful substances found in waste
Sustainable urban livingA city with minimal damage to the environment, a sound economic base with resources allocated fairly and secure jobs, and a strong sense of community with local people involved in decisions
Grey water recyclingReusing wastewater from sinks and showers, for example for toilet flushing or irrigation
CHPCombined Heat and Power — generates electricity and useful heat simultaneously, so far less energy is wasted

subsections.heading: Wording that costs marks
subsections.html:
Don't writeWrite
urbanisation is when cities growurbanisation is the increase in the proportion of a population living in towns and cities; the growth in city size is urban growth
people move to cities for a better lifename the factor and develop it — "pushed by poor harvests, so food and income are unreliable; pulled by better-paid factory work"
cities in LICs grow quickly because lots of people move theremigration and natural increase — and migrants are aged 18–35, so the birth rate rises too
a megacity is a really big cityan urban area with a population of at least 10 million
Rio has lots of favelasaround 1,000 favelas holding roughly 1.5 million people — about 24% of the city
there is a lot of pollution in Rioclassify it — air pollution (5,000 deaths a year), water pollution (150 tonnes a day into Guanabara Bay), waste (under 2% recycled)
the Favela-Bairro Project improved quality of lifegive the mechanism — legal land title → 100% mortgages and low-interest loans → residents invest in brick houses that are safer on the slope
a city in BrazilRio de Janeiro, around Guanabara Bay in south-east Brazil, an NEE — a named place, or the mark scheme caps you at Level 2
London is important because it's the capitalthree tiers — earnings £6,000 above average locally, 22% of UK GNI nationally, 30 million tourists and 6 airports internationally
social opportunities like meeting peoplesocial opportunities are access to education and health care — the examiners' report names "socialising" as the commonest error on this section
regeneration made the area betterStratford went from the most polluted site in Western Europe to a 250-hectare park with Westfield's 10,000+ jobs
regeneration was a successa success for some — house prices rose 50%+ since 2012, so original low-income residents were priced out
East Village is sustainablewater use 50% below average, energy 30% below average from biomass CHP, 99% of parkland waste recycled
trains are better for the environmentfinish the chain — faster than driving, therefore commuters switch, so fewer cars, so congestion and NO₂ fall
Figure 2 shows povertylift and use it — "Figure 2 shows a median age of 23, which means most residents are of reproductive age, so natural increase will keep the population rising"

The 9-mark frame

Three paragraphs plus a conclusion, and the school's rule is that evaluation inside every paragraph beats evaluation saved for the end. The structure is P.E.E.L. — Point, Explanation, Evidence, Link — and in this section the classification is almost always S.E.E.: social, economic, environmental.

  1. One-sentence intro naming the place and your line. "Rio de Janeiro, an NEE city of 13 million grown around Guanabara Bay, has created substantial social and economic opportunities through urban growth, but they are very unevenly distributed." Name the case study in the first sentence — the examiners' commonest complaint is a "geography of anywhere".
  2. Paragraph 1 — the first category, with figures. Point (the opportunity or challenge), explanation (why it follows from urban growth), evidence (the number), then evaluate — how big, who benefits, who doesn't. "Rio has over 400 secondary schools and a literacy rate of 97% against Brazil's 93%; however only 50% of children continue beyond 14, and Rio das Pedras has 50,000 people and two schools, so the opportunity exists but is not shared."
  3. Paragraph 2 — the second category, same shape. If the question says "social and economic", do one of each and compare their size. If it says "to what extent", your evaluative sentence belongs here.
  4. Paragraph 3 — the third category, or the counter-case. For a "has it worked?" question this is where the limits go: uneven coverage, funding cut after 2008, gentrification, displacement. Say which side is stronger.
  5. A conclusion that decides. Use the school's ladder — definitely / mostly / partly / slightly / not at all — and tie it to the words of the question. Two sentences, no new material.

Sentence starters that earn the AO3 marks:

  • "Figure 2 shows that… which means… and therefore…"
  • "This is a significant opportunity because… and as a result…"
  • "However, this benefit is limited to…, whereas…"
  • "The most significant challenge is…, because it causes…, which in turn…"
  • "Urban change created more economic than social opportunity, although the two are linked, since tax revenue funds…"
  • "Overall, I mostly agree with the statement, because… outweighs…"

SPaG (3 marks). Spell these right: urbanisation, Rio de Janeiro, favela, Favela-Bairro, Guanabara Bay, Rocinha, Stratford, Elizabeth Line, ULEZ, gentrification, counter-urbanisation, Seropédica. Use the specialist terms — the top band wants "a wide range of specialist terms as appropriate".
