drill.intro:
What each command word actually wants

Section A is Question 01 on Paper 2 — 1 hour 30 minutes, 88 marks, three compulsory-plus-optional sections. The question types are marked in completely different ways, so answer each in its own shape. This is the school's exam technique guide plus what the examiners' reports say was going wrong.

  • 1 mark — state / give / name / "what is…?" One clear point, or the correct definition. The guide's warning: people "do not read the instructions clearly" and these questions "hide on a busy page". Don't lose them. For "shade one circle only", shade one.
  • 2 marks — outline / describe / give two. Usually point + development, not two bare statements: "it is rare that just a straightforward statement suffices". Use because, this means that, therefore. If it says "give two", two separate points are fine.
  • 3 marks — suggest / outline. Three linked steps in one chain, or three separate developed points. The 2025 scheme for a 3-marker shows a chain earning all three: "economic development increases wages (1) and therefore tax receipts (1) which can be spent on better sanitation (1)".
  • 4 marks — explain / suggest, usually with a figure. Two developed points, or four basic ones. Make a point and explain it, twice, with specific detail. You must refer to the figure — "Figure X shows that…" — and then use it. The report's complaint is students "merely lift text and repeat it".
  • 6 marks — explain / assess / discuss / "to what extent", level marked. Two or three developed paragraphs with evidence and explanation. If the command is discuss, assess or to what extent, you also need limitations or counter-arguments and a short judgement; if it is explain, explanation alone is enough. A named example is often required — the mark scheme caps you at Level 2 without one.
  • 9 marks (+3 SPaG) — assess / evaluate / discuss / "to what extent", level marked. A one-sentence intro naming the case study, two or three P.E.E.L. paragraphs with evaluation inside each, and a one or two sentence conclusion that decides. Classify with S.E.E. (social, economic, environmental). The three AOs carry 3 marks each: AO1 place knowledge, AO2 understanding of the process, AO3 application to this question and this figure. "Simply repeating case study information is knowledge (AO1) and cannot gain credit" in the AO2/AO3 part — so every fact needs a therefore.

Twelve questions in the real spread: two short, four 4-markers, four 6-markers and two 9-markers. The 6- and 9-mark answers are written as plans, because AQA marks them in levels rather than by ticking points — treat the mark points as a coverage target, not a tick list.

modules.title: The Changing Economic World
modules.standfirst: Section B of Paper 2 Challenges in the Human Environment — measuring development, the Demographic Transition Model, the causes and consequences of uneven development, the strategies for closing the development gap (aid, trade, debt relief, intermediate technology, Fairtrade, microfinance), tourism in Jamaica, the Nigeria case study, and the changing UK economy from de-industrialisation to science parks, Torr Quarry, rural change, transport and the north–south divide. The biggest 9-marker on the paper usually lives here, and it is almost always Nigeria or the UK economy.

subsections.html:
What they actually ask

Every Section B question from the June 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 papers, with marks. The maths is relentless — mean, median, interquartile range, range, percentage and best-fit lines all appear — and AQA states that 10% of the whole paper's marks are mathematical.

  • The Nigeria case study — the 9-marker in 2019, 2023 and 2025, plus TNCs and Shell in 2022 and manufacturing in 2024.
  • The changing UK economy — in all five papers, including the 2024 9-marker on transport and infrastructure.
  • Measuring development, and the maths — 2023, 2024, 2025: median, interquartile range, and the limitations of a measure.
  • The Demographic Transition Model and population structure — 2019, 2022, 2025: plotting, percentages, and explaining a stage.
  • Reducing the development gap — Fairtrade 2019, debt relief 2023; the school's list adds tourism (2020) and aid (2021), so Jamaica and aid are overdue.
  • Uneven development and OS map skills — causes and consequences in 2024 and 2025; map work in 2019 and 2023.

Examiners' refrain: say why a measure misleads, learn the interquartile range, and anchor the 9-marker in Nigeria with Shell detail.

Every Section B question from 2019–2025, with the exact wordings

Every Section B question from the June 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 papers, with marks. The maths is relentless — mean, median, interquartile range, range, percentage and best-fit lines all appear — and AQA states that 10% of the whole paper's marks are mathematical.

  • Measuring development and its limitations — "Which measure of development combines income, life expectancy and education levels?" (2023, 1 mark); "Outline one physical cause of uneven development" (2023, 2 marks); "Outline the limitation(s) of one social measure of development such as access to clean water" (2025, 2 marks); "Calculate the median value for the GNI data" (2024, 2 marks); "Calculate the interquartile range for the data in Figure 8" (2023, 2 marks); "What is the difference in access to safe water supply between high income and [low income countries]?" (2025, 1 mark).
  • The Demographic Transition Model and population structure — "Plot the following data on to Figure 5" and "Draw a best fit line" (2019, 1 mark each); "'Japan is in stage 5 of the Demographic Transition Model (DTM) and is a highly developed country.' Explain this statement. Use Figure 5 and your own understanding" (2019, 3 marks); "Complete Figure 8 using the following data" and "Using Figure 8, calculate the percentage (%) of children aged 0–4 years old" (2022, 1 mark each); "What is meant by infant mortality rate?" (2022, 2 marks); "Using Figure 9, suggest how population change in Stage 3 may have economic benefits" (2022, 3 marks); "Calculate the mean population change in the 65+ age groups" (2025, 1 mark); "What is the range between the largest percentage increase and largest percentage [decrease]?" (2025, 1 mark).
  • Causes and consequences of uneven development — "Suggest how international migration can be a consequence of uneven development" (2024, 6 marks); "Explain one or more causes of uneven development" (2025, 4 marks). The school's list adds the earlier "Suggest how economic development affects peoples' quality of life" stems.
  • Reducing the development gap — "Explain how fairtrade can reduce the development gap" (2019, 4 marks); "Suggest how debt relief can help reduce the development gap. Use Figure 9 and your own understanding" (2023, 4 marks). The school's question list adds "Tourism is an effective way of reducing the development gap. Do you agree?" (2020, 6 marks) and "'Aid is the best way to reduce the development gap.' To what extent do you agree?" (2021, 6 marks) — so Jamaica and aid are both overdue.
  • The Nigeria case study (LIC/NEE) — "Using a case study of a LIC/NEE, evaluate the effects of economic development on the population's quality of life" (2019, 9 marks + 3 SPaG); "'Transnational corporations (TNCs) bring more disadvantages than advantages to a host country.' Do you agree? Explain your answer" (2022, 6 marks); "Suggest how economic development can bring improvements to quality of life but at a cost to the environment. Use a case study of a LIC/NEE in your answer" (2023, 9 marks + 3 SPaG); "You have studied a LIC/NEE country" + "Outline one way in which your chosen country is regionally important" (2024, 1 and 2 marks); "Explain how manufacturing industry can stimulate economic development in your chosen country" (2024, 4 marks); "Evaluate the impacts of a transnational corporation (TNC) on a host country. Use a case study of a LIC/NEE" (2025, 9 marks + 3 SPaG); "Use Figure 10 to suggest how economic development affects peoples' quality of life" (2025, 3 marks).
  • The changing UK economy — "Suggest how the UK is moving towards a post-industrial economy. Use Figure 8 and your own understanding" (2019, 6 marks); "Outline one or more reasons for the decline of traditional industries in the UK" (2022, 3 marks); "Suggest how changing economic and political links may affect the UK's place in the wider world. Use Figure 7 and your own understanding" (2022, 6 marks); map evidence for a science park site (2023, 2 marks, Southampton Science Park on the OS map); "To what extent are modern industrial developments environmentally sustainable? Use Figure 6 and your own understanding" (2023, 6 marks); "Outline how globalisation has caused economic change in the UK" (2024, 3 marks); "'The economic future of different parts of the UK will be affected by improvements and developments in transport and infrastructure.' Explain this statement. Use Figure 11 and your own knowledge" (2024, 9 marks); "Suggest how population decline can lead to social and economic changes in the rural landscape in the UK. Use Figure 9 and your own knowledge" (2025, 6 marks).
  • OS map skills — direction from one grid square to another, and two pieces of map evidence for a science park site (2023, 3 marks); six-figure grid references, straight-line distance and photographer direction (2019, 3 marks). Easy marks, taken in Section B as well as Section A.

What the examiners keep saying. On measuring development (2023 02.5): "the best answers gave reasons for the inaccuracy of the measure. However, these were rare, as few stated a disadvantage about birth rates, instead saying what they were not." On the interquartile range (2023 02.8): "students either knew how to calculate the interquartile range or they didn't. The majority didn't." On debt relief (2023 02.9): students struggled "because of a poor understanding of debt relief, often conflating it with loans". And on the 9-marker (2023 02.10): "the best answers used Nigeria and had good place specific detail linked to Shell".

How Section B is built, in full

Section B is compulsory, worth about 30 marks, and always Question 02. It runs in a fixed order: measuring development (a calculation plus a 2-marker on limitations), the DTM and population structure (a graph completion, a calculation, a 3-marker), uneven development and the development gap (a 4- or 6-marker), the Nigeria case study, and the changing UK economy. The 9-marker sits at the very end and alternates between a case study of an LIC/NEE and the UK. In 2022 there was no 9-marker here at all — the marks moved to Section A — so check the mark allocation before you plan your time.

subsections.heading: Measuring development — the indicators and why they mislead
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.1 · CEW Revision Workbook pp. 7–9; AQA List of Key Terms

  • GNI — total national income divided by population, including income earned from investments overseas.
  • HDI is the composite — GDP per capita plus life expectancy plus adult literacy, combined into one index.
  • Every measure is an average — so it hides the regional and social inequality inside a country.
More detail

Development is the progress of a country in terms of economic growth, the use of technology and human welfare. Measures split into economic (GNI, employment structure) and social (health, education, water).

MeasureWhat it isLimitation
GNI per headTotal national income divided by population, including income earned from investments overseasAn average, so it hides enormous internal inequality; says nothing about how income is spent or about healthcare and education
Birth rateBirths in a year per 1,000 of the populationAffected by culture and religion as well as development; can fall for reasons unrelated to wealth
Death rateDeaths in a year per 1,000 of the populationMisleading on its own: an HIC with many elderly people can have a higher death rate than an LIC with a young population
Infant mortalityDeaths of infants under 1 year per 1,000 live births per yearA good indicator of healthcare, but depends on deaths being registered, which is unreliable in the poorest countries
Life expectancyAverage number of years a person might be expected to liveAn average pulled down sharply by high infant mortality, so it understates adult life expectancy
People per doctorPopulation divided by number of doctorsSays nothing about where the doctors are — in Rio the hospitals are in affluent districts, and in Nigeria urban areas take the greater share
Literacy ratePercentage with basic reading and writing skillsDefinitions and testing vary between countries, so figures are not strictly comparable
Access to safe waterPercentage of the population with a safe supply"Access" is defined generously, and the national figure hides the urban–rural gap
HDIGDP per capita, life expectancy and adult literacy combined into a single index figure, allowing countries to be rankedStill an average, and the three components can move in opposite directions

The overarching limitation, which earns the mark on its own: economic and social measures are averages for the whole country, so they conceal differences between regions, between urban and rural areas and between rich and poor. Nigeria is the worked example — GDP per head is US$3,617 in the south against US$292 in the poorest region, so a single national figure describes nobody.

Nigeria against the UK, from the school's booklet: infant mortality 94 per 1,000 live births against 5; life expectancy 54 against 81; internet users 47% against 93%; HDI rank 164th against 13th.

  • Development defined — the progress of a country in economic growth, the use of technology and human welfare.
  • Three groups — LICs, NEEs and HICs, separated by GNI per head and by the characteristics that go with it.
  • Social measures — birth rate, death rate, infant mortality, life expectancy, people per doctor, literacy, access to safe water.
  • Every single measure is an average — so it hides regional and social inequality inside a country, which is the limitation examiners want.

✗ "Birth rate is not a very good measure." — the 2023 report: students said what the measure was not rather than giving a reason it is inaccurate.
✓ "Access to safe water is recorded as a national percentage, so it hides the gap between urban and rural areas — Nigeria's figure rose from 46% to 85% between 1990 and 2019, yet urban areas still take a far greater share of public services than the countryside."

subsections.heading: The Demographic Transition Model
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.1 · CEW Revision Workbook pp. 11–12; 2019 Q02.4 and 2022 Q02.9

  • Stage 2 early expanding — death rate falls (clean water, food, medicine) while births stay high, so population rises fast.
  • Stage 3 late expanding — birth rate falls fast (contraception, women in work, lower infant mortality); population still rising.
  • Stage 4 low fluctuating — both rates low, population high and stable; most HICs, including the UK.
  • Stage 5 natural decrease — death rate slightly exceeds birth rate, so population falls and ages; Japan is the example.
More detail

The Demographic Transition Model shows how populations should change over time in terms of their birth rates, death rates and total population size. It is a model, so it describes the European experience and does not fit every country — a point worth making if you are asked to evaluate it.

StageBirth and death ratesLinks to developmentExample
1 High fluctuatingBoth high and variable; population low and stableSubsistence farming, no healthcare, disease and famine; children needed to workRemote tribal groups
2 Early expandingDeath rate falls sharply; birth rate stays high; population rises rapidlyClean water, better food supply and basic medicine cut deaths, but attitudes to family size have not yet changedNigeria, Afghanistan
3 Late expandingBirth rate falls rapidly; death rate low; population still rising but more slowlyContraception available, women enter paid work, infant mortality falls so fewer children are needed, education costs moneyBrazil, Mexico, India
4 Low fluctuatingBoth low; population high and stableIndustrial and post-industrial, good healthcare, small families the normUK, USA
5 Natural decreaseDeath rate slightly above birth rate; population falls and agesVery high living costs, career priorities, very long life expectancy, so the elderly outnumber birthsJapan, Germany, Italy

The Japan 3-marker (2019). "Japan is in stage 5 of the DTM and is a highly developed country. Explain this statement." The chain: Japan has 28% over 65 and only 12% under 15, so deaths exceed births and the population is falling (1); this is possible only because healthcare is excellent and life expectancy very high, which requires wealth (1); and the low birth rate reflects expensive housing, women in long careers and very low infant mortality, all features of a highly developed economy (1).

The Stage 3 economic benefits 3-marker (2022). In Stage 3 the birth rate falls while the large cohort born in Stage 2 reaches working age, so the working-age population grows relative to dependents (1); fewer children per family means women can enter paid employment, increasing the workforce and household income (1); and with fewer dependents, more income can be saved, invested or taxed, funding infrastructure and education — the demographic dividend (1).

  • What it models — how birth rate, death rate and total population change as a country develops, in five stages.
  • Stage 1 high fluctuating — high birth and death rates, so population stays low and stable; almost no country now.
  • Stage 3 late expanding — birth rate falls rapidly (contraception, women in work, lower infant mortality); population still rising.

The population structures AQA expects you to recognise

  • Mexico, 2020 — 45% under 15, 4% over 65. A wide-based pyramid: Stage 2–3, a youthful population with a high dependency ratio of children.
  • Japan, 2020 — 12% under 15, 28% over 65. Top-heavy: Stage 5, an ageing population with a shrinking workforce.
  • Nigeria — life expectancy 54, infant mortality 94 per 1,000: Stage 2 moving into Stage 3.
  • The UK — Stage 4, with rural areas such as the Outer Hebrides locally in Stage 5 through out-migration of the young.

subsections.heading: Causes of uneven development
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.2 · CEW Revision Workbook pp. 14–15; Revision Mat — Development Gap

  • Three families of cause — physical, economic and historical. Name the family, then the mechanism.
  • Physical — extreme weather and climate, difficult relief, being landlocked, tropical disease, and water shortage.
  • Economic — poverty traps, and trade: LICs export low-value primary goods and import high-value manufactures.
  • Historical — colonialism, slavery, and borders drawn across ethnic groups, which left unstable states and extractive economies.
More detail

Physical causes. Weather and climate — extremes of drought and flood destroy harvests, so farmers have nothing to sell and no surplus to invest; a reliable growing season is the foundation of a farming economy. Relief — steep, mountainous land is hard to farm and expensive to build roads and railways across, so interior regions stay cut off. Landlocked countries — with no coastline there is no port, so trade must cross a neighbour's territory, adding cost and political risk. Tropical environments — disease, including malaria, reduces the working population and diverts spending into healthcare. Water shortages — without reliable water, irrigation, industry and sanitation are all limited.

Economic causes. Poverty is self-reinforcing: low incomes mean low tax revenue, so the government cannot fund the schools, clinics and infrastructure that would raise incomes. Trade is the bigger structural cause — LICs typically export primary products (raw materials and crops) whose prices are low and volatile, and import manufactured goods whose prices are high. Because raw materials are exported before being refined, the profit from processing them accrues elsewhere. Nigeria is the example: oil is 98% of export earnings but only 14% of GDP, and the country still imports chemicals and machinery.

Historical causes. Colonisation organised economies around extracting raw materials for the colonial power rather than developing industry; the slave trade removed millions of working-age people; and borders drawn by colonial powers cut across ethnic and religious groups, leaving states with internal tensions. Nigeria became independent of the UK only in 1960, is multi-ethnic with the Yoruba at 21% of the population, and has a Christian south and Muslim north — and "economic inequality and regional differences have created ethnic tensions".

Consequences. Wealth — 34% of global wealth is held in North America, which has a small fraction of the world's people. Health — 400,000 people died of malaria in 2019, almost all in LICs; Nigeria's infant mortality is 94 per 1,000 against the UK's 5. International migration — 590,000 people have fled Syria, where 80% of the remaining population live below the poverty line and unemployment is 55%.

  • Landlocked is the clearest — no coast means no port, so every import and export pays to cross a neighbour's territory.
  • Consequences — disparities in wealth and health, and international migration.

✗ "Some countries are poor because they have a bad climate." — asserted, not explained, and the 2023 report says wrong answers came from "not understanding what physical causes were".
✓ "A tropical climate supports mosquitoes carrying malaria, which killed 400,000 people in 2019; illness removes adults from work, so output and tax revenue fall and the money that might have been invested in development is spent on treatment instead."

subsections.heading: Consequences of uneven development — and international migration
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.2 · Case Study Summary Booklet quiz facts; 2024 Q02.4

  • Wealth — 34% of global wealth sits in North America, so investment concentrates where money already is.
  • Health — 400,000 malaria deaths in 2019; Nigeria's infant mortality is 94/1000 against the UK's 5.
  • Economic migration — the pull of higher wages, jobs, healthcare and education in HICs; the push of unemployment and poverty.
  • Forced migration — conflict and environmental disaster; 590,000 have fled Syria, 80% of those left in poverty.
More detail

The 2024 6-marker — "Suggest how international migration can be a consequence of uneven development" — wants the mechanism, in both directions.

Why uneven development causes migration. Where development is low, there are few well-paid jobs, healthcare is limited, schooling is poor and basic services are unreliable; where it is high, wages, services and security are all better. People therefore move from LICs towards NEEs and HICs. Conflict, which is itself often a consequence of poverty and competition for resources, forces far larger movements: 590,000 have fled Syria, where 80% of the remaining population lives below the poverty line and 55% are unemployed.

Why it also widens the gap. Migrants are predominantly young, healthy and often the better-educated, so the source country loses exactly the workers it needs — the brain drain. Against that, remittances sent home can exceed the value of official aid, and returning migrants bring skills and capital.

The receiving-country side, worth a sentence for balance: London's migrant streams were dominated by the former British Empire and then Eastern Europe, 37% of Londoners were born outside the UK, and migrants contributed £20 billion to UK public finances between 2000 and 2011 — while also increasing competition for housing, school places and jobs.

  • Migration is the third consequence — people move from where opportunity is absent to where it exists.
  • Forced migration — conflict and environmental disaster; 590,000 have fled Syria, with 80% of those left below the poverty line.
  • It feeds back — remittances help the source country, but the loss of skilled workers (brain drain) widens the gap further.

subsections.heading: Reducing the development gap — the eight strategies
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.3 · Revision Mat — Development Gap; Case Study Summary Booklet quiz facts

  • Learn all eight — investment, industrial development, tourism, aid, intermediate technology, Fairtrade, debt relief, microfinance.
  • The common mechanism — each creates employment, which raises incomes, which raises tax revenue, which funds services.
  • Fairtrade — a guaranteed fair price plus a community premium; 90% of eastern Uganda's coffee farmers joined Gumutindo.
  • Microfinance — very small loans to start a business; the Grameen Bank has lent $12.5 billion.
More detail
  • Fairtrade — a guaranteed fair price plus a premium invested in the community; 90% of small coffee farmers in eastern Uganda joined the Gumutindo co-op.
  • Debt relief is cancellation, not a loan — $75 billion was written off across 19 HIPCs, freeing money for roads and healthcare.
  • Microfinance — very small loans to start a business; the Grameen Bank has lent $12.5 billion, including $200 to a woman to buy a phone.
  • Aid — the UK gives 0.5% of GNI, including about £300 million a year to Pakistan, where 35% live in poverty.

The eight strategies, with the figures that make them specific

  • Investment. Countries, organisations such as the World Bank, and TNCs invest in LICs to increase their own profits. The investment improves infrastructure (road networks, airports), services (water, sanitation, electricity), dams and reservoirs for hydro-electric power, and industrial developments.
  • Industrial development. Brings employment in construction, manufacturing and services. Increased individual wealth leads to improvements in health, education and service provision through the payment of more taxes — that tax link is the mechanism, and it is what the mark schemes credit.
  • Tourism. See Jamaica below. The engine is the multiplier effect: visitor spending → jobs and tax → public spending → better infrastructure → more visitors.
  • Aid. Money, goods and services given by one government, or by a multilateral institution such as the World Bank or IMF, to improve another country's quality of life and economy. Long-term aid funds development projects — sanitation, water supply, education; short-term aid responds to natural disasters. The UK gives 0.5% of GNI as aid, including about £300 million a year to Pakistan, where 35% of the population lives in poverty. Oxfam runs Goat Aid.
  • Intermediate technology. Simple, easily learned and easily maintained technology serving local needs — the point is that it can be repaired locally without imported parts or expertise. A 15 m dam built at Adis Nifas provides irrigation; the Chambamontera micro-hydro scheme in Peru is the same idea applied to energy.
  • Fairtrade. Producers in LICs are given a better price for what they grow — usually cocoa, coffee or cotton — plus a premium invested in the local community, and fair wages for the workforce. 90% of small coffee farmers in eastern Uganda have joined the Gumutindo Co-operative. The better price improves income and reduces exploitation.
  • Debt relief. In the 1970s and 1980s many countries borrowed heavily for large-scale development projects and then fell into debt repaying loans at high interest. Debt relief cancels money owed, so the repayments can be redirected into development — road building, health care, education. Total debt relief across the 19 Heavily Indebted Poor Countries was $75 billion.
  • Microfinance loans. Very small loans to individuals or community groups to start a small business. If the business succeeds it creates jobs and raises incomes. The Grameen Bank has lent $12.5 billion in total and lends around $200 to a woman to buy a phone she can rent out.

✗ "Debt relief gives countries money to develop." — the 2023 report's exact complaint: candidates conflated debt relief with loans.
✓ "Debt relief cancels debt that already exists, so the money a government was spending on interest repayments — across the 19 HIPCs, $75 billion of debt was written off — can instead be spent on roads, clinics and schools."

subsections.heading: Tourism and the development gap — Jamaica
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.3, named example · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 17; Revision Mat — Development Gap

  • The scale — tourism was 35% of Jamaica's GDP in 2019, with 4 million visitors a year.
  • The money — generates about $2 billion a year, and over 50% of Jamaica's foreign exchange earnings.
  • Employment — the main source of jobs: over 200,000 people employed directly and indirectly.
  • The limits — benefits cluster in wealthy areas such as Montego Bay, and pockets of poverty persist.
More detail
  • Infrastructure — new port and cruise liner facilities at Falmouth; a new water treatment plant at Logwood.
  • Environment — the Negril Marine Nature Park shows conservation paying for itself through tourist income.
  • The limits — the benefits cluster in wealthy areas such as Montego Bay, pockets of poverty persist, and roads came late.

Tourism in Jamaica — the facts and figures

  • Economy. In 2019 tourism contributed 35% of Jamaica's GDP, with 4 million visitors a year. It generates $2 billion each year and over 50% of the country's total foreign exchange earnings. Taxes paid to the government allow more public spending — the multiplier effect.
  • Growth. Visitor arrivals grew almost exponentially between 1994 and 2016. Total visitor expenditure rose from US$128,706,000 in 1975 to US$2,608,798,000 in 2016. Arrivals still rose in 2009, but more slowly, because the recession cut disposable income — a reminder that tourism is vulnerable to events elsewhere.
  • Employment. Tourism is the main source of employment, with over 200,000 people employed directly and indirectly — the second largest employer in the country.
  • Infrastructure. New port and cruise liner facilities at Falmouth; a new water treatment plant at Logwood, which benefits residents as well as hotels.
  • Quality of life. Local farmers benefit by supplying hotels, which keeps the money in the Jamaican economy rather than leaking abroad.
  • Environment. The Negril Marine Nature Park attracts many tourists, so protecting the reef and marine life becomes economically worthwhile.
  • The limits. Wealthier parts such as Montego Bay have benefited far more than others; pockets of poverty still exist; and infrastructure such as roads came much later because the authorities prioritised port and airport investment — so the benefit to ordinary Jamaicans lagged behind the benefit to the tourist industry.

subsections.heading: Nigeria — location, importance and context
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.4, Case Study Five · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 18; Revision Mat — Nigeria

  • Where — West Africa, bordering Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon, with the Gulf of Guinea to the south.
  • Globally — 2.2% of the world's oil, the 13th largest oil producer, and the 7th largest population in the world.
  • Regionally — the largest economy and largest population in Africa, with the continent's third-largest manufacturing sector.
  • Internal contrast — semi-desert far north, forest in the wet south; GDP per head US$3,617 against US$292.

Nigeria — the figures that win marks

  • Where and how big — West Africa, bordering Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon, with the Gulf of Guinea south; the 7th largest population in the world.
  • Why it matters — 2.2% of the world's oil and the 13th largest producer; the largest economy in Africa; Nollywood is the world's second largest film industry.
  • Context — independent of the UK in 1960; member of OPEC and ECOWAS; corruption, and Boko Haram since 2002; Christian south, Muslim north.
  • Inequality inside the country — GDP per head US$3,617 in the south against US$292 in the poorest region, a twelvefold gap.
  • Industrial structure — agricultural employment down 40%; manufacturing 27% and the fastest growing sector; services 53%.
  • Over-dependence on oil — oil is 14% of GDP but 98% of export earnings, so national income tracks the world oil price.
  • Shell, for — in Nigeria since 1958; 90% of contracts to Nigerian firms, 3,000 scholarships, healthcare spending and major tax revenue.
  • Shell, against — registered in Bermuda so less tax; spills at Bodo in Ogoniland, contamination 1,000× higher, 42,000 residents sued.
  • Environmental cost — 96% of forests destroyed, around 40 oil spills, 94% exposed to high air pollution, 10,000 tonnes of waste a day.
  • Quality of life, and the judgement — life expectancy up 9 years (2015–19) and safe water from 46% to 85%, but 60% still live in poverty and Malaysia and Singapore have moved far ahead.
More detail
  • Nollywood — the second largest film industry in the world, ahead of the USA and behind India.
  • Political context — independent of the UK in 1960; member of OPEC and ECOWAS; corruption, and Boko Haram since 2002.
  • Internal contrast — semi-desert in the far north, forest in the wet south; GDP per head US$3,617 in the south against US$292 in the poorest region.

Nigeria — location, importance and context

  • Location. West Africa, sharing borders with Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon; to the south it borders the Gulf of Guinea, part of the Atlantic Ocean.
  • Global importance. Produces 2.2% of the world's oil and is the 13th largest oil producer; around the 27th largest GDP in the world; the 7th largest population; the second largest film industry in the world — Nollywood — ahead of the United States and behind India; and a major contributor of troops and police to United Nations peacekeeping since the 1960s.
  • Regional importance. The largest economy in Africa and the highest GNP on the continent; it had the highest GDP in Africa in 2014 and is one of the fastest growing economies in Africa; the largest population in Africa; the third-largest manufacturing sector; the largest agricultural output and the highest number of cattle. A founder figure of the Organisation of African Unity (now the African Union) was Nigeria's president in 1963, and Nigeria now plays a leading political role in Africa.
  • Political context. Became independent of the UK in 1960. Political corruption is a persistent problem, and the terrorist group Boko Haram emerged from 2002. Nigeria is a member of OPEC (the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries) and of ECOWAS, the trading group of West African countries.
  • Social and cultural context. A multi-ethnic country — the Yoruba are 21% of the population — with a religious divide between the Christian south and the Muslim north. Economic inequality and regional differences have created ethnic tensions. Nigerian music, cinema, literature and sport create a rich and varied culture.
  • Regional variation. Urban areas have a greater share of public services. GDP per head is highest in the south at US$3,617 and lowest at US$292 in the poorest region — a twelvefold gap inside one country.
  • Environmental context. The far north is semi-desert; southern Nigeria has high temperatures and high rainfall, and much of it is forest with crops such as rubber and palm oil.
  • Development indicators against the UK. Infant mortality 94 per 1,000 live births against 5; life expectancy 54 against 81; internet users 47% against 93%; HDI rank 164th against 13th.

✗ "Nigeria is important because it has oil." — one word of a one-mark answer, and the 2022 report notes that "few showed understanding of regional".
✓ Match the tier to the question. Regionally: the largest economy and largest population in Africa, with the continent's third-largest manufacturing sector. Globally: 2.2% of the world's oil, the 7th largest population, and Nollywood, the world's second largest film industry.

subsections.heading: Nigeria — industrial structure, manufacturing and TNCs
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.4 · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 18; 2025 Q02.10 mark scheme

  • The shift — from agriculture to manufacturing and services; agricultural employment has fallen by 40%.
  • Oil dominates exports — 14% of GDP but 98% of export earnings, which is the over-dependence problem.
  • Shell, for — tens of thousands employed, 90%+ of contracts to Nigerian firms, 3,000 scholarships, healthcare spending.
  • Shell, against — registered in Bermuda so less tax is paid, and oil spills at Bodo in Ogoniland destroyed livelihoods.
More detail
  • The balance now — manufacturing 27%, services 53%; manufacturing is the fastest growing sector.
  • TNCs — around 40 operate in Nigeria, and 920 Chinese companies; Shell has been there since 1958.
  • Shell, for — tens of thousands employed, 90%+ of contracts to Nigerian firms, 3,000 scholarships, healthcare spending.

Nigeria's economy and the role of Shell

  • Main exports. Oil, natural gas, rubber, cocoa and cotton. Oil accounts for 14% of GDP and 98% of export earnings, so the national income rises and falls with the world oil price.
  • The changing structure. Employment in agriculture has fallen by 40%, through mechanisation and better pay in other sectors. Manufacturing now accounts for 27% of the economy and is the fastest growing sector; the service sector is 53%, with considerable growth in IT.
  • How manufacturing stimulates development. It creates better-paid, more secure work than subsistence farming; wages are spent locally so other businesses grow (the multiplier effect); companies and workers pay tax, giving the government money for schools, clinics and infrastructure; processing raw materials in Nigeria rather than exporting them raw keeps the value added in the country; and it reduces reliance on imported manufactured goods such as chemicals and machinery.
  • TNCs in Nigeria. Around 40 transnational corporations operate in the country, and 920 Chinese companies. Countries such as the USA, China and South Africa have invested heavily.
  • Shell — the case study TNC. An Anglo-Dutch oil TNC, in Nigeria since 1958 with the discovery of oil and controversial extraction operations in the Niger Delta.
  • The advantages of Shell. $250,000 spent on healthcare; 3,000 scholarships to local schools; 90% of contracts awarded to local companies (AQA's 2025 mark scheme gives 91%, with direct employment of 65,000 Nigerians and 250,000 more indirectly, while an updated textbook figure is 2,700 direct employees and 9,000 contractors, 97% of them Nigerian). Shell makes significant contributions to Nigeria's tax revenue, increasing national wealth.
  • The disadvantages of Shell. Less tax is paid because the company is registered in Bermuda. Oil spills have caused water pollution, with two massive spills at Bodo in Ogoniland in the Niger Delta; 42,000 residents took out a lawsuit against Shell; contamination in Ogoniland is 1,000 times higher than elsewhere; gas flaring continues, adding greenhouse gases and causing respiratory problems. Oil wealth has provoked armed conflict and groups such as the Niger Delta Avengers, costing lives and government revenue.
  • The general case against TNCs. Profits leave the country and benefit shareholders, often in HICs; wages are lower than in the TNC's home country; environmental damage is caused without responsibility for cleaning it up; a TNC can withdraw if circumstances change; powerful TNCs can exert pressure on governments; and raw materials are exported before being refined, which reduces the profit retained in LICs and NEEs.

subsections.heading: Nigeria — trade, political links and international aid
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.4 · Revision Mat — Nigeria; Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 18

  • Now diversified — most trade is with the EU, USA and India, with links to China growing fast.
  • Still an unequal trade — exports are raw oil and crops; imports are manufactured chemicals and machinery.
  • Aid in action — Christian Aid reached 360,000 people with life-saving health care and trained 1,000 local people.
  • The problems with aid — government corruption diverts it, donors may demand political influence, and dependence can follow.
More detail
  • Colonial legacy — as part of the British Empire, Nigeria's links ran almost entirely to the UK.
  • Aid received — 6% of all aid given to African countries, but only 0.8% of Nigeria's annual GNI.

Nigeria's changing relationships and its aid

  • Trade. Nigeria was originally part of the British Empire, so most political and economic links ran to the UK and other Empire members. Since independence in 1960 it has kept strong links with the UK but now conducts most of its trade with some of the world's largest economies — the EU, USA and India — and links with China are growing. Oil became its main commodity export after independence, but it still imports manufactured goods such as chemicals and machinery.
  • Political links. Nigeria plays a leading political role in Africa, is a member of OPEC and ECOWAS, and has been a major contributor to UN peacekeeping since the 1960s.
  • Why aid is needed. 60% of the population — about 100 million people — live on less than US$1 a day, and over 50% live in poverty.
  • How much. Nigeria receives 6% of the aid given to African countries, which represents only 0.8% of its annual GNI — so aid is a small part of its economy compared with oil.
  • Named examples. Christian Aid — 360,000 people received life-saving health care and 1,000 local people were trained. The UK Department for International Development funded a health and HIV programme. The IMF approved £3.4 billion post-Covid for economic redevelopment.
  • The problems. Corruption in government means aid is lost or does not reach the right people; there have been claims that aid money was used to supply the Navy; donors may demand political influence over who benefits and may use donations to promote themselves; and aid can create dependence rather than self-sufficient growth.

subsections.heading: Nigeria — environmental impacts and quality of life
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.4 · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 18; Revision Mat — Nigeria

  • Deforestation — 96% of Nigeria's forests have been destroyed by logging, agriculture and urban expansion.
  • Oil spills — around 40 spills; Ogoniland contamination 1,000× higher than elsewhere; 42,000 residents sued Shell.
  • But quality of life has risen — life expectancy up 9 years since 2015; safe water from 46% to 85%.
  • The judgement — 30 years ago Nigeria was level with Malaysia and Singapore, which have moved far ahead.
More detail
  • Air — 94% of the population is exposed to high air pollution; gas flaring causes respiratory illness.
  • Waste — 10,000 tonnes a day, and electronic waste is imported from Europe.
  • But quality of life has risen — life expectancy up 9 years between 2015 and 2019; safe water access up from 46% to 85% since 1990.
  • The comparison that makes the judgement — 30 years ago Nigeria was level with Malaysia and Singapore, which have since moved far ahead.

Nigeria — the environmental cost, and the gains in quality of life

  • Deforestation. 96% of Nigeria's forests have been destroyed through logging, agriculture and urban expansion, removing habitat and the carbon sink.
  • Mining and oil. Around 40 oil spills; contamination in Ogoniland is 1,000 times higher than elsewhere; 42,000 residents took out a lawsuit against Shell; oil spills have destroyed aquatic ecosystems and ruined fishermen's livelihoods. Burning and flaring gas associated with oil extraction causes air pollution, releases greenhouse gases and causes respiratory problems. Tin mining has caused soil erosion and polluted water supplies. 94% of the population is exposed to high air pollution levels.
  • Waste. 10,000 tonnes a day; lack of sanitation and inadequate waste disposal cause land and water pollution; electronic waste is imported from Europe and dismantled unsafely.
  • Urban growth. Rapid urban growth has caused urban sprawl, swallowing up countryside, while emissions from cars and industry contribute to climate change.
  • The gains. Between 2015 and 2019 life expectancy increased by 9 years. Between 1990 and 2019 access to safe water rose from 46% to 85%. Manufacturing and services now provide better-paid, more secure employment than subsistence agriculture.
  • The limits. 60% still live in poverty; the religious divide between Christian south and Muslim north remains; corruption and over-dependence on oil persist. Thirty years ago Nigeria was at a similar stage of development to Malaysia and Singapore, and both have moved much further ahead — the sharpest single piece of evidence that economic development has not translated fully into quality of life.
  • The future challenges. Overcoming socio-economic inequality; tackling government corruption so wealth reaches everyone; addressing soil erosion, water pollution, desertification and oil spills; maximising oil revenue and investing it in other sectors; handling ethnic and religious conflict sensitively; providing basic sanitation for all; and further investment in healthcare and education.

✗ "Economic development in Nigeria has been bad for the environment." — one-sided, so capped at Level 2 on a question that says "improvements to quality of life but at a cost".
✓ Pair them: "Access to safe water rose from 46% to 85% and life expectancy rose 9 years in four years, but 96% of the forests have gone, 94% of people breathe polluted air, and Ogoniland is contaminated at 1,000 times the level found elsewhere — so quality of life improved while the environment that sustains it deteriorated."

subsections.heading: De-industrialisation and globalisation in the UK
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.5 · Revision Mat — UK Changing Economy; 2022 Q02.3, 2024 Q02.8

  • De-industrialisation — the reduction of industrial activity or capacity, especially heavy industry and manufacturing.
  • What declined — coal mining, shipbuilding and steel manufacturing, as raw materials ran out and markets were lost.
  • Three causes — mechanisation replacing workers, exhaustion of raw materials, and competition from NEEs with lower wages.
More detail

De-industrialisation is the reduction of industrial activity or capacity in a region or economy, especially of heavy industry or manufacturing industry. AQA's own definition adds the causes: "due to exhaustion of raw materials, loss of markets and competition from NEEs".

How the UK's employment structure changed in the 20th century. A decrease in the number of people working in manufacturing, as mechanisation — the introduction of robots and automated plant — replaced jobs, and as competition from abroad increased. A dramatic increase in the service sector, through the introduction of public services, the growth of financial services, and an increase in leisure time and disposable income. And since the 1980s, the research and development sector has become increasingly important.

What de-industrialisation involved in practice: the closure of coal mines and shipyards; a negative multiplier effect, as the smaller businesses that supplied and supported heavy industry closed too, affecting thousands more people; huge job losses and rising unemployment in North East England as factories and industrial sites closed; and a skills problem — many of those employed in heavy industries struggled to find new jobs with the skills they had.

Globalisation's six effects on the UK, from the school's revision mat:

  • Migration — migrants fill jobs where the UK has a shortage of skilled workers, such as healthcare and construction.
  • Less manufacturing — fewer goods are made in the UK because they can be imported more cheaply from countries such as China where wages are lower.
  • Inequality — the gap between the best-paid and lowest-paid jobs is increasing.
  • Outsourcing — jobs are moved to other countries where wages are lower.
  • Economic growth — in most years the UK economy grows by 1–2%, mainly through trade with other countries.
  • Foreign investment — foreign companies invest in the UK, bringing new ways of working and new technology; and cheaper goods and services follow from more competitive wages and production.

The environmental legacy of heavy industry: coal mining created spoil heaps, vast mounds of waste removed during extraction; burning coal to generate electricity caused considerable air pollution in cities across the UK; and toxic waste materials from heavy industry polluted land and water supplies.

  • The negative multiplier — suppliers and support businesses closed too, so job losses spread; the North East was hit hardest.
  • Globalisation cuts both ways — cheaper goods, foreign investment and 1–2% growth a year, against outsourcing and widening inequality.
  • Skills mismatch — workers from heavy industry struggled to find new jobs with the skills they had.

subsections.heading: The UK's post-industrial economy — science parks and sustainable industry
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.5, named example · Revision Mat — UK Changing Economy; Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 19

  • Post-industrial economy — one where most employment is in service industries; 80% of the UK economy is tertiary.
  • IT is the engine — 1.3 million people work in IT, and digital firms grew 2.6 times faster than the economy.
  • Science parks — on the edge of university cities, with good transport links; they employ around 75,000 people in the UK.
  • Modern industry can be greener — Nissan's plant has 10 wind turbines, 19,000 solar panels, and CO₂ down 22.4%.

The UK's post-industrial economy — the figures that win marks

  • Services — 80% of the UK economy comes from the tertiary sector, and 1.7% from research.
  • Information technology — 1.3 million people are employed in IT, and digital firms grew 2.6 times faster than the overall economy.
  • Science parks — on the edge of university cities with good transport links; they employ around 75,000 people in the UK.
  • Named parks — Southampton Science Park opened in 1986 close to the M3; 21% of South Cambridgeshire works in hi-tech.
  • Torr Quarry, Somerset — a 2.5 km² limestone quarry worth £15 million a year locally: the named example for industry's impact on the environment.
  • Torr Quarry, made sustainable — 80 hectares landscaped with the Somerset Wildlife Trust to create biodiverse-rich landscapes.
  • Nissan, Sunderland — 10 wind turbines and 19,000 photovoltaic panels; CO₂ down 22.4% since 2005; electric and hybrid cars.
More detail

The 2023 OS map question asked for two pieces of map evidence showing why grid square 4018 was a good location for Southampton Science Park. The report's warning: "too many students tended to name anything they saw on the map without any consideration of why this would be a good site". So pair each piece of evidence with the reason — a motorway junction nearby means staff and freight can reach it quickly; the university in the next grid square means research links and a supply of graduates; woodland and open space means the attractive environment that high-tech employers use to recruit.

And the 2023 6-marker on environmental sustainability: the report says the students who reached Level 3 did so "by properly examining the photograph and considering the carbon footprints of construction and employee transportation" — in other words, by arguing that an edge-of-city science park on a greenfield site generates car commuting, so it is only partly sustainable.

  • IT is the engine — 1.3 million people work in IT, and digital firms grew 2.6 times faster than the economy.
  • Named parks — Southampton Science Park opened 1986 near the M3; 21% of South Cambridgeshire works in hi-tech.
  • Torr Quarry — a 2.5 km² limestone quarry in Somerset worth £15 million a year locally, with 80 hectares landscaped.
  • Modern industry can be greener — Nissan's plant has 10 wind turbines and 19,000 solar panels, and cut CO₂ 22.4% since 2005.

Torr Quarry, Somerset — industry and the physical environment

  • What it is. A 2.5 km² limestone quarry in Somerset — a working extractive industry in a rural area.
  • Economic value. It contributes £15 million a year to the local economy.
  • Environmental impacts. Quarrying removes the landscape itself and generates dust, noise and lorry traffic; this is the reason the spec pairs it with "how modern industrial development can be more environmentally sustainable".
  • How it is made more sustainable. 80 hectares have been landscaped, and the Somerset Wildlife Trust works with the quarry to create biodiverse-rich landscapes on the restored ground — so the site is being handed back as habitat rather than left as a hole.
  • The exam use. This is the named example for "the impacts of industry on the physical environment", and it answers the 2023 6-marker "to what extent are modern industrial developments environmentally sustainable?" from the extractive side, where Nissan and the science parks answer it from the manufacturing side.

The post-industrial economy — the figures

  • Services. 80% of the UK economy comes from the tertiary sector; 1.7% comes from research.
  • Information technology. 1.3 million people are employed in IT; home-working and self-employment have grown because of the internet; the UK is viewed as one of the top IT countries in the world and receives overseas investment as a result; technological developments have driven specialist manufacturing, services and research; information can be accessed anywhere on mobile devices. The turnover of digital technology companies grew by 4.5% between 2016 and 2017 against 1.7% growth in UK GDP — 2.6 times faster than the overall economy; London-based technology businesses raised £9 billion between 2015 and 2018; and the UK accounts for 5% of all high-growth technology workers employed globally.
  • Science parks. Typically located on the edge of university cities, sometimes within university grounds; they have good transport links and usually attractive environments; graduates are employed to apply their knowledge to innovative businesses; and businesses have close links to local universities and tap into their research and development. Science parks employ around 75,000 people in the UK. Southampton Science Park opened in 1986 and sits close to the M3; 21% of the population of South Cambridgeshire is employed in hi-tech industries.
  • Sustainable modern industry — the Nissan plant. 10 wind turbines generating 6.6 MW and 19,000 photovoltaic panels; Nissan is developing electric and hybrid cars; CO₂ levels have been reduced by 22.4% since 2005; and the Skills Academy for Sustainable Manufacturing and Innovation (SASMI) provides specialist training.

subsections.heading: Rural change, infrastructure, the north–south divide and the UK in the wider world
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.2.5 · Revision Mat — UK Changing Economy; Case Study Summary Booklet quiz facts

  • Rural change — growth areas gain services and jobs; the Outer Hebrides has lost 50% of its population since 1901.
  • Infrastructure — road, rail, ports and airports; A303 £2bn, Crossrail £19bn, Liverpool2 £400m and 5,000 jobs.
  • The north–south divide — longer life expectancy, higher incomes and house prices in the south-east; higher unemployment in the north.
  • Closing it — devolution, HS2, northern business parks, 43 Enterprise Zones, and LEPs — one created 11,000 jobs.
More detail

Rural areas with population growth (North Somerset, Cambridgeshire): an increased population leads to higher demand for goods and services, which helps secure the future of rural shops, schools and businesses; it provides balance to rural–urban migration, particularly as young people move away in search of better opportunities; new people are more likely to invest in new local businesses; and new developments provide jobs.

Rural areas with population decline (the Outer Hebrides, Mid Wales): the population of the Outer Hebrides has fallen by 50% since 1901. The 2025 mark scheme sets out the mechanism: younger people leave in search of opportunities, leaving a higher proportion of older residents, which closes schools and makes the community less varied, and creates social care and health pressures; economically, the cost of providing services rises because smaller populations reduce economies of scale, and a reduced, less varied population makes businesses less viable — which is why the figure described rural shops as a "lifeline".

Transport and infrastructure. The four aspects being developed are the road network, rail network, ports and airports. The widening project on the A303 will cost £2 billion; Crossrail cost £19 billion to build; Liverpool2 cost £400 million and created 5,000 jobs; the new runway at Heathrow is expected to cost £19 billion, boost the economy by £61 billion and create 75,000 new jobs.

The north–south divide is the term used to describe the social, economic and cultural disparities between London and the south-east of England and the rest of the UK. People living in the south-east typically have a longer life expectancy, higher income and better standard of living; house prices are higher because demand is higher; and rates of unemployment are higher in the north as regions continue to adjust to de-industrialisation. AQA's own definition adds "clear differences in health conditions, house prices, earnings, and political influence".

Strategies to reduce it: devolution of powers to regional authorities; HS2 and other transport links; business and science parks in the north of England; 43 Enterprise Zones across the UK offering tax breaks and simplified planning; and Local Enterprise Partnerships — one received £1 billion of investment and created 11,000 jobs.

The UK in the wider world. Links run through trade, culture, transport and electronic communication, and through two institutions. The European Union was formed to reduce trade barriers and increase cooperation, with free movement of workers between member states — the UK's departure changed the terms of that relationship. The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of 53 independent and equal sovereign states, mostly former territories of the British Empire, home to 2.2 billion citizens, united by language, history, culture and shared values rather than legal obligation. The 2022 6-marker — "suggest how changing economic and political links may affect the UK's place in the wider world" — set the two against each other explicitly: does leaving the EU mean taking back control of money, laws and borders, or can the Commonwealth provide the trading future instead?

  • Rural growth areas — more demand secures shops, schools and businesses; new residents invest; new development brings jobs.
  • Rural decline areas — the Outer Hebrides has lost 50% of its population since 1901, closing schools and shops.
  • Heathrow's third runway — £19bn to build, a £61bn economic boost and 75,000 new jobs.
  • Closing it — devolution, HS2, northern business parks, 43 Enterprise Zones, and LEPs — one created 11,000 jobs from £1bn.

The facts you cannot sit Section B without

Measuring development: GNI = total national income ÷ population, including overseas investment income · HDI = GDP per capita + life expectancy + adult literacy · social measures: birth rate, death rate, infant mortality, life expectancy, people per doctor, literacy, access to safe water · the limitation of every measure is that it is an average, hiding internal inequality.

Nigeria v UK: infant mortality 94 v 5 per 1,000 · life expectancy 54 v 81 · internet users 47% v 93% · HDI rank 164th v 13th.

DTM: 1 high fluctuating · 2 early expanding (death rate falls) · 3 late expanding (birth rate falls) · 4 low fluctuating · 5 natural decrease. Mexico 2020: 45% under 15, 4% over 65. Japan 2020: 12% under 15, 28% over 65 (Stage 5).

Uneven development — causes: physical (weather and climate, relief, landlocked, tropical disease, water shortage) · economic (poverty trap, trade in low-value primary exports) · historical (colonialism, slavery, borders cutting across ethnic groups).

Uneven development — consequences: 34% of global wealth in North America · 400,000 malaria deaths in 2019 · 590,000 fled Syria, 80% of those remaining below the poverty line, 55% unemployment.

Closing the gap — eight strategies: investment · industrial development · tourism · aid · intermediate technology · Fairtrade · debt relief · microfinance. Figures: Gumutindo co-op 90% of small coffee farmers in eastern Uganda · $75bn debt relief across 19 HIPCs · Grameen Bank $12.5bn lent, $200 for a phone · UK aid 0.5% of GNI, ~£300m/yr to Pakistan (35% in poverty) · Oxfam Goat Aid · 15 m dam at Adis Nifas.

Jamaica: tourism 35% of GDP (2019) · 4m visitors/yr · $2bn a year · over 50% of foreign exchange earnings · 200,000+ employed · expenditure US$128.7m (1975) → US$2.6bn (2016) · Falmouth cruise port · Logwood water treatment plant · Negril Marine Nature Park · but Montego Bay gained most, pockets of poverty persist, roads came late.

Nigeria — importance: West Africa, borders Benin, Niger, Chad, Cameroon, Gulf of Guinea south · 2.2% of world oil, 13th largest producer · ~27th largest GDP · 7th largest population · Nollywood = 2nd largest film industry · largest economy and population in Africa, 3rd largest manufacturing sector · independent 1960 · OPEC and ECOWAS · Boko Haram from 2002 · Yoruba 21% · Christian south / Muslim north · GDP per head US$3,617 south v US$292 poorest region · far north semi-desert, south forest with rubber and palm oil.

Nigeria — economy: exports oil, gas, rubber, cocoa, cotton · oil = 14% of GDP but 98% of export earnings · agriculture employment −40% · manufacturing 27% (fastest growing) · services 53% · 40 TNCs, 920 Chinese companies.

Shell: Anglo-Dutch, in Nigeria since 1958, Niger Delta. For: $250,000 on healthcare · 3,000 school scholarships · 90% of contracts to local companies (AQA 2025: 91%, 65,000 direct and 250,000 indirect jobs; updated figures 2,700 direct and 9,000 contractors, 97% Nigerian) · large tax contributions. Against: registered in Bermuda so less tax · Bodo oil spills in Ogoniland · 42,000 residents sued · contamination 1,000× higher · gas flaring · Niger Delta Avengers.

Nigeria — aid: 60% (100 million) on under US$1/day · receives 6% of African aid = 0.8% of GNI · Christian Aid: 360,000 given life-saving health care, 1,000 trained · UK DfID health and HIV programme · IMF £3.4bn post-Covid · problems: corruption, political strings, dependence.

Nigeria — environment and quality of life: 96% of forests destroyed · ~40 oil spills · 94% exposed to high air pollution · 10,000 tonnes of waste a day · e-waste imported from Europe · life expectancy +9 years 2015–2019 · safe water 46% → 85% (1990–2019) · 60% still in poverty · 30 years ago level with Malaysia and Singapore.

UK — de-industrialisation: decline of coal mining, shipbuilding, steel · causes: mechanisation, exhausted raw materials, loss of markets, NEE competition · negative multiplier effect · North East England worst hit · skills mismatch.

UK — globalisation: migration fills skills gaps · less manufacturing (cheaper imports from China) · widening inequality · outsourcing · 1–2% growth a year from trade · foreign investment · cheaper goods.

UK — post-industrial: 80% tertiary, 1.7% research · 1.3 million in IT · digital turnover +4.5% (2016–17) v GDP +1.7%, 2.6× faster · London tech raised £9bn 2015–18 · UK = 5% of global high-growth tech workers · science parks employ ~75,000, on the edge of university cities · Southampton Science Park opened 1986, near the M3 · 21% of South Cambridgeshire in hi-tech.

Torr Quarry: 2.5 km² limestone quarry in Somerset · £15 million a year to the local economy · 80 hectares landscaped · Somerset Wildlife Trust creating biodiverse-rich landscapes. Nissan: 10 wind turbines (6.6 MW), 19,000 solar panels, CO₂ −22.4% since 2005, SASMI training academy.

UK — rural and regional: Outer Hebrides population −50% since 1901 · A303 widening £2bn · Crossrail £19bn · Liverpool2 £400m, 5,000 jobs · Heathrow runway £19bn, £61bn boost, 75,000 jobs · 43 Enterprise Zones · one LEP: £1bn invested, 11,000 jobs · Commonwealth 53 states, 2.2 billion citizens.

subsections.heading: Quotes and figures to learn
subsections.html:
Section B is the most figure-dependent part of the paper, and the 2023 report says the best 9-mark answers "used Nigeria and had good place specific detail linked to Shell". The front of each card names the case study and what the figure measures; the back says what you use it to argue.

Development gap — wealth and health34% of global wealth is held in North America; 400,000 people died of malaria in 2019; Nigeria's infant mortality is 94 per 1,000 live births against the UK's 5Used to argue: uneven development is measurable and extreme, and its consequences are wealth, health and migration — the three the spec names
Uneven development — Syria and forced migration590,000 people have fled Syria; 80% of the remaining population live below the poverty line; unemployment is 55%Used to argue: international migration is a consequence of uneven development — conflict and poverty push people out, and HIC wages and services pull them in
The limitation of every measureNigeria's GDP per head is US$3,617 in the south and US$292 in its poorest region — a twelvefold gap inside one countryUsed to argue: national averages describe nobody, which is the limitation examiners want when they ask about any single measure of development
Population structure — Japan and MexicoJapan 2020: 12% under 15, 28% over 65 (Stage 5). Mexico 2020: 45% under 15, 4% over 65 (Stage 2–3)Used to argue: the DTM stage follows from development — Japan's ageing structure requires the wealth and healthcare that produce very long life expectancy, Mexico's youthful one does not
Fairtrade — Gumutindo90% of small coffee farmers in eastern Uganda have joined the Gumutindo Co-operativeUsed to argue: Fairtrade works at scale when farmers organise — a guaranteed price plus a community premium raises income and reduces exploitation
Debt relief — the HIPCsTotal debt relief across the 19 Heavily Indebted Poor Countries was $75 billionUsed to argue: debt relief cancels existing debt rather than lending more, so repayments can be redirected into roads, clinics and schools — the distinction the examiners say most candidates miss
Microfinance — the Grameen BankThe Grameen Bank has lent $12.5 billion in total, including loans of about $200 to women to buy a phoneUsed to argue: very small loans create self-employment where banks will not lend, and successful businesses then create jobs and raise local incomes
UK aidThe UK gives 0.5% of GNI as aid, including around £300 million a year to Pakistan, where 35% of the population lives in povertyUsed to argue: aid is substantial in absolute terms but small relative to a recipient economy — Nigeria's aid is only 0.8% of its GNI, which is why aid alone cannot close the gap
Jamaica — tourism's share of the economyTourism contributed 35% of Jamaica's GDP in 2019, with 4 million visitors a year generating about $2 billion and over 50% of the country's foreign exchange earningsUsed to argue: tourism can reduce the development gap, because the tax on that income funds public spending — the multiplier effect in a named place
Jamaica — jobs and infrastructureOver 200,000 people employed directly and indirectly; a new cruise port at Falmouth and a new water treatment plant at Logwood; the Negril Marine Nature ParkUsed to argue: tourism income builds infrastructure residents also use, and gives conservation an economic value — but note that roads came late because ports and airports were prioritised
Jamaica — the limits of tourismExpenditure rose from US$128.7 million in 1975 to US$2.6 billion in 2016, yet pockets of poverty persist and wealthy areas such as Montego Bay have benefited mostUsed to argue: the counter-case for "tourism is an effective way of reducing the development gap" — growth was enormous but its distribution was uneven, and 2009 showed how exposed it is to recession abroad
Nigeria — global and regional importance2.2% of the world's oil and the 13th largest producer; around the 27th largest GDP; the 7th largest population; Nollywood is the world's second largest film industry; the largest economy and population in AfricaUsed to argue: importance in tiers — global through oil, population and film, regional through being Africa's largest economy with its third-largest manufacturing sector
Nigeria — the oil dependency figureOil accounts for 14% of GDP but 98% of export earningsUsed to argue: over-dependence on one commodity — national income rises and falls with the world oil price, which is why diversifying into manufacturing (27%) and services (53%) matters
Nigeria — the industrial shiftEmployment in agriculture has fallen 40%; manufacturing is now 27% of the economy and the fastest growing sector; services are 53%Used to argue: manufacturing stimulates development — better-paid secure jobs, local spending through the multiplier, tax revenue for services, and value added retained in Nigeria instead of exported raw
Shell in Nigeria — the case forIn Nigeria since 1958; $250,000 spent on healthcare; 3,000 scholarships to local schools; around 90% of contracts awarded to Nigerian companies; large contributions to national tax revenueUsed to argue: a TNC brings employment, local contracts, training and tax a host government could not otherwise raise — the "advantages" half of the 2022 and 2025 TNC questions
Shell in Nigeria — the case againstRegistered in Bermuda so less tax is paid; two massive oil spills at Bodo in Ogoniland, where contamination is 1,000 times higher than elsewhere; 42,000 residents took out a lawsuit; gas flaring continuesUsed to argue: the disadvantages half — profits and tax leave the country while the environmental cost stays, which is the sharpest evidence for "TNCs bring more disadvantages than advantages"
Nigeria — the environmental cost of development96% of Nigeria's forests have been destroyed; 94% of the population is exposed to high air pollution; 10,000 tonnes of waste a day, with electronic waste imported from EuropeUsed to argue: economic development has carried a severe environmental cost — the "but at a cost to the environment" half of the 2023 9-marker
Nigeria — the quality of life gainsLife expectancy rose by 9 years between 2015 and 2019; access to safe water rose from 46% to 85% between 1990 and 2019Used to argue: development has genuinely improved quality of life — the figures that stop a Nigeria answer being one-sided and cap-limited to Level 2
Nigeria — the comparison that makes the judgement60% of the population still live in poverty, and thirty years ago Nigeria was at a similar stage of development to Malaysia and Singapore, both of which have moved much further aheadUsed to argue: the conclusion to "evaluate the effects of economic development on quality of life" — growth happened, but corruption and oil dependence meant it delivered far less than it should have
UK — the post-industrial economy80% of the UK economy is tertiary and 1.7% is research; 1.3 million people work in IT; digital technology turnover grew 4.5% against GDP's 1.7%, 2.6 times faster than the overall economyUsed to argue: the UK is moving towards a post-industrial economy — services and research replacing the manufacturing lost to de-industrialisation
UK — science parksScience parks employ around 75,000 people in the UK; Southampton Science Park opened in 1986 close to the M3; 21% of the population of South Cambridgeshire works in hi-tech industriesUsed to argue: the named examples for the post-industrial economy and for the OS-map "why is this a good site?" question — motorway access, a university next door, an attractive environment
Torr Quarry — industry and the environmentA 2.5 km² limestone quarry in Somerset contributing £15 million a year to the local economy, with 80 hectares landscaped and the Somerset Wildlife Trust creating biodiverse-rich landscapesUsed to argue: modern industrial development can be made more environmentally sustainable — the extractive-industry example to set beside Nissan's turbines and solar panels
Nissan — sustainable manufacturing10 wind turbines generating 6.6 MW and 19,000 photovoltaic panels; CO₂ reduced 22.4% since 2005; electric and hybrid cars; the SASMI skills academyUsed to argue: "to what extent are modern industrial developments environmentally sustainable?" — substantially, though the carbon footprint of construction and employee commuting limits the claim
UK — rural population declineThe population of the Outer Hebrides has fallen by 50% since 1901Used to argue: population decline closes schools and shops, raises the per-head cost of services and leaves an ageing community — the social and economic changes the 2025 6-marker wanted
UK — transport investmentA303 widening £2 billion; Crossrail £19 billion; Liverpool2 £400 million and 5,000 jobs; the Heathrow third runway £19 billion to build, a £61 billion economic boost and 75,000 new jobsUsed to argue: improvements in transport and infrastructure shape the economic future of different parts of the UK — the figures the 2024 9-marker needed
UK — closing the north–south divide43 Enterprise Zones across the UK; one Local Enterprise Partnership attracted £1 billion of investment and created 11,000 jobs; plus devolution, HS2 and northern business parksUsed to argue: regional differences are being addressed, but house prices, earnings, life expectancy and unemployment still diverge — so "evaluate the success" means partly
UK — the CommonwealthA voluntary association of 53 independent and equal sovereign states, mostly former territories of the British Empire, home to 2.2 billion citizens, with no legal obligation to one anotherUsed to argue: the UK's place in the wider world after leaving the EU — the Commonwealth offers scale but not the single market's legal integration, which is the tension the 2022 6-marker set up

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
DevelopmentThe progress of a country in terms of economic growth, the use of technology and human welfare
Development gapThe difference in standards of living and wellbeing between the world's richest and poorest countries
Gross national income (GNI)Total national income divided by the population, taking into account not just goods and services but also income earned from investments overseas
Human Development Index (HDI)GDP per capita, life expectancy and adult literacy combined into a single index figure, allowing comparison between countries
Birth rateThe number of births in a year per 1,000 of the total population
Death rateThe number of deaths in a year per 1,000 of the total population
Infant mortalityThe average number of deaths of infants under 1 year of age, per 1,000 live births, per year
Life expectancyThe average number of years a person might be expected to live
Literacy rateThe percentage of people who have basic reading and writing skills
Demographic Transition ModelA model showing how populations should change over time in terms of their birth rates, death rates and total population size
Natural increaseBirth rate minus death rate
Industrial structureThe relative proportion of the workforce employed in the different sectors — primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary
GlobalisationThe process which has created a more connected world, with increases in the movements of goods (trade) and people worldwide
TradeThe buying and selling of goods and services between countries
FairtradeWhen producers in LICs are given a better price for the goods they produce, which improves income and reduces exploitation
Debt reliefCancelling money owed, so that more significant investment can be made in development projects — not a new loan
Microfinance loansVery small loans given to people in LICs to help them start a small business
Intermediate technologySimple, easily learned and maintained technology used in economic activities serving local needs in LICs
International aidMoney, goods and services given by one government or a multilateral institution such as the World Bank or IMF to help the quality of life and economy of another country
Transnational Corporation (TNC)A company that has operations in more than one country — factories, offices, research and development, shops
Quality of lifeThe standard of health, comfort and happiness experienced by a person or group
De-industrialisationThe decline of a country's traditional manufacturing industry due to exhaustion of raw materials, loss of markets and competition from NEEs
Post-industrial economyThe economy of many economically developed countries where most employment is now in service industries
Service (tertiary) industriesEconomic activities that provide services — commercial, professional, social, entertainment and personal
Science and business parksBusiness parks are purpose-built areas of offices and warehouses, often at the edge of a city on a main road; science parks are located near university sites, with high-tech industries and research carried out in co-operation with the university
Information technologiesComputer, internet, mobile phone and satellite technologies, especially those that speed up communication and the flow of information
InfrastructureThe basic physical systems of a country — roads, railways, ports, airports, power, water and communications
North–south divide (UK)Economic and cultural differences between southern England and northern England, with clear differences in health conditions, house prices, earnings and political influence
European UnionAn international organisation of European countries formed to reduce trade barriers and increase cooperation, with citizens able to live and work in any member country without a work permit
CommonwealthA voluntary association of 53 independent and equal sovereign states, mostly former territories of the British Empire, home to 2.2 billion citizens, with no legal obligation to one another
Multiplier effectWhen new investment or employment generates further knock-on growth — wages are spent locally, so other businesses grow and tax revenue rises

subsections.heading: Wording that costs marks
subsections.html:
Don't writeWrite
GNI is how much money a country hastotal national income divided by the population, including income earned from investments overseas
birth rate isn't a very good measuregive the reason it misleads — "it is affected by culture and religion as well as development, so it can fall for reasons unrelated to wealth"
HDI measures developmentHDI combines GDP per capita, life expectancy and adult literacy — the measure that "combines income, life expectancy and education levels"
