drill.intro:
What each command word actually wants

Section B is Question 02 on Paper 2 — compulsory, around 30 marks, and the home of the paper's maths. The AQA command words have fixed meanings, taken here from the school's command word table and exam technique guide.

  • Describe — say what you see. Trends, extremities, data, anomalies. No reasons.
  • Explain — say why or how. Causes and processes, developed with because, this means that, as a result. Make explicit reference to the figure if there is one.
  • Suggest — a reasonable explanation you have worked out from the figure plus your own knowledge; a broad range of valid answers is accepted, so long as each is developed.
  • Outline — a brief but developed point; on a 2-marker, point + development, and on a 3-marker, a three-step chain.
  • Discuss — present key points about different sides of an argument. Open with one side, make multiple points to support it, make counter-arguments, finish with a clear conclusion that links back to the question. It does not have to be balanced.
  • Assess — a judgement of the size or significance of the problem. Which factor is most significant? How large a problem is this? State which factors are most to least important in the conclusion and justify the choice.
  • Evaluate — judge from evidence, weighing up both sides, and rank the arguments from most to least important or convincing. Use however and on the other hand.
  • To what extent — the same as evaluate, but the conclusion must land on the ladder: definitely, mostly, partly, slightly, not at all.
  • Maths. 10% of the paper's marks are mathematical. Mean, median, interquartile range, range, percentage change, best-fit lines, plotting and graph completion all appear. Read the rounding instruction — "to one decimal place", "to the nearest whole percentage" — because the 2022 and 2023 reports both say the commonest error was not rounding. Show your working: if the answer is wrong but the method is right you still get a mark.

Twelve questions in the real spread: two short, four 4-markers, four 6-markers and two 9-markers. The 6- and 9-mark answers are written as plans, because AQA marks them in levels — treat the mark points as a coverage target rather than a tick list.

modules.title: Resource Management
modules.standfirst: Section C of Paper 2 Challenges in the Human Environment — the global distribution of food, water and energy, then the UK's own food, water and energy situation in Question 03 (compulsory), followed by the energy option in Question 06: global demand and supply, the impacts of energy insecurity, the strategies for increasing supply including the Camisea gas project in Peru, and sustainable energy including the Chambamontera micro-hydro scheme. Answer Question 03 and Question 06 only — the school's first rule is "don't answer the wrong questions".

subsections.html:
What they actually ask

Every Question 03 and Question 06 question from the June 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 papers, with marks. Question 03 wanders freely across food, water and energy, so revise all three at overview level even though you only sit the Energy option.

  • Q06 — rising demand and energy insecurity — in all five papers: the impacts, the political and physical factors, and conflict.
  • Q06 — global energy patterns and data skills — 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025: plot, complete, describe a trend, describe a distribution, calculate a percentage.
  • Q06 — the 6-marker on increasing supply — fossil fuel extraction or renewables in 2019, 2023 and 2024. Camisea answers all three.
  • Q06 — sustainable energy — Chambamontera in 2022, and energy conservation in homes, workplaces and transport in 2025.
  • Q03 — UK food — in all five papers, with 6-markers on changing demand and the carbon footprint in 2023 and 2024.
  • Q03 — UK water and UK energy — water 6-markers in 2019, 2022 and 2025; the changing energy mix in 2023 and 2024 (and 2018 on the school's list).

Examiners' refrain: develop the figure rather than lifting it, write energy insecurity not deficit, and practise the percentage calculation.

Every Q03 and Q06 question from 2019–2025, with the exact wordings

Every Question 03 and Question 06 question from the June 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 papers, with marks. Question 03 wanders freely across food, water and energy, so revise all three at overview level even though you only sit the Energy option.

  • Q03 — the global resource overview — "Which of the following continents has the largest number of countries with a score of 0–0.57?" on a map of women's well-being (2022, 1 mark); "Calculate the median well-being score for the nine lowest scoring countries… to two decimal places" and "Suggest one reason for higher well-being scores in a country" (2025, 2 and 1 marks).
  • Q03 — UK food — "Calculate the percentage increase in mango imports into the UK between 2012 and 2016" and "State one environmental effect of the increase" (2019, 2 and 1 marks); "Outline one advantage of sourcing food locally in the UK" (2019, 2 marks); "Explain how changing demand for food has affected the UK's carbon footprint" (2022, 4 marks); "'Trying to reduce the carbon footprint of food in the UK creates opportunities and challenges.' Use Figure 11a and Figure 11b to explain this statement" (2023, 6 marks); "Discuss how changing demand for food in the UK creates opportunities and challenges" (2024, 6 marks); "Explain how changing demand for food has affected organic farming in the UK" (2025, 2 marks).
  • Q03 — UK water — "Discuss the challenges of managing water quality and pollution in the UK. Use Figure 10 and your own understanding" (2019, 6 marks); "Suggest how poor water supply may affect social well-being" (2022, 3 marks); "Discuss the challenges of the changing demand for water in the UK. Use Figure 11 and your own understanding" (2022, 6 marks); "'Managing water quality and water pollution in the UK is a significant challenge.' To what extent do you agree with this statement? Use Figure 12 and your own understanding" (2025, 6 marks).
  • Q03 — UK energy — "What is solar energy?" (2023, 1 mark); "Suggest how the energy mix used to generate the UK's electricity has changed in the last 30 years. Use Figure 10 and your own understanding" (2023, 2 marks); "Explain why demand for different energy sources has changed in the UK" (2023, 3 marks); "Calculate the percentage change in gas prices shown in Figure 12" (2024, 2 marks); "Give one reason for reduced domestic supplies of gas in the UK" (2024, 1 mark); "Why might increasing gas prices mean that renewables become increasingly [important]?" (2024, 2 marks). The school's list adds "Using Figure 10 and your own understanding, discuss the issues arising from the UK's changing energy mix" (2018, 6 marks).
  • Q06 — global patterns of energy — "Plot the following data on to Figure 14", "Which country is identified by the following data?", "Describe the relationship between GNI and energy consumption shown in Figure 14" and "Outline one or more reasons for the link between GNI and energy consumption" (2022, 1, 1, 2 and 3 marks); "Describe the distribution of countries which produced 0–20% of their electricity from renewable sources in 2019" (2023, 2 marks); "Complete Figure 16 using the following data for North America", "What is the difference in energy consumption between Europe and [Africa]?" and "Using Figure 16, describe the trend for Asia 1980–2020" (2024, 2, 1 and 2 marks); "Complete Figure 15 using the following data" and "Name one country where 5–9.9% of households could not afford to heat their home" (2025, 2 and 1 marks).
  • Q06 — rising demand and energy insecurity — "Suggest how energy supply issues can lead to conflict" (2019, 3 marks); "Give two impacts of energy insecurity" (2022, 2 marks); "What is energy insecurity?" and "Explain how political factors can affect energy supply" (2023, 1 and 2 marks); "Outline the link between increasing economic development and rising energy [consumption]" (2024, 3 marks); "Outline one or more ways that physical factors can affect energy supply" (2025, 3 marks).
  • Q06 — increasing supply, and the fossil fuel example — "State two alternatives to large solar energy farms suggested in Figure 15" (2019, 2 marks); "'Extraction of fossil fuels can bring both advantages and disadvantages.' Explain this statement using an example you have studied" (2019, 6 marks); "To what extent can wind and tidal power and other strategies increase energy supply? Use Figure 17 and your own knowledge" (2023, 6 marks); "Explain how the extraction of a fossil fuel has both advantages and disadvantages" (2024, 6 marks). Camisea is the answer to all of these.
  • Q06 — sustainable energy — "Suggest how energy supplies have been made more sustainable. Use an example of a local renewable energy scheme in an LIC/NEE" (2022, 6 marks) — Chambamontera; "Explain how strategies to conserve energy in homes and workplaces and in transport can lead to increased sustainability of energy supply" (2025, 6 marks).

What the examiners keep saying. On the 6-markers (2023 06.5): "many students merely lifted information from the resource. As a result, they wrote a lot without developing their ideas and left little room to discuss other examples… Understanding of the reliability of tides and wind power allowed appropriate discussions in the best responses." On the definitions (2023 06.3): "most correct unless students defined energy deficit" — the mark scheme wants insecurity. On "political factors" (2023 06.4): "war and conflict were the common choices, with many answers reflecting the current situation in Ukraine". On the distribution questions (2023 04.2, 05.2): "many were let down by poor locational knowledge". And on the maths, every year: "a significant minority were unable to perform a percentage calculation".

How Section C is built, in full

Section C is in two parts and the rubric matters. Question 03 is compulsory and covers the resource overview plus the UK's food, water and energy — so you can be asked about all three whichever option you sit. Then you answer one of Question 04 (Food), Question 05 (Water) or Question 06 (Energy). Your class does Energy. The structure of Q06 is almost identical every year: a graph or map data question, a 1-mark count or definition, a 2-mark describe, a 2–3 mark "explain how X affects energy supply", and a 6-marker at the end. The 2023 examiner's report confirms there is "an even spread of answers to the 3 options", so nothing about Energy is easier or harder — but Q06 is where Camisea and Chambamontera earn their marks.

subsections.heading: What a resource is, and why food, water and energy
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.3.1 · Resource Management Revision Mat; AQA List of Key Terms

  • A resource — something human society attaches value to because of its usefulness.
  • Resource management — the control and monitoring of resources so that they are not depleted or exhausted.
  • The three the spec names — food, water and energy, because each is needed for economic and social well-being.
More detail

A resource is something which human society attaches value to due to its usefulness. Resource management is the control and monitoring of resources so that they do not become depleted or exhausted.

The spec's framing is that all three resources are "significant for economic and social well-being", so the 1- and 3-mark questions at the start of Question 03 are usually about why, not where:

  • Food — calories are the fuel for our bodies, needed to work and to enjoy ourselves. Without them, undernutrition follows: people "do not eat enough nutrients to cover their needs for energy and growth, or to maintain a healthy immune system".
  • Water — we drink it to survive, and we also need it to wash, dispose of wastes, grow and process food, and for industrial manufacturing. Poor supply therefore affects health, education (time spent collecting water), income and dignity at once — which is what the 2022 3-marker on "social well-being" wanted.
  • Energy — needed to keep ourselves warm, construct houses, transport goods and people, process food and power machinery.

The 2025 paper opened Question 03 with a map of well-being for women, and the mark scheme's accepted reasons for a high score are worth knowing because they are generic resource geography: the country is an HIC with high standards of living; most high scorers are in northern Europe with a temperate climate and few natural hazards; they are stable democracies; and almost all are conflict free.

  • Food — calories are the fuel our bodies need in order to work and to enjoy ourselves.
  • Water — needed to drink to survive, and to wash, dispose of waste, grow and process food, and manufacture.
  • Energy — needed to keep warm, build houses, transport goods, process food and power machinery.

subsections.heading: Global inequalities in the distribution of food, water and energy
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.3.1 · Resource Management Revision Mat; Energy Workbook pp. 5–7

  • Food surplus — large areas of Europe, Asia and North and South America produce more than they consume.
  • Food deficit — most of sub-Saharan Africa, plus India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan; 50 countries face food insecurity.
  • Water shortage — Africa, the Middle East and Australia are prone to shortage and drought.
  • Energy consumption — highest in HICs; North America is the clearest cluster of very high per-capita use.
More detail

Food. Large areas of Europe, Asia and North and South America produce a food surplus. In a large proportion of countries in sub-Saharan Africa there is a food deficit, and this is also the case in some Asian countries such as India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan. Around 50 countries face food insecurity, and more than 800 million people live every day with hunger or food insecurity.

Water. Africa, the Middle East and Australia are prone to water shortages and drought. Europe, South East Asia, northern South America and northern North America have a water surplus. A water surplus exists where supply is greater than demand; a water deficit where demand is greater than supply.

Energy. Consumption per person is highest in HICs — North America, with the USA and Canada, has some of the highest levels in the world. The key relationships the 2022 scatter-graph question tested are:

  • GNI and energy consumption are positively correlated — richer countries use more energy per person, because they own more appliances, drive more, heat and cool buildings, and run more industry.
  • Consumption and reserves do not match. The countries holding the largest fossil fuel reserves are often not the largest consumers, so energy has to be traded — which is the root of energy insecurity and of energy conflict.
  • Energy insecurity is almost universal. The workbook's framing: high levels of insecurity are experienced by both HICs and LICs/NEEs; the countries with the lowest insecurity tend to be those rich in resources; insecurity can occur at both high and low levels of consumption; and even a country with a high supply can be insecure if demand is higher still.

The Arctic is the frontier: 30% of the world's unexploited natural gas is thought to lie there, which is why the region is becoming politically contested as the ice retreats.

  • Water surplus — Europe, South East Asia, northern South America and northern North America.
  • Reserves and consumption do not match — the countries that use most energy are rarely the countries that hold the fossil fuels.

✗ "Africa has less water than Europe." — the 2023 report says the distribution questions were "hampered by a lack of ability to describe distribution and poor locational knowledge".
✓ Describe it properly: name continents and regions, give the general pattern, then the anomaly. "Countries with very low renewable generation are concentrated in the Middle East and North Africa, with a second cluster in eastern Europe; the exception is Norway, which is surrounded by low-renewable countries but generates almost all its electricity from hydro."

subsections.heading: The UK's food situation
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.3.1 · Resource Management Revision Mat; Case Study Summary Booklet quiz facts

  • Four demand changes — high-value exotic exports, all-year seasonal food, organic produce, and a bigger carbon footprint.
  • Imports — 12% of the food eaten in the UK comes from LICs, which raises food miles and carbon.
  • Agriculture's own footprint — 12% of the UK's total greenhouse gas emissions come from farming.
  • Agribusiness — larger farms, hedgerows removed, more mechanisation and chemicals, so yields rise.
More detail
  • Imports — 12% of the food eaten in the UK comes from LICs, which raises food miles and the carbon footprint.
  • Local sourcing — cuts food miles and supports the local economy, but limits choice and seasonality.
  • Organic — demand is rising because it is seen as better for the environment and healthier, so organic area is expanding.

The UK's changing demand for food — the four strands

  • High-value exotic foods. Growing demand for high-value food exports such as Madagascan vanilla and specialist honey. These travel long distances, raising food miles — the distance covered supplying food to consumers — and so the carbon footprint of the UK diet.
  • All-year seasonal food. Growing demand for foods such as strawberries out of season, which can only be grown in the UK in summer; the rest of the year they are flown or shipped in, or grown in heated glasshouses.
  • Organic produce. Growing demand because it is seen as better for the environment and healthier. Organic produce is grown with environmentally and animal-friendly methods: artificial fertilisers are banned and farmers build fertile soil by rotating crops and using compost, manure and clover, with no synthetic additives such as pesticides and dyes. So UK farmers convert land to organic, which lowers yields per hectare but commands a higher price.
  • Agribusiness. The application of business skills to agriculture. It increases food production because farming takes place on a greater scale: farm size increases as hedgerows are removed when farms are combined, and the greater use of mechanisation and chemicals raises crop yields. The cost is habitat loss and chemical runoff.
  • The figures to quote. 12% of the food eaten in the UK comes from LICs. 12% of the UK's total greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture. Around 50 countries face food insecurity.
  • Local sourcing. A method of food production and distribution that is local rather than national or international — food is grown and harvested close to consumers' homes and distributed over much shorter distances. Advantages: far fewer food miles and so a lower carbon footprint; fresher produce; money stays in the local economy, supporting farmers and shops; and consumers know how it was produced. Disadvantages: limited choice, strictly seasonal, and often more expensive per unit.

subsections.heading: The UK's water situation
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.3.1 · Resource Management Revision Mat; 2019, 2022 and 2025 Q03.4

  • The mismatch — rainfall is greatest in the west; the greatest demand is in the driest part, the south-east.
  • So water is transferred — from areas of surplus in the west and north to the deficit south-east.
  • Rising demand — 310 litres per person a day, and demand is expected to exceed supply by 2034.
  • Pollution effects — pesticides kill wildlife, fertilisers cause eutrophication, drinking water is polluted, fishing and tourism lose money.
More detail
  • The UK has enough water — the problem is that rainfall patterns do not match demand.
  • So water is transferred — from areas of surplus in the west and north to the deficit areas of the south-east.
  • Rising demand — average UK consumption is 310 litres per person a day, and demand is expected to exceed supply by 2034.
  • Pollution causes — agricultural chemicals and pesticides, oil from boats, untreated industrial waste, transport runoff, sewage.

The UK's water — supply, demand and quality

  • Why transfer is needed. The UK receives enough water to meet its demands, but rainfall patterns do not match demand. Rainfall is greatest in the west of the country while the east receives less, and the greatest demand comes from the south-east, which is the driest area in the UK and has a water deficit. Water therefore has to be transferred from the west to the south-east.
  • Rising demand. Average daily consumption in the UK is 310 litres per person, and demand is expected to exceed supply by 2034. The drivers: a rising population increasingly concentrated in the south; more water-using appliances — UK dishwasher ownership rose from 22% in 1998 to 49% in 2018 — and an increasing trend for UK houses to have more than one bathroom.
  • Causes of water pollution. Chemicals and pesticides from agriculture; oil from boats and ships; untreated industrial waste; oil and heavy metals from transport; sewage pumped into rivers and seas.
  • Effects of water pollution. Pesticides kill wildlife; fertilisers cause eutrophication — nutrients from farmland and sewage produce algae which reduce oxygen levels in the water; drinking water is polluted; and fishermen and the tourist industry suffer economic losses.
  • The scale of the problem, from the exam figures. The 2019 paper quoted the Environment Agency naming population growth, climate change and plastic pollution as the main future threats to water quality. The 2025 paper quoted MPs: "No river in England is clean" — agriculture and water companies have caused raw sewage, microplastics and farm waste to be present in all of England's rivers, along with car tyre particles, oils and wet wipes, so people using rivers are now at risk.
  • Management strategies. Water transfer schemes, which attempt to make up for shortages by constructing systems of canals, pipes and dredging to move water from one river basin to another; groundwater management to regulate levels, pollution and use; limits on over-abstraction, which is when water is used faster than it is replaced; and water conservation — metering, efficient appliances and grey water recycling.

subsections.heading: The UK's energy situation and its changing energy mix
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.3.1 · Resource Management Revision Mat; Case Study Summary Booklet quiz facts; 2023 Q03.2–03.3, 2024 Q03.1–03.3

  • The shift — away from fossil fuels and (slightly) nuclear, towards renewables.
  • The figures — 47% of UK energy was "green" in 2020; 35% of UK energy was imported in 2019.
  • Why fossil fuels fell — their environmental impact, and declining domestic supplies as North Sea reserves are depleted.
  • The costs of renewables — £22bn for a new nuclear station and £4m for a commercial wind turbine.
More detail
  • Why renewables rose — environmental benefits and the UK's legally binding carbon reduction targets.
  • Cost drives the switch — rising gas prices make renewables relatively cheaper, so investment moves.
  • The costs of renewables — £22bn for a new nuclear station, £4m for a commercial wind turbine, and high set-up costs generally.

The UK's changing energy mix — the facts

  • What the energy mix is. The range of energy sources of a region or country, both renewable and non-renewable.
  • The change. There is a shift from fossil fuels and nuclear to renewable energy sources. Nuclear energy has fallen slightly. The use of fossil fuels has decreased because of their environmental impact and declining supplies within the UK. There has been an increase in the use of renewables because of their environmental benefits and because they help the UK meet its targets to reduce carbon emissions.
  • The figures. In 2020, 47% of UK energy was "green". In 2019, 35% of UK energy was imported. The target for UK renewables by 2030 is 65%.
  • Why domestic gas supply has fallen. North Sea reserves are being depleted and the remaining fields are harder and more expensive to exploit, so the UK imports more — which exposes it to world prices and to the politics of supplier countries.
  • Why rising gas prices favour renewables. Once gas is expensive, the electricity it generates is expensive too, so wind and solar — which have high set-up costs but almost no fuel cost — become cheaper per unit by comparison; and expensive imported gas is an energy security risk, so there is a political incentive to replace it.
  • The economic issues with renewables. High set-up costs — a new nuclear power station costs around £22 billion to build and a commercial wind turbine around £4 million; tourism can decline where environments become less attractive; and low profitability is a concern.
  • The environmental issues with renewables. They are considered unattractive; wind turbines can affect wildlife, especially birds and bats; in upland areas large areas of land are flooded for reservoirs behind HEP dams; and biomass reduces biodiversity where monoculture crops replace mixed habitat.

✗ "The UK uses more renewables now because they are better for the environment." — one reason, undeveloped; the 2023 3-marker wanted the demand for different sources to change, with reasons.
✓ Three linked reasons: fossil fuels are declining domestically and their emissions drive climate change, so demand has fallen; renewables are needed to meet the UK's carbon targets — 65% by 2030 — so demand has risen; and because rising gas prices make gas-fired electricity expensive, renewables become comparatively cheaper, so investment follows.

subsections.heading: Why global energy demand is rising, and global supply
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.3.4 · Energy Workbook pp. 9–10; 2024 Q06.4

  • Three drivers — economic development, population growth, and technology.
  • Economic development — industry, car ownership, appliances, heating and cooling all rise with income.
  • Population growth — more people need more homes, food, transport and goods, so total demand rises.
  • Technology also raises supply — fracking, deep-water drilling and Arctic exploration reach reserves that were previously inaccessible.
More detail

Energy consumption is increasing due to economic development, rising population and technology.

Economic development. As a country develops, industry expands and manufacturing is energy-intensive; incomes rise so people buy cars, fridges, washing machines, air conditioning and electronics; cities grow and need lighting, transport and construction; and services such as hospitals and offices need continuous power. This is why the 2022 scatter graph of GNI against energy consumption showed a clear positive relationship — the richer the country, the more energy each person uses. The 2024 3-marker asked for exactly this link.

Population growth. A larger population needs more homes to heat and light, more food to grow and process, more transport and more manufactured goods, so total national demand rises even where efficiency improves.

Technology — the positive and negative sides. Negatively, technology creates demand that did not exist: more devices per person, data centres, and the electrification of heating and transport. Positively, technology improves efficiency — LED lighting, better insulation, more efficient engines and smart controls all reduce the energy needed for the same output — and it increases supply, because fracking, deep-water drilling and polar exploration make reserves accessible that previously were not. 30% of the world's unexploited natural gas is in the Arctic.

The four factors affecting energy supply, which the spec names and the exam asks about one at a time:

  • Physical factors. Geology determines where fossil fuels and geothermal heat exist; climate determines where solar, wind and HEP work — the UK's position in the mid-latitude westerlies suits wind, and upland relief with high rainfall suits HEP; a coastline with a large tidal range suits tidal power. The 2025 3-marker asked for these directly.
  • Cost of exploitation and production. Deep, remote or small reserves cost more to extract than they are worth, so they stay in the ground until prices rise. Set-up costs for renewables are high — £22 billion for a nuclear station, £4 million for a wind turbine.
  • Technology. A reserve is only a resource if the technology exists to reach it. Fracking opened shale gas; improved turbine design made offshore wind viable.
  • Political factors. Governments decide whether to allow fracking or build nuclear; international agreements set carbon targets; and conflict interrupts supply — the 2023 examiner's report notes that most students answered this with "the current situation in Ukraine and the impact on Russian energy supplies".
  • The evidence — GNI and energy consumption per person are positively correlated across the world's countries.
  • Population growth — more people need more homes, food, transport and goods, so total demand rises even if per-head use does not.
  • Technology cuts both ways — it creates new demand (devices, data centres) and reduces it (efficiency, LEDs, insulation).

subsections.heading: Energy insecurity and its impacts
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.3.4 · Energy Workbook pp. 12–13; AQA List of Key Terms; 2019 Q06.4, 2022 Q06.6, 2023 Q06.3

  • Energy insecurity — when supply cannot meet demand reliably or affordably; it is not an "energy deficit".
  • Industrial output falls — factories cannot run, so production, exports and jobs are lost.
  • Food production suffers — no power for irrigation, processing or refrigeration, so yields and food security fall.
  • Exploration of difficult environments and conflict — insecurity pushes countries into fragile areas and into disputes over supply.
More detail
  • Energy security — the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price.
  • Prices rise and fuel poverty follows — in 2021 a measurable share of European households could not afford to heat their homes.

The impacts of energy insecurity

  • Industrial output. Manufacturing needs continuous, affordable power; blackouts and price spikes stop production, so output, exports and employment all fall and the economy shrinks.
  • Food production. Energy runs irrigation pumps, fertiliser manufacture, farm machinery, food processing and refrigeration. Energy insecurity therefore becomes food insecurity, and in LICs it can tip into undernutrition.
  • Industry and services. Hospitals, schools and water treatment all need power; in Rio, favela residents illegally tap the grid precisely because supply is unreliable, which is dangerous as well as insecure.
  • Rising prices and fuel poverty. Shortage raises prices, and households spend a greater share of income on heating and transport. The 2025 paper's figure measured the percentage of households in each country that could not afford to heat their homes in 2021 — a direct measure of insecurity in HICs as well as LICs.
  • Exploration of difficult and environmentally sensitive areas. Insecurity makes expensive, risky extraction worthwhile — deep-water drilling, tar sands, the Arctic (which holds 30% of the world's unexploited natural gas) and tropical rainforest, as at Camisea in Peru.
  • Conflict. Where supply and demand are in different countries, energy becomes political. Countries fight or threaten to fight over reserves and over the routes that carry them; a supplier can shut off a pipeline to apply pressure; disputed territory such as the Arctic or the South China Sea becomes contested because of what lies beneath it; and inside a country, extraction can provoke armed resistance — the Niger Delta is the clearest case.

✗ "Energy insecurity is when a country doesn't have enough energy." — the 2023 report says the only common error was defining energy deficit instead.
✓ "Energy insecurity is when energy availability is not enough to ensure the population enjoys good health, livelihood and earnings — the opposite of energy security, which is the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price." Note the two halves: uninterrupted and affordable.

subsections.heading: Strategies to increase energy supply — renewable and non-renewable
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.3.4 · Energy Workbook pp. 15–17; Resource Management Revision Mat; 2023 Q06.5

  • Renewables — biomass, wind, HEP, tidal, geothermal, wave, solar. Learn one advantage and one disadvantage each.
  • Reliability is the discriminator — tidal is predictable, HEP and geothermal are constant, wind and solar are intermittent.
  • Fossil fuels — still needed now, because renewables cannot yet meet demand, but finite and polluting.
  • Nuclear — reliable, low-carbon and high-output, but £22 billion a station, with waste that stays radioactive for millennia.
More detail

Non-renewable energy in the short term. Fossil fuels will continue to supply the majority of world energy for some time, because the infrastructure — power stations, pipelines, refineries, vehicle fleets — already exists, because renewables cannot yet meet total demand and are intermittent, and because fossil fuels remain cheaper in many places. Known reserves are still substantial and new technology keeps adding to them.

Non-renewable energy in the long term. They are finite, so supplies will eventually be exhausted; extraction becomes progressively more expensive as the easy reserves are used; and their emissions drive climate change, so international agreements and national targets — the UK's 65% renewables by 2030 — will force them out regardless of what remains underground.

Nuclear power. The energy released by a nuclear reaction, using fuel made from mined and processed uranium to make steam and generate electricity. It is reliable, very high output and almost carbon-free in operation, which is why the UK retains it. The concerns are the cost — around £22 billion for a new station — the radioactive waste, which remains dangerous for thousands of years and has no permanent disposal solution, the risk of accident, and the link to weapons technology.

The 2023 6-marker, "to what extent can wind and tidal power and other strategies increase energy supply?" The examiner's report is explicit about what separated the best answers: "understanding of the reliability of tides and wind power allowed appropriate discussions". So the argument is that tidal is predictable and wind is not, which is why wind needs backup capacity while tidal does not — and that the phrase "and other strategies" is an instruction to bring in nuclear, biomass, solar, HEP and fossil fuels rather than writing only about the figure.

  • Two families — renewable (not diminished by use) and non-renewable (finite, so depleted by use).
  • Fossil fuels in the short term — still needed, because renewables cannot yet meet demand and the infrastructure exists.
  • Fossil fuels in the long term — finite and polluting, so they must be replaced; the question is how fast.

The renewable sources — advantages and disadvantages

SourceAdvantagesDisadvantages
WindNo fuel cost and no emissions in operation; the UK's position in the mid-latitude westerlies makes it among the windiest countries in Europe; offshore turbines are out of sight of most peopleIntermittent — no output when the wind drops or blows too hard; considered visually unattractive; can affect birds and bats; £4 million per commercial turbine
SolarNo fuel cost, no emissions, scalable from a single roof to a desert farm, and ideal for remote off-grid use — 150 panels on roofs in Rio's Santa Marta favelaIntermittent and seasonal, and weakest in winter when UK demand peaks; large farms take agricultural land, which is why conservation groups in the 2019 paper's Balearics article preferred rooftop panels and undersea cables instead
Hydro-electric (HEP)Reliable and controllable — output can be raised to match demand within minutes; very long-lived; the reservoir also stores waterIn upland areas large areas of land are flooded behind the dam, displacing people and drowning habitat; huge construction cost and carbon footprint; depends on relief and rainfall
TidalPredictable — tides are known years in advance, which is its decisive advantage over wind and solar; very high energy density; the UK has one of the world's largest tidal rangesOnly works where the tidal range is large; barrages damage estuary ecosystems and bird feeding grounds; very high capital cost; generates only around the tides, not continuously
WaveThe UK's Atlantic coast has among the best wave resources in Europe; no emissionsStill largely experimental; equipment must survive storms; output varies with weather
GeothermalEnergy generated by heat stored deep in the Earth — constant, 24 hours a day, with a tiny surface footprintOnly economic where hot rock is near the surface, so geographically very restricted; drilling is expensive
BiomassRenewable organic material — wood, crops or waste — burned directly or processed into biofuels such as ethanol and methane; the carbon released was recently absorbed, and it uses waste; Brazil cut petrol consumption by 40% by introducing bio-ethanolReduces biodiversity where monoculture replaces mixed habitat; competes with food crops for land; still produces air pollution when burned

subsections.heading: Extracting a fossil fuel — the Camisea gas project, Peru
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.3.4, named example · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 20

  • Why gas — it is the cleanest of the fossil fuels, with 45% less CO₂ emissions than the alternatives.
  • The economics — could save Peru US$4 billion and earn US$34 billion over the project's 30-year life.
  • The environmental cost — deforestation along the pipeline destroys habitat, and clearing routes has caused landslides.
  • The human cost — impacts on indigenous tribes, who may lack immunity to diseases brought in by developers.
More detail
  • What it is — a natural gas extraction and pipeline project in the Peruvian rainforest, in the Camisea region.
  • The economics — could save Peru US$4 billion in energy costs and earn US$34 billion over the project's 30-year life.
  • Employment — the gas industry built around it employs 1.2 million people.

The Camisea Natural Gas Pipeline Project, Peru

  • Location. The Camisea region of the Peruvian Amazon rainforest, with a pipeline carrying gas across the Andes to the coast.
  • Advantage — national energy costs. The project could save Peru US$4 billion in energy costs, because domestic gas replaces imported fuel.
  • Advantage — export earnings. Peru could make US$34 billion over the 30-year life of the project from exports, which is government revenue available for development.
  • Advantage — the cleanest fossil fuel. Natural gas produces 45% less CO₂ than the alternatives, so switching to it reduces emissions relative to coal or oil.
  • Advantage — employment. The industry employs 1.2 million people, with further employment opportunities in construction and operation.
  • Advantage — infrastructure. Improved infrastructure could benefit locals — the roads, power and services built for the project remain afterwards.
  • Disadvantage — deforestation. The deforestation associated with the pipeline destroys habitats, in one of the most biodiverse environments on Earth.
  • Disadvantage — landslides. Clearing routes for pipelines has led to landslides, because removing the forest removes the root network that binds steep Andean slopes.
  • Disadvantage — indigenous people. There is a direct impact on indigenous tribes whose land the project crosses, and locals may not have immunity to diseases brought by developers — a risk that has been lethal in previously uncontacted Amazonian groups.
  • Disadvantage — the method. Fracking is a controversial process, with concerns about groundwater contamination and induced seismicity.

✗ "Extracting fossil fuels damages the environment but makes money." — unnamed and ungrounded; the 2024 mark scheme caps you at the top of Level 2 if the fossil fuel is not named or cannot be inferred, and again if you use a local renewable scheme by mistake.
✓ Name it in the first line — "the Camisea natural gas project in the Peruvian Amazon" — then pair each advantage with its cost, with the figures: US$34 billion over 30 years against deforestation and landslides in primary rainforest.

subsections.heading: Sustainable energy — conservation, and Chambamontera, Peru
subsections.html:
Spec 3.2.3.4, named example · Case Study Summary Booklet 2026, p. 21; Energy Workbook pp. 19–22; 2025 Q06.5 mark scheme

  • Four conservation strands — home and workplace design, transport, reducing demand, and more efficient use of fossil fuels.
  • Chambamontera — a micro-hydro scheme in the Andes of Peru, supported by the charity Practical Action.
  • Community ownership — the community paid part of the cost, US$51,000 in total, about $750 per family.
  • The outcomes — reliable electricity, electric street lighting, low maintenance and running costs, low environmental impact.
More detail
  • Sustainable energy supply — energy savings, efficiency measures and renewable sources, used without harming future generations.
  • Why there — isolated communities are cut off from the national grid, so local generation is the only realistic option.

Chambamontera micro-hydro scheme, Peru

  • Where. The Andes mountains, Peru — steep relief and reliable rainfall, which is exactly what micro-hydro needs.
  • Why it was introduced. Isolated communities are cut off from the main electricity power network, and extending the national grid to them would be prohibitively expensive, so there is a need for local power generation.
  • What it is. Hydroelectric power generation on a micro scale, supported by the charity Practical Action. The community had to pay some of the cost — US$51,000 in total, about $750 per family — which gives local people ownership of the scheme and a reason to maintain it.
  • Why it is sustainable. It uses renewable energy; it has a low environmental impact, because a micro-hydro scheme needs no large dam and floods no valley; it has low maintenance and running costs, so the community can keep it working without outside help — this is intermediate technology: simple, easily learned and easily maintained, serving local needs.
  • Benefits to the community. Electricity is reliable, and there is now electric street lighting, which improves safety and lets social and community life continue after dark. Light in homes extends the hours available for study, and power allows refrigeration of food and medicine.
  • Economic benefits. Electricity creates economic opportunities — small businesses can run machinery and lighting, produce can be processed and stored rather than sold immediately, and people are not spending income on kerosene or batteries.
  • Environmental benefits. No fossil fuels are burned, so there are no greenhouse gas emissions and no indoor air pollution from kerosene lamps or wood fires; no forest is cleared for fuelwood.

Energy conservation — the four strands, with AQA's own examples

  • Designing homes and workplaces. Insulating houses — cavity wall and loft insulation, double glazed windows — to keep heat in or out, reducing the need for heating or air conditioning; thermostats on radiators, computerised heating controls and smart meters; energy saving appliances; encouraging people to turn devices off rather than leave them on standby; large windows to make use of natural light; and LED lighting or lights with motion sensors in offices.
  • Transport. More fuel-efficient cars; carbon fibre cars that are lighter and more aerodynamic; electric and hybrid cars; car tax that encourages people to drive less polluting vehicles; investment in public transport, including hydrogen buses and electric trams; park and ride schemes; and clean air zones that charge vehicles to enter — London's ULEZ cut NO₂ by 44% in the original zone.
  • Reducing energy demand. Public information, pricing and regulation — appliance efficiency standards, building regulations, and the habit changes that follow from smart meters showing real-time cost.
  • Using technology to improve the efficiency of fossil fuels. Combined Heat and Power, which captures the heat a conventional power station wastes — East Village in Stratford uses a biomass CHP system and runs 30% below average energy use; more efficient turbines; and carbon capture.
  • Why each of these is sustainable, which is the half of the 2025 question most candidates skipped: less energy is needed to heat, cool and light buildings, so finite fossil fuels are used more slowly; decreased fossil fuel use means fewer greenhouse gas emissions from power stations, which contribute to climate change; less petrol and diesel means less oil extraction, which damages fragile environments and leaks during transport; fewer vehicles means fewer pollutants and better human health; schemes that cut congestion and raise public transport use reduce travel times, bringing economic benefits to business; and encouraging walking and cycling benefits health and wellbeing.

✗ Writing about a national renewable scheme, or about Camisea, for the "local renewable energy scheme in an LIC/NEE" question. The 2024-style mark scheme caps a fossil-fuel answer at Level 2 if a local renewable is used, and the reverse applies too.
✓ Match the example to the question. Camisea = extraction of a fossil fuel, advantages and disadvantages. Chambamontera = a local renewable scheme providing a sustainable supply in an LIC/NEE. They are not interchangeable.

The facts you cannot sit Section C without

The rubric: answer Question 03 and Question 06 (Energy) only. Q03 covers the overview and UK food, water and energy, so revise all three.

Resources: a resource = something society values for its usefulness · resource management = control and monitoring so resources are not depleted · food, water and energy are the three the spec names.

Global distribution: food surplus in Europe, Asia, North and South America · food deficit in sub-Saharan Africa plus India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan · 50 countries face food insecurity · 800 million live with hunger · water shortage in Africa, the Middle East, Australia · water surplus in Europe, SE Asia, northern South America, northern North America · energy consumption highest in North America · GNI and energy consumption positively correlated · 30% of the world's unexploited natural gas is in the Arctic.

UK food: 12% of food eaten in the UK comes from LICs · 12% of UK greenhouse emissions come from agriculture · rising demand for high-value exotics (Madagascan vanilla, specialist honey), all-year seasonal food (strawberries) and organic produce · agribusiness: larger farms, hedgerows removed, more mechanisation and chemicals · local sourcing cuts food miles but limits choice.

UK water: enough water overall but rainfall doesn't match demand — wettest west, highest demand in the driest south-east, so water is transferred · 310 litres per person per day · demand expected to exceed supply by 2034 · dishwasher ownership 22% (1998) → 49% (2018) · pollution causes: agricultural chemicals and pesticides, oil from boats, untreated industrial waste, transport runoff, sewage · effects: pesticides kill wildlife, fertilisers cause eutrophication, polluted drinking water, losses to fishing and tourism · Environment Agency: population growth, climate change and plastic pollution are the main future threats · 2025: "No river in England is clean," say MPs.

UK energy: shift from fossil fuels and nuclear to renewables; nuclear fallen slightly · 47% of UK energy "green" in 2020 · 35% imported in 2019 · target 65% renewables by 2030 · fossil fuels down because of environmental impact and declining domestic supply · renewables up for environmental benefit and carbon targets · new nuclear station ~£22bn · commercial wind turbine ~£4m · renewables: high set-up costs, low profitability, tourism decline, visually unattractive, wildlife impact, land flooded for reservoirs, biomass reduces biodiversity.

Rising demand: three drivers — economic development, population growth, technology. Four supply factors: physical, cost of exploitation and production, technology, political.

Energy security = uninterrupted availability at an affordable price. Energy insecurity impacts: industrial output falls · food production suffers (irrigation, processing, refrigeration) · prices rise and fuel poverty follows · exploration of difficult and sensitive environments · conflict (Ukraine and Russian supply is the standard example; the Niger Delta for internal conflict).

Reliability ranking (the 2023 discriminator): geothermal and HEP constant · tidal predictable · biomass and nuclear controllable · wind and solar intermittent · wave experimental. Brazil cut petrol consumption 40% with bio-ethanol.

Camisea (Peru) — fossil fuel extraction. For: could save Peru US$4bn in energy costs · US$34bn over the 30-year life from exports · gas is the cleanest fossil fuel, 45% less CO₂ · employs 1.2 million · improved infrastructure benefits locals. Against: deforestation along the pipeline destroys habitat · clearing routes has caused landslides · impacts on indigenous tribes · locals may lack immunity to diseases brought by developers · fracking is controversial.

Chambamontera (Peru) — local renewable scheme. Micro-hydro in the Andes, supported by Practical Action · isolated communities cut off from the main grid, so local generation is needed · community paid part of the cost: US$51,000 total, about $750 per family · renewable, low environmental impact, low maintenance and running costs · reliable electricity and electric street lighting, improving quality of life and economic opportunity.

Energy conservation: homes and workplaces — cavity wall and loft insulation, double glazing, radiator thermostats, smart meters, efficient appliances, no standby, natural light, LEDs and motion sensors. Transport — fuel-efficient and carbon fibre cars, electric and hybrid, car tax, public transport investment (hydrogen buses, electric trams), park and ride, clean air zones (London ULEZ cut NO₂ 44%). Efficiency — CHP (East Village runs 30% below average energy use), carbon capture.

subsections.heading: Quotes and figures to learn
subsections.html:
Section C's extended answers are won with named examples and numbers. The front of each card names the case study and what the figure measures; the back says what you use it to argue.

Global food — the deficit regionsA large proportion of sub-Saharan Africa has a food deficit, as do India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan; around 50 countries face food insecurity and over 800 million people live with hungerUsed to argue: the global distribution of food is deeply uneven, and the deficit regions are the ones with the fewest resources to fix it — the opening of any global resources answer
Global water — surplus and shortageAfrica, the Middle East and Australia are prone to water shortage and drought; Europe, South East Asia, northern South America and northern North America have a water surplusUsed to argue: water insecurity is primarily a question of physical geography reinforced by development — and it gives you the named regions the "describe the distribution" questions demand
Global energy — the Arctic30% of the world's unexploited natural gas is thought to lie in the ArcticUsed to argue: energy insecurity pushes exploration into fragile environments and makes territory politically contested — the link between insecurity, conflict and environmental risk in one figure
UK food — imports and emissions12% of the food eaten in the UK comes from LICs; 12% of the UK's total greenhouse gas emissions come from agricultureUsed to argue: changing demand for food has raised the UK's carbon footprint through food miles — and that even home-grown food carries a substantial emissions cost, so local sourcing is not a complete answer
UK water — the spatial mismatchThe UK receives enough water overall, but rainfall is greatest in the west while the greatest demand comes from the south-east, the driest area, which has a water deficitUsed to argue: why water transfer schemes are necessary in a country that is not short of water — the single most important idea in the UK water topic
UK water — rising demandAverage daily consumption is 310 litres per person, and demand is expected to exceed supply by 2034; dishwasher ownership rose from 22% in 1998 to 49% in 2018Used to argue: demand is rising through population growth, its concentration in the south, and appliance ownership — the evidence for "the changing demand for water in the UK is a challenge"
UK water — quality"No river in England is clean," say MPs — agriculture and water companies have put raw sewage, microplastics and farm waste into all of England's rivers, alongside car tyre particles, oils and wet wipesUsed to argue: managing water quality is a significant challenge, because the sources are numerous, diffuse and legal — the 2025 6-marker's own figure
UK water — eutrophicationNutrients from farmland and sewage produce algae which reduce oxygen levels in the water, killing fish and causing economic losses to fishermen and tourismUsed to argue: the mechanism, not just the fact, of water pollution — name eutrophication and explain the oxygen depletion and you have the AO2 mark
UK energy mix — the shift47% of UK energy was "green" in 2020; 35% was imported in 2019; the target is 65% renewables by 2030Used to argue: the UK's energy mix is shifting from fossil fuels and nuclear towards renewables, driven by environmental impact, declining domestic supply and carbon targets
UK energy — the cost of capacityA new nuclear power station costs around £22 billion to build; a commercial wind turbine around £4 millionUsed to argue: the cost of exploitation and production is one of the four factors limiting energy supply — high set-up costs are the main barrier to renewables, even where the resource exists
Energy security — the definition that earns the markEnergy security is the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price; energy insecurity is when availability is not enough to ensure good health, livelihood and earningsUsed to argue: both halves matter — uninterrupted and affordable — which is why an HIC with plenty of supply can still be insecure if prices spike. Do not define an energy deficit instead
Energy insecurity — fuel poverty in HICsThe 2025 paper measured the percentage of households in each European country that could not afford to heat their homes in 2021Used to argue: energy insecurity is not only an LIC problem — rising prices create fuel poverty in rich countries, which is the "affordable price" half of the definition made concrete
Energy insecurity — conflictSupply and demand sit in different countries, so a supplier can shut a pipeline to apply political pressure, disputed territory becomes contested for what lies beneath it, and extraction can provoke armed resistanceUsed to argue: "suggest how energy supply issues can lead to conflict" — the examiners report that the best answers used Russia, Ukraine and European gas supply
Reliability — the discriminatorTidal power is predictable years in advance and geothermal and HEP are effectively constant, whereas wind and solar are intermittent, so they need backup capacityUsed to argue: "to what extent can wind and tidal power increase energy supply?" — the examiner's report says understanding of reliability is what allowed the best discussions
Biomass — BrazilBrazil has reduced its petrol consumption by 40% by introducing bio-ethanolUsed to argue: biofuel can displace fossil fuels at national scale — with the counter that monoculture for biomass reduces biodiversity and competes with food crops for land
Camisea — the national gainThe project could save Peru US$4 billion in energy costs, and Peru could make US$34 billion over the project's 30-year life from exportsUsed to argue: the advantages of extracting a fossil fuel — domestic supply replaces imports and export revenue funds development, the two figures that make the "advantages" half specific
Camisea — gas as the cleanest fossil fuelNatural gas is the cleanest of the fossil fuels, with 45% less CO₂ emissions; the industry employs 1.2 million peopleUsed to argue: extraction can be defended on climate grounds relative to coal and oil, and on employment — the strongest version of the case for a fossil fuel project
Camisea — the environmental and human costDeforestation along the pipeline destroys habitat, clearing routes has caused landslides, indigenous tribes are directly affected, and locals may lack immunity to diseases brought by developersUsed to argue: the disadvantages half — in primary rainforest the damage is irreversible, and the human risk falls on people who gain least from the project
Chambamontera — why local, not nationalA micro-hydro scheme in the Andes of Peru, introduced because isolated communities are cut off from the main electricity network and need local power generationUsed to argue: the reason a local renewable scheme is the right solution in an LIC/NEE — extending a national grid to remote mountain communities is prohibitively expensive, so decentralised generation wins
Chambamontera — community ownershipSupported by the charity Practical Action, with the community paying part of the cost — US$51,000 in total, about $750 per familyUsed to argue: why the scheme is sustainable rather than a donation — paying for it gives local people ownership and the incentive to maintain it, the defining feature of intermediate technology
Chambamontera — the outcomesRenewable energy with low environmental impact, low maintenance and running costs; electricity is now reliable and there is electric street lighting, improving quality of life and economic opportunitiesUsed to argue: a small renewable scheme delivers social, economic and environmental sustainability at once — the three strands the 6-mark mark scheme rewards
Conservation — insulation and efficiencyCavity wall and loft insulation and double glazing keep heat in; radiator thermostats, smart meters, energy-saving appliances, natural light, LEDs and motion sensors cut demand furtherUsed to argue: conservation in homes and workplaces makes supply more sustainable because finite fossil fuels are used more slowly and power-station emissions fall

equations.name: Global food — the deficit regions
equations.formula: A large proportion of sub-Saharan Africa has a food deficit, as do India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan; around 50 countries face food insecurity and over 800 million people live with hunger
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the global distribution of food is deeply uneven, and the deficit regions are the ones with the fewest resources to fix it — the opening of any global resources answer

equations.name: Global water — surplus and shortage
equations.formula: Africa, the Middle East and Australia are prone to water shortage and drought; Europe, South East Asia, northern South America and northern North America have a water surplus
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: water insecurity is primarily a question of physical geography reinforced by development — and it gives you the named regions the "describe the distribution" questions demand

equations.name: Global energy — the Arctic
equations.formula: 30% of the world's unexploited natural gas is thought to lie in the Arctic
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: energy insecurity pushes exploration into fragile environments and makes territory politically contested — the link between insecurity, conflict and environmental risk in one figure

equations.name: UK food — imports and emissions
equations.formula: 12% of the food eaten in the UK comes from LICs; 12% of the UK's total greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: changing demand for food has raised the UK's carbon footprint through food miles — and that even home-grown food carries a substantial emissions cost, so local sourcing is not a complete answer

equations.name: UK water — the spatial mismatch
equations.formula: The UK receives enough water overall, but rainfall is greatest in the west while the greatest demand comes from the south-east, the driest area, which has a water deficit
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: why water transfer schemes are necessary in a country that is not short of water — the single most important idea in the UK water topic

equations.name: UK water — rising demand
equations.formula: Average daily consumption is 310 litres per person, and demand is expected to exceed supply by 2034; dishwasher ownership rose from 22% in 1998 to 49% in 2018
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: demand is rising through population growth, its concentration in the south, and appliance ownership — the evidence for "the changing demand for water in the UK is a challenge"

equations.name: UK water — quality
equations.formula: "No river in England is clean," say MPs — agriculture and water companies have put raw sewage, microplastics and farm waste into all of England's rivers, alongside car tyre particles, oils and wet wipes
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: managing water quality is a significant challenge, because the sources are numerous, diffuse and legal — the 2025 6-marker's own figure

equations.name: UK water — eutrophication
equations.formula: Nutrients from farmland and sewage produce algae which reduce oxygen levels in the water, killing fish and causing economic losses to fishermen and tourism
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the mechanism, not just the fact, of water pollution — name eutrophication and explain the oxygen depletion and you have the AO2 mark

equations.name: UK energy mix — the shift
equations.formula: 47% of UK energy was "green" in 2020; 35% was imported in 2019; the target is 65% renewables by 2030
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the UK's energy mix is shifting from fossil fuels and nuclear towards renewables, driven by environmental impact, declining domestic supply and carbon targets

equations.name: UK energy — the cost of capacity
equations.formula: A new nuclear power station costs around £22 billion to build; a commercial wind turbine around £4 million
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the cost of exploitation and production is one of the four factors limiting energy supply — high set-up costs are the main barrier to renewables, even where the resource exists

equations.name: Energy security — the definition that earns the mark
equations.formula: Energy security is the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price; energy insecurity is when availability is not enough to ensure good health, livelihood and earnings
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: both halves matter — uninterrupted and affordable — which is why an HIC with plenty of supply can still be insecure if prices spike. Do not define an energy deficit instead

equations.name: Energy insecurity — fuel poverty in HICs
equations.formula: The 2025 paper measured the percentage of households in each European country that could not afford to heat their homes in 2021
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: energy insecurity is not only an LIC problem — rising prices create fuel poverty in rich countries, which is the "affordable price" half of the definition made concrete

equations.name: Energy insecurity — conflict
equations.formula: Supply and demand sit in different countries, so a supplier can shut a pipeline to apply political pressure, disputed territory becomes contested for what lies beneath it, and extraction can provoke armed resistance
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: "suggest how energy supply issues can lead to conflict" — the examiners report that the best answers used Russia, Ukraine and European gas supply

equations.name: Reliability — the discriminator
equations.formula: Tidal power is predictable years in advance and geothermal and HEP are effectively constant, whereas wind and solar are intermittent, so they need backup capacity
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: "to what extent can wind and tidal power increase energy supply?" — the examiner's report says understanding of reliability is what allowed the best discussions

equations.name: Biomass — Brazil
equations.formula: Brazil has reduced its petrol consumption by 40% by introducing bio-ethanol
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: biofuel can displace fossil fuels at national scale — with the counter that monoculture for biomass reduces biodiversity and competes with food crops for land

equations.name: Camisea — the national gain
equations.formula: The project could save Peru US$4 billion in energy costs, and Peru could make US$34 billion over the project's 30-year life from exports
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the advantages of extracting a fossil fuel — domestic supply replaces imports and export revenue funds development, the two figures that make the "advantages" half specific

equations.name: Camisea — gas as the cleanest fossil fuel
equations.formula: Natural gas is the cleanest of the fossil fuels, with 45% less CO₂ emissions; the industry employs 1.2 million people
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: extraction can be defended on climate grounds relative to coal and oil, and on employment — the strongest version of the case for a fossil fuel project

equations.name: Camisea — the environmental and human cost
equations.formula: Deforestation along the pipeline destroys habitat, clearing routes has caused landslides, indigenous tribes are directly affected, and locals may lack immunity to diseases brought by developers
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the disadvantages half — in primary rainforest the damage is irreversible, and the human risk falls on people who gain least from the project

equations.name: Chambamontera — why local, not national
equations.formula: A micro-hydro scheme in the Andes of Peru, introduced because isolated communities are cut off from the main electricity network and need local power generation
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the reason a local renewable scheme is the right solution in an LIC/NEE — extending a national grid to remote mountain communities is prohibitively expensive, so decentralised generation wins

equations.name: Chambamontera — community ownership
equations.formula: Supported by the charity Practical Action, with the community paying part of the cost — US$51,000 in total, about $750 per family
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: why the scheme is sustainable rather than a donation — paying for it gives local people ownership and the incentive to maintain it, the defining feature of intermediate technology

equations.name: Chambamontera — the outcomes
equations.formula: Renewable energy with low environmental impact, low maintenance and running costs; electricity is now reliable and there is electric street lighting, improving quality of life and economic opportunities
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: a small renewable scheme delivers social, economic and environmental sustainability at once — the three strands the 6-mark mark scheme rewards

equations.name: Conservation — insulation and efficiency
equations.formula: Cavity wall and loft insulation and double glazing keep heat in; radiator thermostats, smart meters, energy-saving appliances, natural light, LEDs and motion sensors cut demand further
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: conservation in homes and workplaces makes supply more sustainable because finite fossil fuels are used more slowly and power-station emissions fall

equations.name: Conservation — transport and CHP
equations.formula: Electric and hybrid cars, car tax on polluting vehicles, hydrogen buses and electric trams, park and ride, and clean air zones — London's ULEZ cut NO₂ 44%; CHP captures waste heat, and East Village runs 30% below average energy use
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the transport and efficiency strands of the 2025 6-marker, with the health and economic benefits — less oil extraction in fragile environments, fewer pollutants, shorter journey times

The 6-mark frame (and the 9-mark version if it appears)

Section C's extended answer is a 6-marker, not a 9-marker — there is one at the end of Question 03 and one at the end of Question 06. AQA marks them in levels, AO1 3 marks and AO2 3 marks, so the structure is tighter than a 9-marker: two or three developed paragraphs, evidence and explanation, plus discussion if the command word demands it, and no introduction.

  1. Name the example in the first clause. "The Camisea natural gas project in the Peruvian Amazon…" or "The Chambamontera micro-hydro scheme in the Andes of Peru…". The mark scheme states explicitly: max top Level 2 if the scheme is not named or cannot be inferred, and max top Level 2 if you use the wrong kind of scheme.
  2. Refer to the figure if there is one, then use it. "Figure 17 shows that…, which means…, and therefore…". The examiners' standing complaint is lifting without developing.
  3. Paragraph 1 — the first side, developed with figures. Point, explanation of the mechanism, evidence, link back to the question's words. For Camisea: the US$34 billion over 30 years, and why export revenue matters to an NEE.
  4. Paragraph 2 — the other side, same shape. For Camisea: deforestation, landslides, indigenous communities without immunity — and why rainforest damage is irreversible in a way that economic loss is not.
  5. Paragraph 3 or a developed third point. Where the question says "and other strategies", this is where nuclear, biomass, solar and HEP go. Where it says "homes and workplaces and transport", you must cover both — the mark scheme caps you at Level 2 for only one.
  6. A short conclusion that decides. One or two sentences on the ladder, tied to the exact wording. "So extraction brings substantial advantages to Peru as a country, but the disadvantages fall on the rainforest and on the people least able to refuse them — the costs are more permanent than the benefits."

Sentence starters that earn the AO2 marks:

  • "Figure X shows that…, which means…, and as a result…"
  • "This increases supply because…, so…"
  • "However, this is limited because wind is intermittent, whereas tidal power is predictable…"
  • "This is sustainable because it reduces the rate at which finite fossil fuels are used, which in turn reduces greenhouse emissions…"
  • "The most significant disadvantage is…, because it is irreversible, whereas…"
  • "Overall, this strategy can partly increase supply, because…"

SPaG (3 marks only on a 9-marker, but spelling still signals competence): Camisea, Chambamontera, Practical Action, Andes, Peru, eutrophication, abstraction, geothermal, biomass, insecurity, hydro-electric, non-renewable.
