questions.promptHtml: The UK receives more than enough rainfall. So why does it need water transfer schemes?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the water and the people are in different places. Rainfall is greatest in the west — the uplands of Wales, the Lake District and western Scotland, which face the prevailing south-westerly winds and force air to rise. Demand is greatest in the south-east, which is both the most densely populated region and the driest, so it runs a water deficit while the west runs a surplus.

Water transfer therefore moves water between river basins through canals, pipes and dredging — the only way to match a supply pattern set by physical geography to a demand pattern set by human geography.

The complication that earns the evaluation mark: demand is still rising. Consumption averages 310 litres per person per day, the population is increasingly concentrated in the south, dishwasher ownership rose from 22% to 49% between 1998 and 2018, and more homes have more than one bathroom. Demand is expected to exceed supply by 2034 — so transfer alone will not be enough without conservation.

questions.promptHtml: Why is buying local food not automatically better for the environment than importing it?
questions.answerHtml:
Because food miles are only part of the carbon footprint. The other part is how the food was produced, and 12% of the UK's total greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture — fertiliser manufacture, machinery, livestock methane and soil disturbance.

The case that matters is out-of-season produce. A UK strawberry in January has to be grown in a heated, lit glasshouse, which can emit more than a strawberry shipped from a country where it grows in the open air. The same logic applies to tomatoes and salad crops.

What local sourcing does achieve: far fewer food miles for food that is in season; fresher produce; money retained in the local economy, supporting farmers and shops; and transparency about how it was produced. The costs are limited choice, strict seasonality and often a higher price.

The exam point: this is why the 2023 and 2024 questions were phrased as "opportunities and challenges" and "creates opportunities and challenges". A one-sided answer about food miles misses half the marks.

questions.promptHtml: A country can hold huge energy reserves and still be energy insecure. How?
questions.answerHtml:
Because energy security means uninterrupted availability at an affordable price, and reserves deliver neither on their own.

A reserve is not a supply. It becomes usable only if the technology exists to reach it and the cost of exploitation is less than the value of the energy — which is why 30% of the world's unexploited natural gas sits in the Arctic, unexploited. Political factors can also block it: a government may ban fracking or refuse nuclear.

Demand can outrun supply. The workbook's own framing: "even some countries with a high energy supply can experience energy insecurity where demand for energy is high". A rapidly developing economy adds demand faster than it can add capacity.

Distribution and conflict. Nigeria is the clearest case — it produces 2.2% of the world's oil, yet electricity supply is unreliable, oil wealth has provoked armed groups, and the revenue has not built the domestic grid.

And affordability is half the definition. The 2025 figure measured the share of households in each European country that could not afford to heat their homes in 2021 — insecurity in some of the richest countries on Earth.

questions.promptHtml: Why do examiners treat "tidal power is reliable" as a stronger point than "tidal power is clean"?
questions.answerHtml:
Because clean is true of every renewable, so it does not discriminate between them, whereas reliability is the problem renewables actually have.

Electricity demand must be met at the moment it occurs; it cannot wait for the wind. Wind and solar are intermittent — no output when the wind drops, and solar is weakest in winter when UK demand peaks — so every unit of wind capacity needs backup capacity from gas, nuclear or storage, which adds cost and emissions. Tidal is predictable years in advance, because tides are astronomical, so it can be planned into the grid; geothermal and HEP are effectively constant, and HEP can be ramped up within minutes to match a demand spike.

The exam point: the 2023 examiner's report says of the 6-marker on wind and tidal power that "understanding of the reliability of tides and wind power allowed appropriate discussions in the best responses". That one idea is the difference between Level 2 and Level 3.

The counter to keep in reserve: tidal needs a very large tidal range, so it works almost nowhere, and barrages damage estuary ecosystems and bird feeding grounds. Reliability is not the only criterion.

questions.promptHtml: Camisea is described as extracting "the cleanest of the fossil fuels". Does that make it a sustainable project?
questions.answerHtml:
No — "cleanest" is a relative claim, and sustainability is an absolute one.

What the claim does establish. Natural gas produces 45% less CO₂ than the alternatives, so if Camisea's gas displaces coal or oil, emissions fall. It also gives Peru domestic supply instead of imports, saving US$4 billion in energy costs, and US$34 billion of export revenue over 30 years that can fund development.

Why it is still not sustainable. Gas is non-renewable — the project has a stated 30-year life, which is the definition of a resource being depleted rather than sustained. And sustainable development means meeting present needs "without limiting the ability of future generations to meet their own needs": the deforestation along the pipeline, the landslides caused by clearing routes on steep Andean slopes, and the exposure of indigenous tribes to diseases they have no immunity to are all losses future generations inherit.

The contrast that makes the point: compare it with Chambamontera — renewable, low environmental impact, low running costs, community-owned, and with no stated end date. That is what a sustainable energy supply looks like, and it is why AQA pairs the two examples in the same spec bullet.

questions.promptHtml: Why did Practical Action make the Chambamontera community pay $750 per family rather than giving them the scheme?
questions.answerHtml:
Because paying for it changes what happens afterwards. Contributing US$51,000 of the cost gives the community ownership, so the scheme is theirs to run and maintain rather than a donor's project that stops when the donor leaves. That is the whole logic of intermediate technology: simple, easily learned and easily maintained technology serving local needs, which can be repaired locally without imported parts or outside expertise.

It also avoids the problems the development-gap topic identifies with aid: donors deciding priorities, aid being diverted, and recipients becoming dependent rather than self-sufficient. The Chambamontera design makes the community the decision-maker.

Why micro-hydro specifically. The communities are cut off from the main electricity network in the Andes, and extending a national grid across mountains to scattered settlements would cost far more than it could ever recover. Local generation is not a second-best option here — it is the only economic one.

Use it like this: the same argument is the Favela-Bairro argument about legal land title, and the Fairtrade argument about the Gumutindo co-op. Development works when the people affected have a stake in it.

questions.promptHtml: Why do rising gas prices speed up the move to renewables, when renewables have high set-up costs?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the two have completely different cost structures. A gas power station is relatively cheap to build and expensive to run, since it must buy fuel for every unit it generates. A wind turbine costs around £4 million up front — and a nuclear station around £22 billion — but has almost no fuel cost afterwards.

So when the gas price rises, every unit of gas-fired electricity gets more expensive while every unit of wind-generated electricity costs the same as before. Renewables become comparatively cheaper, so new investment moves towards them. This is exactly what the 2024 2-marker asked: "why might increasing gas prices mean that renewables become increasingly [important]?"

The second reason is security, not cost. The UK imported 35% of its energy in 2019 and domestic gas supply is falling as North Sea reserves deplete. Expensive imported gas is an energy security risk as well as an expense, because the price and the supply are both set abroad — so there is a political incentive to replace it, reinforced by the target of 65% renewables by 2030.

The limitation to acknowledge: high set-up costs still need financing, and renewables' intermittency means gas capacity has to be kept for backup even as its use falls. So the switch is slower than the price signal alone suggests.

questions.promptHtml: Energy conservation does not generate a single unit of electricity. Why does the spec treat it as a way of increasing sustainable supply?
questions.answerHtml:
Because what matters is the balance of supply and demand, and reducing demand moves that balance exactly as adding supply would — AQA's own definition is that a sustainable energy supply "is the combination of energy savings, energy efficiency measures and technologies, as well as the use of renewable energy sources". Savings are listed first.

The chain the mark scheme wants. Less energy is needed to heat, cool and light buildings, so fossil fuels — which are running out — are used at a slower rate, which extends the time available to replace them. Decreased fossil fuel use means fewer greenhouse gas emissions from power stations, which contribute to climate change. Fewer petrol and diesel vehicles means less oil has to be obtained, which damages fragile environments during extraction and leaks during transport. And fewer vehicles releasing pollutants has a positive effect on human health.

It is also the cheapest option. Loft insulation costs a tiny fraction of the £22 billion for a nuclear station or the £4 million for a turbine, and it can be installed on existing buildings immediately rather than after a decade of construction.

And it brings co-benefits supply never does: schemes that cut congestion and raise public transport use reduce travel times, bringing economic benefits to businesses, while walking and cycling improve health and wellbeing. That is social, economic and environmental sustainability from one measure.

questions.promptHtml: What is energy insecurity? (2)
questions.answerHtml:
When energy availability is not enough to ensure the population of an area enjoys good health, livelihood and earnings 1

— in other words, the opposite of energy security, which is the uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price, so a country can be insecure through unreliable supply or through cost 1

The 1-mark version needs only the first line. The 2023 report: "most correct unless students defined energy deficit."

questions.promptHtml: Outline one or more ways that physical factors can affect energy supply. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Geology determines where fossil fuels and geothermal heat exist, so a country without suitable rock cannot exploit them whatever its wealth — which is why 30% of the world's unexploited natural gas lies in the Arctic rather than where it is needed 1

Climate determines which renewables work: the UK's position in the mid-latitude westerlies makes it one of Europe's windiest countries, so wind power is viable, whereas solar output is weakest in winter when UK demand peaks 1

Relief and rainfall control hydro-electric power, because HEP needs steep gradients and a reliable flow — which is exactly why the Chambamontera micro-hydro scheme works in the Andes of Peru, and why a tidal scheme needs a coastline with a very large tidal range 1

questions.promptHtml: Explain why demand for different energy sources has changed in the UK. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Demand for fossil fuels has fallen because of their environmental impact: burning coal, oil and gas releases the greenhouse gases that drive climate change, so the UK has committed to cutting emissions and aims for 65% renewables by 2030 1

Domestic supplies of fossil fuels are also declining — North Sea gas reserves are being depleted and the remaining fields are harder and more expensive to exploit — so the UK had to import 35% of its energy in 2019, which is both costly and an energy security risk because the price and supply are set abroad 1

Demand for renewables has therefore risen sharply, and 47% of UK energy was green by 2020; wind suits the UK's position in the mid-latitude westerlies, and renewables have almost no fuel cost once built 1

Rising gas prices accelerate the switch, because gas-fired electricity gets more expensive with every price rise while wind and solar generation costs stay the same — so renewables become comparatively cheaper and new investment moves to them. Nuclear has fallen only slightly, because it is reliable and low-carbon even though a new station costs around £22 billion 1

questions.promptHtml: Suggest how energy supply issues can lead to conflict. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Energy reserves and energy demand are usually in different countries, so supply has to be traded — which gives a supplier political power, because it can raise prices or shut a pipeline to apply pressure, as Europe found over Russian gas 1

That dependence makes importing countries act to secure supply, by forming alliances, intervening in producer regions or racing to develop alternatives, which raises tension between states 1

Unexploited reserves make territory worth fighting over: 30% of the world's unexploited natural gas is thought to lie in the Arctic, so as the ice retreats several states have made overlapping claims to the seabed 1

Conflict also occurs within countries, between a government or TNC and the people whose land is being exploited — in the Niger Delta, oil wealth has provoked armed groups, and at Camisea in Peru the pipeline crosses the land of indigenous tribes who gain least from it 1

questions.promptHtml: Outline the link between increasing economic development and rising energy consumption. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
As a country develops, its industrial base expands, and manufacturing is energy-intensive — so national demand rises with industrial output 1

Rising incomes change household consumption: people buy cars, fridges, washing machines, air conditioning and electronics, and heat and light larger homes, so energy use per person rises as well as in total 1

Development is also urbanising, and cities need continuous power for lighting, transport, construction, water treatment, hospitals and offices — which is why energy consumption per person is highest in HICs, with North America among the very highest in the world 1

The relationship is visible in the data as a positive correlation between GNI per person and energy consumption per person across the world's countries, so a scatter graph of the two shows consumption rising as GNI rises 1

questions.promptHtml: Explain how changing demand for food has affected the UK's carbon footprint. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Demand has grown for high-value exotic foods such as Madagascan vanilla and specialist honey, and 12% of the food eaten in the UK now comes from LICs, so food is travelling much further — raising food miles and therefore the emissions from air and sea freight 1

Demand for all-year seasonal produce has the same effect: strawberries can only be grown outdoors in the UK in summer, so out of season they are imported, or grown in heated and lit glasshouses, which itself consumes energy 1

Agribusiness has raised the footprint of UK-grown food too, because larger-scale farming uses more mechanisation and more chemicals — and fertiliser manufacture is energy-intensive, which is part of why 12% of the UK's total greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture 1

Two changes pull the other way: rising demand for organic produce, which bans artificial fertilisers and builds soil fertility through crop rotation, compost, manure and clover, and rising demand for locally sourced food, which cuts the distribution distance sharply — so the net effect on the carbon footprint depends on which trend grows faster 1

questions.promptHtml: "Extraction of fossil fuels can bring both advantages and disadvantages." Explain this statement using an example you have studied. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Plan: name Camisea in the first clause, three developed advantages, three developed disadvantages, and a closing judgement. Level marked, AO1 3 + AO2 3. The mark scheme caps you at the top of Level 2 if the fossil fuel is not named or cannot be inferred, and again if you use a local renewable scheme instead.

The Camisea natural gas project extracts gas from the Peruvian Amazon and pipes it across the Andes to the coast, and its first advantage is national energy supply: it could save Peru US$4 billion in energy costs by replacing imported fuel with a domestic source, which also improves Peru's energy security because the price is no longer set abroad 1

The second advantage is revenue. Peru could make US$34 billion over the 30-year life of the project from exports, which is government money available for development spending on healthcare, water supply and education — and Peru's own 2025 exam figure showed the president involved in improving water and sanitation 1

The third is employment and infrastructure: the industry employs 1.2 million people, and the roads, power lines and services built for the project remain afterwards and could benefit local communities. Gas is also the cleanest of the fossil fuels, producing 45% less CO₂, so where it displaces coal or oil, emissions fall 1

However, the environmental cost falls on one of the most biodiverse environments on Earth. The deforestation associated with the pipeline destroys habitat permanently, because tropical rainforest regrows slowly on nutrient-poor latosols 1

Clearing routes for the pipelines has also led to landslides, because removing the forest removes the root network binding steep Andean slopes — so the damage spreads well beyond the cleared corridor itself 1

The human cost is sharpest: the project directly affects indigenous tribes whose land it crosses, and locals may not have immunity to diseases brought in by developers, a risk that has proved lethal to previously isolated Amazonian groups. Overall the advantages are real but temporary — the project has a stated 30-year life — whereas lost rainforest and lost lives are permanent, so the disadvantages are the more significant 1

questions.promptHtml: Suggest how energy supplies have been made more sustainable. Use an example of a local renewable energy scheme in an LIC/NEE. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Plan: name Chambamontera, say why local generation was chosen, then show the three strands of sustainability — environmental, economic, social. Level marked; the mark scheme requires a named local renewable scheme, so Camisea would cap you at Level 2.

The Chambamontera micro-hydro scheme in the Andes mountains of Peru generates hydroelectric power for isolated communities that are cut off from the main electricity network, where extending the national grid across mountainous terrain to scattered settlements would be prohibitively expensive — so local generation is the only realistic option 1

It is environmentally sustainable because hydro power is renewable, so the resource is not diminished by use, and no fossil fuels are burned — which means no greenhouse gas emissions and no indoor air pollution from the kerosene lamps or wood fires it replaces 1

Its environmental impact is also low because it is micro-scale: unlike a large HEP dam it floods no valley, displaces nobody and drowns no habitat, which matters because flooding large areas of upland is one of the standard objections to hydro power 1

It is economically sustainable because it has low maintenance and running costs and the community part-funded it — US$51,000 in total, about $750 per family, with support from the charity Practical Action 1

That contribution is the key to its durability: paying for the scheme gives local people ownership of it, and because it is intermediate technology — simple, easily learned and easily maintained — they can repair it themselves without imported parts or outside expertise, so it does not fail when the charity leaves and creates no aid dependence 1

It is socially and economically sustainable in its outcomes: electricity is now reliable and there is electric street lighting, which improves safety, extends the hours available for study and allows community life after dark, while power for machinery, lighting and refrigeration creates economic opportunities and removes the cost of kerosene and batteries. Overall, the scheme is sustainable on all three counts precisely because it was built at the scale the community can own and maintain 1

questions.promptHtml: To what extent can wind and tidal power and other strategies increase energy supply? (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Plan: wind, then tidal, then "other strategies" — and the discriminator is reliability. The 2023 report: students "merely lifted information from the resource… and left little room to discuss other examples", whereas "understanding of the reliability of tides and wind power allowed appropriate discussions in the best responses".

Wind can increase supply substantially in the UK, because its position in the mid-latitude westerlies makes it among the windiest countries in Europe, and offshore turbines avoid most of the visual objection while catching stronger, steadier wind 1

However, wind is intermittent: there is no output when the wind drops or blows too hard, so every unit of wind capacity needs backup from gas, nuclear or storage, which adds cost and emissions. Each commercial turbine also costs around £4 million up front, and turbines can affect birds and bats 1

Tidal power's decisive advantage is that it is predictable — tides are astronomical, so output is known years in advance and can be planned into the grid rather than merely hoped for — and the UK has one of the world's largest tidal ranges, with very high energy density 1

However, tidal only works where the range is large, so it is geographically very restricted; barrages damage estuary ecosystems and the feeding grounds of wading birds; and capital costs are very high, so despite its reliability it contributes little at present 1

Other strategies can contribute more than either in the short term. HEP and geothermal are effectively constant, and HEP output can be raised within minutes to meet a demand spike; biomass uses waste and recently absorbed carbon, and Brazil cut its petrol consumption 40% with bio-ethanol; nuclear is reliable and almost carbon-free, though a new station costs around £22 billion; and solar is ideal for small-scale off-grid use, as at Santa Marta in Rio 1

Judgement: wind and tidal power can increase supply only partly on their own, because the one that is cheap is unreliable and the one that is reliable is geographically restricted and expensive. The UK reached 47% green energy by 2020 and targets 65% by 2030, but it will do so through a mix — renewables backed by nuclear and gas capacity, and reinforced by conservation, which reduces the demand that has to be met at all 1

questions.promptHtml: "Managing water quality and water pollution in the UK is a significant challenge." To what extent do you agree? (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Plan: the sources of pollution, why they are hard to manage, the effects, then what is being managed successfully and a judgement. Level marked; "to what extent" requires both sides and a conclusion.

The challenge is significant first because the sources are numerous and varied: chemicals and pesticides from agriculture, untreated industrial waste, sewage pumped into rivers and seas, oil from boats and ships, and oil and heavy metals washed off roads 1

Several of these are diffuse rather than from a single pipe — fertiliser runs off thousands of fields and tyre particles wash off every road — so there is no single discharge to regulate, which makes enforcement far harder than closing one polluting factory 1

The effects are serious and economically costly: pesticides kill wildlife; fertilisers cause eutrophication, where nutrients from farmland and sewage produce algae that reduce oxygen levels and kill fish; drinking water is polluted; and fishermen and the tourist industry suffer economic losses 1

The scale is confirmed by the evidence put before Parliament — MPs concluded that "no river in England is clean", with raw sewage, microplastics, farm waste, car tyre particles, oils and wet wipes present in all of England's rivers, so people using rivers are now at risk 1

The challenge is also growing rather than shrinking: the Environment Agency names population growth, climate change and plastic pollution as the main future threats, and demand is expected to exceed supply by 2034, which concentrates pollutants in less water 1

However, there are effective strategies, and some have worked: sewage treatment, groundwater management to regulate levels and pollution, limits on over-abstraction, water transfer from the wet west to the dry south-east, and conservation through metering and grey water recycling. Judgement: I mostly agree — the strategies exist and are improving the worst point sources, but because the remaining pollution is diffuse, legal and driven by population growth and climate change, managing quality remains a significant and intensifying challenge 1

questions.promptHtml:
"Reducing demand is more important than increasing supply in achieving a sustainable energy future."

To what extent do you agree with this statement? (9)
questions.answerHtml:
Plan — intro defining sustainable energy supply; the case for conservation; the case for increasing supply; the complication; judgement that ranks them. Level marked. Add 3 SPaG marks if the paper awards them.

Intro. AQA defines a sustainable energy supply as "the combination of energy savings, energy efficiency measures and technologies, as well as the use of renewable energy sources" — so the real question is which of the three does most work, and conservation is listed first for a reason 1

The case for reducing demand — buildings. Cavity wall and loft insulation, double glazing, radiator thermostats, smart meters, energy-saving appliances, natural lighting and LEDs with motion sensors all cut the energy needed for the same comfort, and because they apply to existing buildings they take effect immediately 1

Why that is sustainability, not just saving. Less energy to heat, cool and light buildings means finite fossil fuels are used at a slower rate, which buys time to replace them; and less fossil fuel burned means fewer greenhouse gas emissions from power stations 1

The case for reducing demand — transport. Fuel-efficient and carbon fibre cars, electric and hybrid vehicles, car tax on polluting vehicles, hydrogen buses and electric trams, park and ride and clean air zones all reduce oil use — London's ULEZ cut NO₂ by 44% in the original zone. Less petrol and diesel means less oil extraction in fragile environments and fewer leaks in transport, and fewer pollutants improves human health 1

The cost advantage. Conservation is radically cheaper than capacity: loft insulation costs a fraction of the £4 million for a commercial wind turbine or the £22 billion for a new nuclear station, and it can be installed now rather than after a decade of construction 1

The case for increasing supply. Demand cannot be reduced indefinitely — economic development, population growth and the electrification of heating and transport all push consumption up, and energy is needed for industry, food production, water treatment and health care. Conservation alone leaves a large residual demand that must still be met 1

And supply decides what that demand is met with. The UK reached 47% green energy by 2020 and targets 65% by 2030; local schemes reach people a grid never will, as Chambamontera's micro-hydro does in the Andes, where the community part-funded it for US$51,000. Where there is no supply at all, conservation is meaningless 1

The complication. The two are not alternatives but complements, and conservation makes renewables work: because wind and solar are intermittent while tidal is predictable and geothermal and HEP constant, a grid built on renewables needs demand that is lower and more flexible. Lower demand shrinks the backup capacity needed, which is the main reason renewables still require gas 1

Conclusion. I mostly agree. Reducing demand is the more important strategy, because it is immediate, cheap, applicable to existing buildings and vehicles, and carries social and economic co-benefits that new capacity does not — but it cannot be the whole answer, since development and population growth guarantee a residual demand, and renewable supply is what determines whether that demand is met sustainably 1

questions.promptHtml:
"The UK's changing energy mix creates more opportunities than problems."

Discuss this statement. (9)
questions.answerHtml:
Plan — intro stating what the mix is changing to; the opportunities; the problems, economic and environmental; the security dimension; judgement. Level marked; discuss requires both sides, multiple supporting points, counter-arguments and a clear conclusion.

Intro. The UK's energy mix — the range of sources, renewable and non-renewable — is shifting away from fossil fuels and slightly away from nuclear towards renewables: 47% of UK energy was green by 2020, against a target of 65% by 2030 1

Opportunity — emissions. Renewables produce no greenhouse gases in operation, so the shift directly reduces the UK's contribution to climate change and is what allows it to meet its legally binding carbon targets 1

Opportunity — energy security. The UK imported 35% of its energy in 2019 while North Sea gas reserves decline, which exposes it to prices and politics set abroad; domestic wind, tidal, solar and HEP cannot be shut off by a supplier, so the shift reduces insecurity 1

Opportunity — cost and investment. Renewables have high set-up costs but almost no fuel cost, so when gas prices rise their electricity gets comparatively cheaper — and the construction and operation of offshore wind, tidal and nuclear capacity creates skilled employment and a multiplier effect in coastal and former industrial regions 1

Problem — reliability. Wind and solar are intermittent, and solar is weakest in winter when UK demand peaks, so the grid still needs backup capacity from gas or nuclear; only tidal is predictable, and geothermal and HEP constant, and both are geographically restricted in the UK 1

Problem — economic cost. A new nuclear power station costs around £22 billion and a commercial wind turbine around £4 million; low profitability is a recognised concern; and tourism can decline where environments become less attractive, which is a real cost in upland and coastal areas that depend on scenery 1

Problem — environmental cost. Renewables are not impact-free: turbines are considered visually unattractive and can affect birds and bats; large areas of upland land are flooded for reservoirs behind HEP dams; biomass reduces biodiversity where monoculture replaces mixed habitat; and nuclear produces waste that stays dangerous for thousands of years with no permanent disposal solution 1

Weighing the two. The problems are mostly transitional and technical — intermittency can be managed with storage, interconnectors and demand reduction, and set-up costs fall as deployment scales — whereas the problem the shift solves, climate change, is cumulative and irreversible. The strongest argument on the other side is that the backup capacity needed for intermittency keeps fossil fuels in the system longer than the headline percentages suggest 1

Conclusion. The changing energy mix creates more opportunities than problems, but only if it is paired with conservation: reducing demand through insulation, efficiency and transport measures shrinks the backup capacity intermittency requires, which is what turns a 47% renewable share into a genuinely sustainable supply rather than a renewable veneer on a gas-backed grid 1

drill.intro:
What each command word actually wants

Section C is Question 03 (compulsory) plus Question 06 (Energy), worth around 25 marks. The school's exam technique guide opens with the rubric warning for exactly this section: "Don't answer the wrong questions. Know what options you are to choose." Then:

  • 1 mark — state / give / name / "what is…?" One clear point, or the exact definition. The reports show marks lost here for defining the wrong term — energy deficit instead of energy insecurity, food deficit instead of food insecurity.
  • 2 marks — outline / describe / explain how. Point plus development. For "describe the distribution", name continents and regions, give the overall pattern and then the anomaly — the reports repeatedly blame "poor locational knowledge" and "inaccurate compass points" and the use of "bottom of map" instead of south.
  • 2 marks — calculate. Show your working. Full marks for a correct answer even without working; one mark for correct working if the answer is wrong. Obey the rounding instruction exactly.
  • 3 marks — outline / suggest / explain. Either three separate developed points or one three-step chain. The mark schemes award each link in a chain: "economic development increases wages (1) and therefore tax receipts (1) which can be spent on better sanitation (1)".
  • 6 marks — explain / discuss / "to what extent", level marked, AO1 3 + AO2 3. Two or three developed paragraphs with evidence and explanation, plus counter-arguments and a short judgement if the command word is discuss, assess or to what extent. A named example is usually required: "max top Level 2 if the scheme is not named or cannot be inferred", and "max top Level 2 if a local renewable is used" where a fossil fuel was asked for. If the question names two elements — homes/workplaces and transport, advantages and disadvantages — covering only one also caps you at Level 2.
  • The maths. 10% of the paper's marks. In Section C this is percentage change, median, counting from a choropleth map and converting it to a percentage, graph completion and trend description. The reports say the same thing every year: "a significant minority were unable to perform a percentage calculation".

Twelve questions in the real spread: two short, four 4-markers, four 6-markers and two 9-markers. Section C's own extended answers are 6-markers, so the two 9-mark questions here are built from the Section C content in the shape the paper uses elsewhere — worth drilling, because resource management also underpins the Paper 3 issue evaluation. The 6- and 9-mark answers are written as plans, since AQA marks them in levels.

modules.title: Paper 3: Issue Evaluation and Fieldwork
modules.standfirst: The whole of Paper 3 Geographical applications — Section A issue evaluation from the pre-release booklet (37 marks) and Section B fieldwork (39 marks), plus the geographical skills AQA can test on any of the three papers: OS maps and grid references, photographs, graphs and charts, statistics, and how to describe a distribution or a trend. This is the one module where the marks are not in the content you have learned but in the method you bring to material you have never seen — and in how precisely you can describe your own two enquiries, Brighton and Stratford.

subsections.html:
What they actually ask

Every Paper 3 from 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. The 2022 paper was the Covid-reduced version (56 marks) and had no familiar-fieldwork questions at all — every other year ends with a 9-mark question on your own enquiry. The shape is astonishingly stable: the same question types in the same order, year after year, with only the topic changing.

  • The familiar-fieldwork 9-marker (+3 SPaG) — the same question in six costumes: 2019, 2023, 2024 and 2025, plus 2018 and 2020 on the school's list. Learn Brighton for it.
  • Section A's 9-mark decision question (+3 SPaG) — every year, and three of the five made you tick a Yes/No box first.
  • Familiar fieldwork, Q5 — four questions, almost always 2 + 3 + 6 + 9, walking the six strands; the 6-marker rotates location (2019), presentation (2023), collection (2024).
  • Unseen fieldwork, Q4 — skills marks plus the 4-mark "does the data support the hypothesis" in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025; it always asks you to criticise the method too.
  • Section A's 6-mark discussions — two or three every year, usually broader than the booklet's own location.
  • Skills on the figures, and the OS map — calculations, trends and graph completion every year; map questions whenever there is a map (2022, 2024) — and the 2026 booklet has one.

Never asked: designing a whole enquiry from scratch, or a named statistical test.

Every Paper 3 question from 2019–2025, with the exact wordings

Every Paper 3 from 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. The 2022 paper was the Covid-reduced version (56 marks) and had no familiar-fieldwork questions at all — every other year ends with a 9-mark question on your own enquiry. The shape is astonishingly stable: the same question types in the same order, year after year, with only the topic changing.

  • Section A always ends with one 9-mark decision question (+3 SPaG), and it is always the same job. "The Peruvian government has decided to allow the development of new roads in the Amazon. Do you think that this was the right decision? Yes/No" (2019, 9+3); "The proposal to build the waste incinerator was rejected in June 2020. Do you think that this was the correct decision? Yes/No" (2022, 9+3); "Do you think that the cruise ship terminal and port facility… should go ahead? Yes/No" (2023, 9+3); "To what extent do you think that the Tudeley Village development will be a sustainable settlement?" (2024, 9+3); "The social and economic benefits of the Morecambe Bay and Duddon Estuary tidal gateway project are greater than the environmental costs. To what extent do you agree?" (2025, 9+3). Three of the five made you tick a box first.
  • Section A also carries two or three 6-mark discussions, usually broader than the booklet's location. "Tropical rainforests are important at both the local and global scales. Discuss" and "Some activities in areas of tropical rainforests are more damaging than others. To what extent do you agree?" (2019, 6 each); "Waste should be seen as a resource opportunity rather than a problem. Do you agree?" (2022, 6+3) and "Managing waste is both an economic and an environmental issue. Discuss" (2022, 6); "To what extent can tourism create opportunities for economic development?" and "Suggest why the development of tourism is an example of an economic versus environmental issue" (2023, 6 each); "Suggest how brownfield development could help to regenerate urban areas" and "The housing challenge in England is not just about building more houses. Use information from Figure 1 to discuss this statement" (2024, 6 each); "Explain why energy security is important in helping to achieve social and economic well-being" and "All types of renewable energy generation have an impact on the physical environment. Discuss" (2025, 6 each).
  • Section A short questions are mostly skills on the booklet's own figures. Calculate: "Calculate the temperature range for Manaus" (2019, 1); "Complete the following table by calculating the total spending for an average cruise ship visit" (2023, 1); "What percentage of the UK's electricity energy mix (2020) came from fossil fuels?" (2025, 1). Describe a trend or a relationship: "Describe the trend in the rate of recycling in England between 2000–2019" (2022, 2); "Describe the relationship between average house prices and average household income in England (2019)" (2024, 2); "Describe the changes to total energy consumption in the UK (1990–2021)" (2025, 2). Complete a graph: a bar (2023, 1), pie charts (2019 1, 2023 1, 2025 2), a diagram (2019, 2). Read off a value: a multiple-choice percentage (2022, 1), the largest world region (2023, 1), the year exports peaked (2025, 1), a named country in a 5–9.9% band (2025, 1).
  • If there is an OS map in the booklet, there are OS map questions. "Using map evidence, describe the physical geography of the area surrounding the proposed incinerator development" (2022, 2) and "What is the approximate direct distance from the roundabout (470621) to the proposed incinerator site?" (2022, 1, multiple choice); "In which direction is the settlement of Paddock Wood from the proposed Tudeley Village development?" (2024, 1, multiple choice), "What is the approximate straight-line distance between Tonbridge railway station and the proposed Tudeley Village railway station?" (2024, 1, multiple choice) and "Using the Ordnance Survey map, describe the physical geography (relief and drainage) of the area north of the Tonbridge to Paddock Wood railway line" (2024, 4). The 2026 booklet has an OS map of the Lincolnshire reservoir site, so expect the same three.
  • Section A also asks "why here" and "who objects" questions on the specific proposal. "What does the information in the Peru: development fact file suggest about levels of development in Peru?" (2019, 4); "Why will dealing with waste be a challenge for the Cambridge area in the future?" (2022, 2); "Explain how physical and cultural factors are important in attracting visitors to the Cayman Islands" (2023, 4) and "Explain why the proposed development… is called a multi-use development" (2023, 2); "Suggest two reasons why people might be attracted to live in Tudeley Village" (2024, 2) and "Give two ways urban sprawl can damage the environment" (2024, 2); "Suggest why the proposed Morecambe Bay and Duddon Estuary scheme is a multi-use project" (2025, 4).
  • Unseen fieldwork (Q4) is a run of 1- and 2-mark skills questions plus one 4-mark judgement. Complete a table of calculations (2019, 2); complete a pie chart (2019 1, 2024 1); name the sampling method shown (2019, 1, multiple choice); complete a cross-section and describe the slope (2019, 1+1); complete an isoline map and describe its pattern (2023, 1+2); complete a scattergraph (2023, 1); complete a dispersion graph (2024, 1); complete a desire line map (2025, 2); calculate the total EQS score (2022, 1), the mean and total (2024, 2), a percentage (2024, 1), a mean width and a range (2025, 2), a straight-line distance (2025, 1). "Which of the following would be an appropriate alternative way of presenting…" appeared in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, always multiple choice, always 1 mark.
  • And unseen fieldwork always asks you to criticise the other student's method and conclusions. "Suggest why the type of sampling shown in Figure 6 is not always possible" (2019, 2), "Suggest two ways that students might adapt their method in order to obtain more appropriate data" (2019, 2), "Suggest two additional data collection techniques" (2019, 2), "Assess the usefulness of measures of central tendency, such as median, mean and mode" (2019, 4); "Suggest two ways that the primary data collection methods could be adapted to give more reliable data" (2022, 2); "Suggest two ways that the house price survey could be adapted to make it more useful" (2023, 2) and "Suggest and justify one question that the student might use in their questionnaire" (2023, 2); "Suggest one way that the environmental quality survey could be adapted in order to improve the results" (2024, 1) and "Suggest one way that the data collection method could be improved" (2024, 1); "Suggest two ways that the river investigation could be adapted to allow the students to collect more useful data" (2025, 2) and "Suggest one additional question the students could use" (2025, 1).
  • The 4-mark unseen judgement is always "does the data support the hypothesis". "Which area shown in Figure 6 has the highest residential quality? Use the data in Figure 6 to justify your decision" (2022, 4); "To what extent does the data shown in Figure 6 prove the original hypothesis, The further visitors travelled the longer they stayed?" (2023, 4); "To what extent does the data shown in Figure 6 support the original hypothesis, The velocity (speed) of a river increases downstream?" (2024, 4); "To what extent are the students able to make reliable conclusions about the quality of the two shopping centres from the data in Figure 8?" (2025, 4). There is also a 2-mark version: "state two conclusions that the student might draw" (2022, 2), "Suggest the conclusion(s) that the student might reach in relation to the original hypothesis" (2024, 2), "What conclusions can the students make about the relationship between the width and maximum depth of the river?" (2025, 2).
  • Familiar fieldwork (Q5) is four questions, almost always 2 + 3 + 6 + 9, and they walk the six enquiry strands. Location and risk: "Suggest why one set of data you collected in your physical fieldwork enquiry may not have been accurate" (2019, 2) and "Identify one potential risk in your physical geography fieldwork and explain how the risk was reduced" (2019, 3); "Suggest one reason why the chosen location was suitable for data collection in your human geography enquiry" (2023, 2); "For one of your geographical enquiries, outline one reason why it was important to complete a risk assessment in your planning" (2024, 2); "Outline how using secondary data can be useful in a fieldwork enquiry" (2025, 2). Methods: "Justify one primary data collection method used in your physical geography enquiry" (2023, 3); "suggest the advantage(s) of one sampling strategy you used for collecting primary data" (2025, 3) and "Justify the use of your data collection method(s)" in the human enquiry (2025, 6). Presentation: "Justify the use of one data presentation technique, for example a graph or a map, in your human geography enquiry" (2024, 3); "Assess the effectiveness of your data presentation technique(s) in your physical geography enquiry" (2023, 6). The 6-marker rotates between location ("Assess the suitability of the location chosen for your human geography enquiry", 2019), presentation (2023) and collection ("Assess the effectiveness of one or more of the data collection method(s) used in your physical geography enquiry", 2024).
  • The familiar-fieldwork 9-marker is the same question in four costumes. "To what extent did the data collected for one of your enquiries allow you to reach valid conclusions?" (2019, 9+3); "For one of your fieldwork enquiries, to what extent did the data collected help you to obtain accurate results and reach a valid conclusion(s)?" (2023, 9+3); "For one of your fieldwork enquiries, to what extent did your results and conclusions answer the enquiry question or hypothesis?" (2024, 9+3); "Evaluate the effectiveness of one of your fieldwork enquiries and suggest how your enquiry could be improved" (2025, 9+3). School's own list adds the 2018 and 2020 wordings: "assess the extent to which the accuracy of the results and the reliability of the conclusions could be improved" (2018) and "to what extent did your results and conclusions meet the original aims of your enquiry?" (2020). Learn one enquiry in enough depth to answer all six wordings — the school's advice is to learn Brighton for this question because it is the more straightforward to analyse.

What has never come up: no paper in these five years asked you to design a whole enquiry from scratch, and none asked for a named statistical test. The statistics are confined to mean, median, mode, range, percentage and totals — with interquartile range named in the specification and offered in the 2019 mark scheme as a better alternative, which is exactly how to use it.

How Paper 3 is built, in full

Paper 3 is 1 hour 15 minutes, 76 marks, 30% of the GCSE, and it is the only paper where you are told what is coming. Section A — Issue evaluation, 37 marks is set on a pre-release resources booklet released about twelve weeks before the exam; you work through it in class, then sit the paper with a clean copy. Section B — Fieldwork, 39 marks splits in two: Question 4 is unseen fieldwork, somebody else's enquiry presented as data you have to read, analyse and criticise; Question 5 is familiar fieldwork, your own two enquiries, which you have to name on the paper. Six marks of SPaG are available, three on the Section A 9-marker and three on the Section B 9-marker.

The assessment objective split is what makes this paper different. Papers 1 and 2 are mostly AO1 (knowledge) and AO2 (understanding). Paper 3 is heavily AO3 — interpret, analyse and evaluate information to make judgements — and AO4 — select, adapt and use skills and techniques. That is why the examiners keep saying the same thing: copying the booklet is Level 1, using the booklet as evidence is Level 2, and linking points across the booklet to support a judgement is Level 3.

subsections.heading: Section A: how the pre-release booklet actually works
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3.1 Issue evaluation · Pre-Release Teaching Slides 2026, Lesson 1

  • Released twelve weeks early — the 2026 booklet came on 19 March 2026, so yours lands in late March 2027.
  • Three figures, always — the general problem, the range of possible solutions, then one specific proposed scheme with stakeholder views.
  • You annotate your copy in class, then hand it back — a clean, unmarked copy is issued in the exam.
More detail

The specification promises that the sources "could include maps at different scales, diagrams, graphs, statistics, photographs, satellite images, sketches, extracts from published materials, and quotes from different interest groups". In practice the three figures do three different jobs, and knowing which is which tells you which figure to quote in which question:

FigureJob2026 version2024 version2023 version
Figure 1The general problem, with the national statistics and the graphsWater supply and demand in the United KingdomEngland's housing challengeTourism and development
Figure 2The range of possible solutions, plus the OS map or site map of the proposalWater futures (and the OS map of the reservoir site)The proposed Tudeley Village developmentA new cruise ship terminal and port for the Cayman Islands
Figure 3One specific proposed scheme, with the stakeholders arguing about itThe proposed Lincolnshire reservoirDifferent perspectives on the Tudeley Village developmentDifferent views about the proposed cruise ship and port facility

The 2023 examiner's report makes the point explicitly, and it is the most useful sentence in all five reports: "There will be questions that specifically relate to the particular location of the issue and other questions that are more generally linked to the subject under discussion." In 2023, questions 2.2, 2.4 and 3 were about the Cayman Islands; questions 1.4 and 2.6 were broad discussions about tourism and development, and candidates who narrowed those two down to the Cayman Islands limited their own marks. The same trap works in reverse: a 2022 candidate who answered the general "waste as a resource opportunity" question entirely through the Cambridge incinerator was marked as self-limiting.

The twelve weeks are not for memorising the booklet — you get it back in the exam. They are for three things: annotating the figures so you know where every statistic lives, categorising the impacts of the proposal (social, economic, environmental; positive, negative), and ranking them by significance so that when a 9-marker asks for a judgement you already have one.

  • Released twelve weeks early — the 2026 booklet was issued on Thursday 19 March 2026, so yours lands in late March 2027.
  • The issue is synoptic — it is driven by one part of the course but reaches across the whole specification.
  • It always has a human and a physical side — the examiners call it the "human–environmental interface".
  • Some questions are about the place, some are general — read which, because answering the wrong one is self-limiting.

subsections.heading: Reading the resources: using evidence rather than copying it
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3.1 · Pre-Release Teaching Slides 2026, "Geographical applications – 9-marker advice"

  • Copying the booklet is Level 1 — even when the copied sentence is exactly the right sentence.
  • Developing the point is Level 2 — take the statistic, then say what it means and what it causes.
  • Linking across the booklet is Level 3 — this paper is synoptic, so joined-up points outscore separate ones.
  • Always name the figure — "Figure 3 shows that…", "I can see from Figure 1 that…".
More detail

The teaching slides give the model of a Level 3 link, and it is worth learning the shape of it rather than the content: "the scheme will result in 50 families losing their homes, however in order to meet the rising housing demand of the area, water supply must be increased. The reservoir will provide water to 500,000 homes, including the 175,000 new homes which are planned to be built in Lincolnshire over the next 5 years". That is one sentence doing three things — a cost, a counter-argument, and a figure from a different page of the booklet that settles the comparison.

The school's own list of what separates the levels:

LevelWhat it looks like
Level 1 (basic)A limited number of appropriate points, mainly from one figure, largely copied or with limited development. An unsubstantiated judgement.
Level 2 (clear)Not just quoting — the points taken from the figures are developed. A structured response (intro, one way it is, one way it isn't). Good clarity and flow.
Level 3 (detailed)All of the above, plus an understanding of the synoptic nature of the issue: links between different aspects. Very clear grasp of the key concept (usually sustainability), a considered discussion of how complex the judgement is, specific points quoted, and evaluative observations throughout rather than only at the end.

Two further habits from the exam technique guide. For a photograph you cannot read, draw a mental cross through it and find one point in each quadrant. For any source-based answer, use the source as the structure: the headings in the figure become the paragraphs of your answer, which saves you planning time you do not have in 75 minutes.

  • Choosing which figure to use is itself a skill — you have the whole booklet, so pick the strongest evidence.
  • Don't argue against your own choice — balance is fine, but the stronger evidence must support your position.

✗ "Over 2000 local people have signed a petition to stop the development and 50 families will lose their homes." — accurate, relevant, and Level 1, because it is the booklet's words with nothing added.
✓ "Over 2000 local people have signed a petition, and more than 50 families will lose their homes — but the reservoir would supply 500 000 homes, including the 175 000 planned for Lincolnshire in the next five years, so the loss falls on a small local population while the benefit is regional. The scale of the two is not comparable, which is why I judge the scheme socially sustainable overall."

subsections.heading: The short Section A questions — what each mark size wants
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3.1 and 3.4 · DC Exam Technique Guide; examiner's reports 2022 and 2023

  • 2 marks for one reason — point plus development; a bare statement scores one, and most candidates stop there.
  • 3 and 4 marks — develop with "this means that…", "as a result…", and refer to the figure by name.
  • 6 marks — two or three developed paragraphs with evidence; if the command is discuss, include the counter-argument.
  • Answer the command word — describe a pattern is not list the values, and explain is not identify.
More detail

The command words, with what the top answers do (from the school's command word sheet):

CommandWhat it requiresStructure
DescribeSay what you see — trends, extremities, clusters, anomalies — supported with dataOverall pattern → highest and lowest → rate of change → anomaly
SuggestOffer a plausible reason; you are not expected to know it for certainReason → "this means that…" → consequence
ExplainSet out purposes or reasons — say why or how, with explicit reference to the figure"Figure X shows that… This could cause… Consequently…"
DiscussPresent both sides of the argument; it does not have to be balancedOne side → multiple supporting points → counter-arguments → conclusion
AssessJudge the size of the problem or effect, not just its existenceState the issue → explain it → give facts → assess its relative importance and why
EvaluateJudge from evidence, weighing both sides, and rank your pointsPoint → explain → evidence → evaluate; conclusion names the most important factor
To what extentCommit to a degree — definitely, mostly, partly, slightly, not at allMini intro with your overall position → paragraphs → mini conclusion

Two structural rules from the guide. For a 6-marker: two or three main paragraphs with evidence and explanation, no introduction needed, but keep referring back to the question. For a 9-marker: a one-sentence introduction defining key terms and stating your overall argument, two or three paragraphs, and a one-to-two-sentence conclusion that reiterates the judgement.

Medium-length answers (3–6 marks) are rarely point-marked. Develop each point rather than adding more points, and do not worry about stating the obvious — the guide is explicit that this is often required.

  • 1 mark — read off, calculate or shade. The examiners expect "a high degree of accuracy"; bring a ruler and a calculator.
  • 2 marks for one reason — point plus development. A bare statement scores one and the examiners say over half of candidates stop there.
  • 2 marks for two things — two separate points, no development needed. Read which version you have.

✗ 2023 Q4.2, "Suggest what the map shows about the pattern of house prices": a list of areas A–G with their prices. Not creditworthy at all — listing values is not describing a pattern.
✓ "The highest prices are in the town centre and on the western edge; prices fall towards the east, so there is a clear west-to-east decline with a high-value core."

✗ 2023 Q5.1, "Suggest one reason why the chosen location was suitable": "It was near school." One mark only — the examiner's report says most candidates stopped exactly there.
✓ "It was near school, so travel took little time and we had longer on site to collect data." Point + development = two marks. Better still, link the development to the enquiry's aim.

subsections.heading: The 9-mark decision question — how to justify a choice
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3.1 · Pre-Release Teaching Slides 2026, Lesson 3; AQA mark schemes 2019–2025

  • It is nearly all AO3 — 6 marks AO3, 3 AO4, plus 3 for SPaG: the marks are for judgement, not recall.
  • Two legitimate structures — by social / economic / environmental, or by positives / negatives. Pick one and hold it.
  • Short term versus long term is the easiest route to Level 3 — schemes hurt locally now and help regionally later.
  • Finish with a conclusion that decides — the mark scheme penalises "a largely unsubstantiated judgement".

The structure the school teaches, worked on "Assess the sustainability of the proposed Lincolnshire reservoir project. [9]"

  1. Introduction — outline your argument. Overall, is the project socially, economically and environmentally sustainable? Define sustainability in one clause.
  2. Paragraph 1 — socially sustainable? Evidence and explain the social benefits, then recognise the short-term negative social impacts for local people.
  3. Paragraph 2 — environmentally sustainable? Evidence and explain the environmental positives and negatives.
  4. Paragraph 3 — economically sustainable? Evidence and explain the economic positives and negatives.
  5. Short conclusion — reiterate the argument and judge overall sustainability, referring to long-term impacts and whether the scheme will meet the region's rising demand.

The alternative structure — positives then negatives — works equally well, but it makes the synoptic links harder, because the link you want is usually between a social cost and an economic benefit.

More detail
  • It is nearly all AO3 — AO3 6 marks, AO4 3 marks, plus 3 for SPaG. The marks are for judgement, not recall.
  • Tick the box if there is one — and then use your strongest evidence on the side you ticked.
  • Sustainability is the recurring concept — meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.
  • Short term versus long term is the easiest route to Level 3 — most schemes hurt locally now and help regionally later.

✗ Choosing "No", then spending two-thirds of the answer on the advantages. The 2022 and 2023 reports both flag this: candidates "appeared to use evidence which was contrary to their choice, which was slightly self-defeating".
✓ Consider both sides — that is legitimate and often necessary — but make the stronger half of the evidence support your chosen position, and write a conclusion that brings the discussion back to it.

subsections.heading: Worked example, part 1: the UK's water problem (2026 Figures 1 and 2)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3.1 · Geography Pre-Release Booklet 2026, pages 2–5

  • The problem is a mismatch — the wet north and west have the water; the dry, crowded south-east has the demand.
  • Supply is falling, demand is rising — supply down 7% by 2045, demand up 4 billion litres a day by 2050.
  • Two families of solution — increase supply (reservoirs, transfers, desalination, recycling) or reduce demand (efficiency, leakage, behaviour).
More detail

The booklet's water balance graph is the one diagram worth being able to explain, because a "describe the pattern" question on it is nearly free marks. It shows rainfall per day against evaporation per day across the year, in four phases:

PhaseWhat is happening
Groundwater surplusRainfall exceeds evaporation, so water soaks in and fills aquifers; supply can rely on rainfall and surface water.
Groundwater utilisationEvaporation rises above rainfall, so surface water alone is not enough and water is extracted from aquifers.
Groundwater deficitToo much has been taken; aquifers run low and rainfall is still too low to refill them.
Groundwater rechargeRainfall climbs back above evaporation, so rain percolates down and refills the aquifers.

The four key terms the slides define, which are the ones to use in any answer on UK water: groundwater — water that infiltrates and percolates through soil into rock and is stored in aquifers; surface water — water that stays on the surface and flows into rivers and streams, including lakes and reservoirs; water storage — a large volume of water kept, naturally in lakes or artificially in reservoirs; water transfer — the artificial movement of water by pipe and pump from an area of surplus to an area of deficit.

The single most useful analytical sentence about Figure 1, and the one the slides lead with: the South-East has the lowest rainfall in the UK but the highest water demand. Every 6-marker on "why is managing UK water increasingly difficult" starts there and then adds the three multipliers — population growth concentrated in the driest region, climate change cutting supply and making droughts twice as likely, and rising per-person consumption.

On the solutions, the slides set a specific task worth repeating for your own booklet: annotate each strategy as affecting supply or demand, then rank them by effectiveness. The ranking is the part that becomes evaluation marks later. A defensible ranking here: leakage reduction first (20% of supply, no new infrastructure), then water-efficient homes and rainwater harvesting (toilets alone are 30% of use), then reservoirs and transfers (big, slow, expensive, but the only thing that adds real volume), then desalination last (expensive to build and run, energy-hungry for a country that is not short of rain overall).

This is the 2026 booklet. Yours, in 2027, will be about something else entirely — so what matters here is the method, not the content. Work it through anyway: the questions AQA builds on a booklet are the same questions whatever the topic, and you will not get a second worked example on a real booklet.

  • Supply is falling, demand is rising — supply down 7% by 2045 from climate change, demand up 4 billion litres a day by 2050.
  • Leakage is the free win — over 3 billion litres a day lost in England, roughly 20% of supply.
  • People massively underestimate their own use — 57 litres estimated against 140 litres actual.
  • Water quality is part of the supply problem — polluted rivers are sources you cannot use.

UK water supply and demand — the figures that earn marks

  • Supply. Water companies supply over 16 billion litres a day, mostly to residential customers. Surface water is 64% of supply in England and 93% in Wales; England and Wales have 2259 groundwater sources and Scotland 86.
  • The rainfall gradient. Annual average rainfall 1991–2020 ranges from over 2000 mm in the north and west to under 800 mm in the south-east — which is the most heavily populated part of the UK. "Effective rainfall", the part left after evaporation and plant use, runs from more than 2500 mm a year in parts of the north-west to less than 200 mm in parts of eastern England.
  • Seasonal demand. Summer demand can rise by over 20% just as rainfall is lowest; in the hot, dry June of 2020 some companies reported demand up over 70%. Within a day, use spikes in the afternoon and evening as people water gardens.
  • Rising demand. Average household water use is up 70% since 1985. Demand is forecast to rise by about 4 billion litres a day by 2050, and it will not be spread evenly: of the increase in England 2020–2050, the South East takes 50%, the West 20%, Central and East 18%, the North 6% and the South West 6%.
  • Falling supply. Total supply is predicted to fall 7% by 2045 because of climate change, while groundwater use needs to come down for environmental reasons. Between 2020 and 2050 a year with drought restrictions is twice as likely as in the past. The Environment Agency's line: without action there will not be enough water in about 20 years.
  • Per-person use. The average person uses 140 litres a day; the Environment Agency thinks 100 litres or less is achievable within 20 years. Government targets: 122 litres per person per day by 2038 and 110 by 2050. A 2023 survey found people estimated their own use at 57 litres against an actual 140.
  • Where household water goes. Flushing toilets 30%, personal washing 25%, washing machines 21%, washing up 8%, garden 7%, drinking 4%, other 5%. Toilets being the biggest slice is why rainwater harvesting into an underground tank is the strongest home measure.
  • Leakage. Over 3 billion litres a day lost in England, about 20% of supply. Fixing it reduces abstraction from rivers and aquifers as well as serving customers.
  • Pollution. The Environment Agency recorded 325 category 1 and 2 incidents in 2021, up 24% on 2020's 263; 2022 was 307. Causes: illegal dumping, waste treatment, discharged untreated sewage and farming. The two most common pollutants in rivers were untreated sewage and agricultural slurry.
  • The solutions on offer. Water recycling; greywater from showers, baths and washing machines reused in the garden; desalination — the Thames plant makes 140–150 million litres a day, but plants are expensive to build and run; reservoirs storing winter surplus for transfer; reducing pollution; and awareness campaigns.

subsections.heading: Worked example, part 2: the proposed Lincolnshire reservoir (2026 Figure 3)
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3.1 · Geography Pre-Release Booklet 2026, pages 5–7; Pre-Release A3 Evaluation Grid

  • The scale is the argument for it — 55 million m³, 500 000 homes and £2.6 billion of investment.
  • The locality is the argument against it — over 50 families lose homes, farmland floods, construction closes roads.
More detail
  • Anglian Water's proposal — a new reservoir and water transfer system south-east of Sleaford, Lincolnshire.
  • It works by seasonal storage — take winter water from the Trent and Witham, store it, treat it, supply it in summer.
  • The site was chosen on physical factors — suitability of local river systems and geology, assessed against other options.
  • The scale is the argument for it — 55 million m³, up to 166 million litres a day, 500 000 homes, £2.6 billion of investment.
  • Everyone agrees water is needed — including the NFU, so the dispute is about this scheme at this scale, not about reservoirs.

The proposed Lincolnshire reservoir, Anglian Water — facts and figures

  • Location. South-east of Sleaford, Lincolnshire, between the villages of Scredington, Helpringham and Swaton. Lincolnshire is one of the driest parts of the UK and has a rapidly growing population, with 175 000 new homes planned over the next five years.
  • Mechanism. Water is taken from the River Trent and River Witham in winter when levels are highest, transferred to the reservoir, then treated and supplied in the hotter summer months. An overflow drain manages levels and reduces winter flood risk.
  • Capacity. 55 million cubic metres of water; supplying up to 166 million litres a day to 500 000 homes; bringing £2.6 billion of direct and indirect investment to the area.
  • Design concessions. Embankments deliberately gently sloping to be less visually intrusive; the shape designed to encourage wildlife and to be attractive to visit; local habitats to be restored on completion, increasing the diversity of wildlife.
  • Stakeholders consulted. The Environment Agency, Natural England, local authorities, the agricultural industry, and local community groups.
  • Opportunities. Open for public use: sailing, wind surfing, cycling, walking. A network of footpaths and cycle tracks; an education centre and visitor centre; new wildlife and wetland habitats; improved public transport; renewable energy opportunities. Expected to attract thousands of visitors a year, creating opportunities for local business.
  • Opposition. Over 2000 local people signed a petition against it. More than 50 families will lose their homes; local businesses will suffer and jobs will go. During construction some local roads will close and others become congested — narrow country roads carrying construction traffic, with an increased risk of accidents. One resident's alternative: smaller reservoirs nearer major towns, plus tackling leakage and pollution.
  • The farmers. Flooding a large area removes homes and livelihoods. The uncertainty is itself damaging — it is affecting mental health and makes further investment in the farms pointless, at a time when farmers are being encouraged to grow and sell more food locally. Other businesses, such as horse-riding stables, will go too.
  • The NFU's position — the most useful source in the booklet, because it is on both sides. It fully supports expanding water supply infrastructure as a response to climate change and population growth, and says farming businesses will benefit from the extra water and that resilience in domestic food production matters. But it warns that large-scale schemes significantly harm local farm businesses and communities, and insists reservoirs be designed to fit the local environment, disruption be minimised, and local people be actively involved in decision-making at every stage.
  • The honest caveat, in Anglian Water's own words. The outlined area on the map is "only indicative and is likely to change as proposals develop" — worth quoting, because it supports the Local-Authority-style point that there is a gap between a plan and a reality.

The evaluation grid, filled in — this is what you build for your own booklet

PositiveNegative / limitation
Social166 million litres a day to 500 000 homes meets rising demand, including from the 175 000 new Lincolnshire homes. Other strategies — cutting consumption, improving efficiency — matter but cannot meet that demand alone. Open to the public for sailing, wind surfing, cycling and walking, with new footpaths and cycle tracks.Conflict with local people: over 2000 signed a petition; farmers especially oppose it over loss of farmland. More than 50 families lose their homes and local businesses suffer. Road closures during construction cut access and congest other routes. One farmer reports the uncertainty is harming mental health.
EnvironmentalEnvironmental concerns built into the design — gently sloping embankments, a shape chosen to encourage wildlife. Habitats restored on completion, increasing diversity. Stores excess winter water for drier months, making the area more drought-resistant: an important adaptation to climate change in a region whose rainfall reliability is falling.Floods a large area of mostly greenfield land, including farmland — harming biodiversity, reducing habitat and losing trees. Residents argue the scale could be reduced or avoided by attacking leakage and pollution and promoting greywater systems instead.
Economic£2.6 billion of direct and indirect investment. Thousands of visitors a year creating opportunities for local business and supporting regional economic growth. The NFU accepts that farm businesses need the water and that expanding supply builds resilience in food production.Flooding the land removes farmers' homes and livelihoods and closes other leisure businesses such as riding stables. Local businesses lose trade and people lose jobs. The NFU warns large-scale schemes significantly harm local farm businesses and communities.

Then do the two things the slides ask for and most students skip: within each box, number the points from most to least significant, and decide where your overall judgement sits. That is the difference between having notes and having an answer.

subsections.heading: Section B: the six enquiry strands, and the vocabulary that scores
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3.2 Fieldwork · Fieldwork Revision Booklet 2026, Part 1

  • Every Section B question maps onto one of six strands — question, methods, presentation, analysis, conclusion, evaluation.
  • You must name both enquiries on the paper — titles have their own lines, and the answers must match them.
  • Six buzz words carry the evaluation marks — accurate, representative, reliable, valid, subjective, bias.
  • Risk assessment has six stages — and the score is severity (1–5) × likelihood (1–5), maximum 25.
More detail
StrandWhat AQA can ask about it
1. A suitable questionWhat makes a question or hypothesis suitable; the geographical theory or concept underpinning it; appropriate sources of primary and secondary evidence, including the choice of location; the risks of human and physical fieldwork and how they are reduced.
2. Selecting, measuring and recording dataPrimary versus secondary data; identifying and selecting appropriate physical and human data; the pros and cons of different sampling methods; describing and justifying collection methods.
3. Processing and presenting dataThe range of visual, graphical and cartographic methods available; selecting and using one accurately; describing, explaining and adapting presentation methods.
4. Describing, analysing and explaining dataDescribing, analysing and explaining results; establishing links between data sets; using statistical techniques — percentage increase and decrease, spread, median, mean, mode, range, quartiles and interquartile range; identifying anomalies.
5. Reaching conclusionsDrawing evidenced conclusions in relation to the original aims.
6. EvaluationProblems with the collection methods; limitations of the data collected; other data that would have been useful; the extent to which the conclusions were reliable.

The six words the school tells you to get into your answers, with what each one actually means:

WordWhat it is aboutWorked on John's fieldwork
AccurateHow close a measurement is to the true value — did everyone collect it the same way?The drop from the top of a Brighton groyne to the beach was often more than a metre, and the groynes did not have straight edges, so a one-metre ruler introduced error.
RepresentativeWhether the sample reflects what is actually happening; usually a sampling questionReadings every 2 m along a 30 m groyne — systematic and fine. Five surveys of people in a park the size of the Olympic Park — not representative of that population.
ReliableConsistency and repeatability — would the same method on another day give the same result?One October day at Brighton; a sunny weekday morning at Stratford. Neither is repeatable across seasons or across the week.
ValidWhether the conclusion is genuinely supported by the data, given its accuracy and reliabilityInternal validity: do the conclusions hold for this beach? External validity: do they hold for all beaches?
Subjective / biasData that depends on the observer's judgement, and the systematic distortion that followsBi-polar and environmental quality surveys. Classmates scored the same sites differently; a standardisation survey at one agreed point, then adjusting to the group average, reduces it.
AnomalyA reading that does not fit the pattern — identify it, suggest why, say what it does to the conclusionA single groyne with unexpected sediment, or one EQS site scoring against the trend because of where you stood.

Sampling. It is never possible to measure everything — nobody is sizing every pebble on Brighton beach — so you sample, and the point of sampling is to reduce bias. Random sampling is based on chance, so everything has an equal probability of selection and bias is minimised, but coverage can be patchy. Systematic sampling takes readings at regular intervals — every 2 m along the groyne — which guarantees even coverage and is easy to justify, but can miss variation between the intervals and can coincide with a pattern in the landscape. Stratified sampling divides the population into groups and samples each in proportion, which is what the Stratford questionnaire needed and did not have: three random people per site missed whole age groups.

Risk assessment has six stages: identify the hazards; decide who might be at risk and how; work out the level of risk as severity (1–5) × likelihood (1–5), maximum 25; decide how it can be reduced or managed; record the findings and act on them; review and update. A 2-mark question — "outline one reason why it was important to complete a risk assessment" (2024) — wants the reason, not the list.

  • You must name both enquiries on the paper — titles have their own lines, and the answers must match the title you wrote.
  • The school used questions, not hypotheses — deliberately, because a question allows a "partly" answer when the evidence is mixed.
  • Two enquiries, contrasting environments, one physical and one human — and at least one must show physical–human interaction.
  • Risk assessment has six stages — and the risk score is severity (1–5) × likelihood (1–5), to a maximum of 25.

subsections.heading: John's physical enquiry: groynes at Brighton Beach
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3.2, strands 1–6 · Brighton Fieldwork Model Answers; Fieldwork Evaluation Summary

  • The title — "Evaluate the success of groynes as a method of coastal management on Brighton beach."
