  • The theory — groynes interrupt longshore drift, trapping sediment updrift and maintaining a protective beach.
  • The conclusion — the groynes work: they stop longshore drift and build a protective beach.
  • Learn this one for the 9-marker — the school's explicit advice, because it is more straightforward to analyse.

Brighton — the enquiry in one panel

  • Question. Evaluate the success of groynes as coastal management on Brighton beach — success means stopping longshore drift and maintaining the protective beach. Drift runs west to east, so west is updrift.
  • Methods. Beach slope profiles at 2 m systematic intervals either side of three adjacent concrete groynes from a 3 km stretch, plus a bi-polar survey from −3 to +3 on erosion vulnerability, aesthetics, lifespan and disturbance.
  • Presentation. The profiles as line graphs (continuous data), the bi-polar scores as a bar chart (category data).
  • Data and conclusion. Far more sediment on the west side and a clear deficit east, so the groynes are successful: they interrupt longshore drift and build a protective beach.
  • Evaluation. Only three concrete groynes out of 3 km and nothing measured between the intervals; one day in October, so no seasonal comparison; the bi-polar scores are subjective.
  • Improvements. More groynes along the 3 km, two contrasting seasons, concrete against wooden, a standardised bi-polar scale, and the results mapped with GIS.
More detail
  • Two methods — beach slope profiles at 2 m systematic intervals, and a bi-polar analysis survey from −3 to +3.
  • The result — far more sediment on the west (updrift) side, a clear deficit on the east (downdrift) side.

Brighton, East Sussex — the enquiry in the detail the exam wants

  • Aim. To investigate whether groynes have been a successful method of coastal management on Brighton beach. To count as successful they must stop longshore drift and help maintain the protective beach.
  • Location, and why it suited. A coastal town in East Sussex, approximately 80 km south of London — accessible by coach in a day. It is a tourist beach, so relatively safe. And there are many groynes along this stretch, giving a choice of sample sites for measuring the success of coastal management. Longshore drift here runs west to east, so west is updrift and east is downdrift.
  • Risk, and how it was reduced. Powerful destructive waves were approaching the coastline, so measurements were taken at a safe distance from the breaking waves, and teachers had checked tide times to ensure enough safe beach. Alternatively: the steep pebble beach risked slipping, so appropriate footwear was worn and work was done sensibly in small groups.
  • Method 1 — beach slope profiles. Measuring the build-up and depletion of sediment on the updrift (west) and downdrift (east) side of a groyne, to see whether the groynes were stopping longshore drift. Measured from just before the waves broke (for safety) inland towards the sea wall, at 2 m systematic intervals for a detailed picture. Done on three adjacent groynes, all concrete, out of a roughly 3 km stretch of coast.
  • Method 2 — bi-polar analysis survey. Rating each management strategy from −3 to +3 on four variables: vulnerability to erosion, aesthetic value, lifespan, and disturbance to natural processes and habitats. This turns a qualitative judgement into a number that can be plotted, and allows the groynes to be compared with the sea wall.
  • Presentation. Two slope profiles drawn as line graphs, one for each side of the groyne — appropriate because sediment height is continuous data and a line shows how height and angle change from shoreline to sea wall. The groyne shaded grey and the beach yellow so the two profiles could be compared visually. A bar chart of the bi-polar scores comparing the sea wall with the groynes — appropriate for category data, and the negative half of the y-axis shows where each strategy fails.
  • Analysis and conclusion. The west side of the groyne had markedly more sediment, because longshore drift was interrupted and sediment trapped; the east side had a significant deficit, suggesting the groyne was blocking sediment transport along the beach. Conclusion: the groynes are a successful method of coastal management — they stop longshore drift and build up a protective beach.
  • Evaluation — accuracy. Only three groynes out of a 3 km stretch, so no complete picture of the whole coastline; only concrete groynes, so no comparison with wooden ones. Sampling at 2 m intervals leaves variation between intervals unmeasured. Tape measures not laid completely flat, and the drop from the top of the groyne often exceeded a 1 m ruler, on edges that were not straight. Beach profiles are also strongly affected by tide — low tide is needed for reliable access — and ranging poles can sink or go out of alignment while clinometer readings vary between people.
  • Evaluation — reliability. Data collected on one day in October, so no seasonal comparison. Geographical theory says destructive waves in winter produce steeper beaches and constructive waves in summer gentler profiles, so October's stronger winds and more powerful destructive waves may have shaped both profiles. The bi-polar survey is subjective: scores from other groups showed a great range of variation, and judging lifespan or vulnerability to erosion properly needs secondary data the class did not have.
  • Improvements. Repeat measurements on more groynes along the full 3 km; collect in two contrasting seasons; compare concrete with wooden groynes; standardise the bi-polar scoring before starting; plot the bi-polar results on a digital map using GIS so different parts of the beach can be compared spatially.

subsections.heading: John's human enquiry: Olympic regeneration at Stratford
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3.2, strands 1–6 · Stratford Fieldwork Model Answers; Fieldwork Evaluation Summary

  • The title — "To what extent has the Olympic Regeneration of Stratford been successful?"
  • The theory — regeneration of a brownfield site brings social, economic and environmental change, unevenly.
  • The conclusion — largely successful, especially environmentally, but not evenly across the area.
  • The weakness is the sample — three people per site, one weekday, probably more tourists than residents.

Stratford — the enquiry in one panel

  • Question. To what extent has the Olympic regeneration of Stratford been successful — social, economic and environmental change on a brownfield site, 2012 Games but ongoing.
  • Methods. A three-question questionnaire (age band, a closed benefit question, an open three-word question) with three people at each of five sites, plus environmental quality surveys at sites A–E scoring buildings, traffic, open space and general quality.
  • Presentation. Four bar charts, one per EQS category, and a word cloud of the open question per site.
  • Data and conclusion. Every site positive, Site B the London Blossom Garden highest at +23, Hackney Wick lowest for buildings, 75% of answers "a lot": largely successful but not equally.
  • Evaluation. The EQS is subjective, so a group average removed outliers; three people per site on one weekday midday, probably over-representing tourists rather than residents.
  • Improvements. A larger stratified sample across days and times, results mapped with GIS, and secondary economic data — deprivation indices and BRES.
More detail
  • Two methods — a three-question questionnaire, and environmental quality surveys at five sites A–E.
  • The result — all five sites scored positively, but the inside-the-park sites scored far higher than the fringes.

Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, Stratford, East London — the enquiry in detail

  • Aim. To investigate how successful the regeneration of Stratford has been, as a result of the 2012 Olympic Games and the wider investment in the area.
  • Location, and why it suited. The Olympic Park lies north of the River Thames in East London, 45–60 minutes from school by train or coach — accessible. The Games ended in 2012 but regeneration continued and is ongoing, so the project is contemporary. It is the transformation of a brownfield site, with social, economic and environmental impacts all available to study. The former Athletes' Village is now the residential area East Village.
  • Risk, and how it was reduced. There are canals and waterways in the park, so a safe distance was kept from the water's edge and sensible behaviour was enforced. Alternatively: the site is large and getting lost was a risk, so maps and mobile phones were used and emergency contact numbers carried.
  • Method 1 — questionnaire. Three questions, asked of three people at each of the five sites. Q1 age band (16–25, 25–35, 35–45, 45–55, 60+) to see whether regeneration had affected age groups differently. Q2, a closed question: "To what extent do you think this area has benefited from the Olympic Park redevelopment?" — categories "A lot", "Somewhat", "Unsure", "Not benefited" — giving data that could be categorised. Q3, an open question: three words to describe the environment here, giving a "sense of place" and letting perception be compared with secondary data.
  • Method 2 — environmental quality survey. Five EQSs at five sites A–E, scoring four categories: buildings, traffic, open space and general quality. The class stayed in one position at each site for the whole survey, because sites looked different from different aspects. This allowed quantitative comparison between the sites and a test of whether regeneration had reached all of them equally.
  • The results. Site B, the London Blossom Garden, ranked highest with an EQS score of +23; every site scored positively. Site A, near Hackney Wick station, scored lowest for building quality — it is peripheral to the park, has grown since the 1990s with artists in converted warehouses, and has graffiti and more traffic. On the questionnaire, 75% of responses to Q2 were "a lot", and 100% were "a lot" or "somewhat".
  • Presentation. EQS data as four bar charts, one per category — bar charts suit discrete, categorical data and let site characteristics be compared visually, and they turn subjective scores into plottable quantities. Questionnaire Q3 as a word cloud per site, which suits subjective qualitative data and sizes the most frequent words for emphasis — clean, safe, green.
  • Analysis and conclusion. Positive change to buildings, traffic and environment across all five sites, but not equally: the sites inside the park (the Blossom Garden, the 2012 Gardens) had the highest environmental quality, while the fringes such as Hackney Wick had been less affected. The questionnaire data aligned with the EQS — people were more positive about inside-the-park sites — which strengthens the conclusion. Conclusion: the regeneration has been largely successful, especially environmentally.
  • Evaluation — accuracy and bias. The EQS is subjective; classmates scored the same sites differently, showing bias. Taking a group average of the total for each site removed outliers and improved accuracy and reliability. Environmental variation within a site can skew the score, and a single observer's results need benchmarking for consistency.
  • Evaluation — the sample. Three people per site is not a large enough sample, which reduces reliability. Data was collected one weekday, in the middle of the day: local residents — the people who actually experience the regeneration — were likely at work, so the sample probably over-represented tourists with a superficial view. A weekend would have reached more locals. Stratified sampling should have been used to guarantee a spread of age groups. Some participants had no historical knowledge of the area, which limits how useful their comparison can be. And a sunny, quiet day may have pushed responses positive.
  • Improvements. A larger and stratified sample across different days and times; bar charts or proportional symbols plotted on a map, ideally using GIS, to give a spatial view of inequality — more traffic by a main road, less by a park. Add secondary economic data, because most of the primary data was qualitative and descriptive: deprivation indices from gov.uk, and local business growth from the government's Business Register and Employment Survey (BRES).

✗ "We did an EQS and it showed the regeneration was successful." No title, no site count, no score, no limitation — and the examiners report that answers like this score one mark out of six.
✓ "At five sites across Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park we scored buildings, traffic, open space and general quality. Site B, the London Blossom Garden, scored +23, the highest; Site A near Hackney Wick scored lowest for building quality. Because the scoring is subjective we took a group average, which removed outliers — so the conclusion that regeneration has been uneven is reasonably valid."

subsections.heading: Unseen fieldwork: answering on somebody else's enquiry
subsections.html:
Spec 3.3.2, "questions based on the use of fieldwork materials from an unfamiliar context"

  • "Adapt" means change what is there — not add a new method; 2022's scheme refused credit for suggesting questionnaires.
  • "Additional" means something not already asked — 2023 refused credit for repeating the distance question in the figure.
  • Criticise the method, not the student — sample size, subjectivity, one day, one time, narrow scale, limited criteria.
More detail

The question types recur so reliably that they can be learned as a list. Seen across 2019–2025:

TypeWhat to do
Suggest a suitable enquiry question from a photograph or mapStart from the theory for that landscape, then phrase it as "How does X change with Y at Z?" — e.g. for a river's long profile: how does velocity, width, depth, gradient or bedload change downstream? (The Bradshaw model is the theory to name.)
Identify a primary technique for that questionMatch the technique to the variable: clinometer for gradient, flowmeter for velocity, tape measure for width, cross-sectional area × velocity for discharge, Power's Roundness Index for bedload shape, EQS or questionnaire or land-use survey or pedestrian count or traffic count for human enquiries.
Identify a secondary sourceData from previous years, OS maps, GIS, historic photographs, newspapers and online articles, Environment Agency flow and depth records, official economic data.
Describe a risk at this locationRiver or coast: deep water, fast flow, cold water, tides, slippery or uneven surfaces, mass movement, the drop from a groyne, water pollution. Upland: poor weather, steep slopes, uneven ground. Urban: working near roads and the need to watch for vehicles.
Say why a measurement may not be accurateInaccurate measurement; poor recording; too few readings to average reliably; and for any bi-polar or EQS, the answer is always that it rests on personal judgement, so it is subjective.
Complete a graph or mapUse a ruler. Pie chart: convert the percentage to degrees (1% = 3.6°). Isoline: join equal values smoothly, keeping higher values on one side. Dispersion graph: one dot per value on the correct line. Desire line: correct direction and a length matching the scale.
Choose an appropriate presentation methodThe 2023 report says only a very small proportion of candidates got this right. Learn the table in the skills section below — categories to bars or a pie, continuous to a line, relationship to a scattergraph, spread to a dispersion graph, land use to a land-use map, flows to flow lines or desire lines, equal values to isolines, density to a choropleth, totals at points to proportional symbols.
Suggest how to adapt or improve the methodMore sites; sites further apart; larger sample or repeated measurements at each site; different days, times or seasons (and qualify which); more accurate or specialist equipment; wider range of criteria; wider numeric scale; avoid an odd-numbered scale so 3 is not a default; describe what each score means to reduce subjectivity; use more observers.
Suggest a conclusion (2 marks)One mark for a conclusion that genuinely relates to the stated hypothesis; the second for developing it or using the data. It must answer the hypothesis in the stem, not the data in general.
"To what extent does the data support the hypothesis" (4 marks)Level 2 needs you to say it appears to support it but then consider the strength of the relationship and name the anomaly, with data. A manipulated calculation with the wrong conclusion is capped at Level 1.

Two mark-scheme details worth knowing because they are counter-intuitive. The 2022 adaptation question refused credit for "reference to questionnaires/asking people" because the question said adapt, so the answer had to be about the methods already in the figure. And 2019's "suggest two ways students might adapt their method to obtain more appropriate data" came after a figure showing the sample was all over-50s surveyed on a Saturday morning in an area where 48% of the population is over 50 and 56% of that group is female — the point being that the data in the stem tells you what is wrong with the method.

  • Read the stem first — it names the aim or hypothesis, and every answer has to be judged against it.
  • It is all AO3 and AO4 — interpretation and skills. Nothing here rewards what you know about the place.
  • Attempt the graph-completion questions — the reports repeatedly note that many candidates skip them for no reason.
  • "Adapt" means change what is there — not add a new method. 2022's mark scheme refused credit for suggesting questionnaires.
  • "Additional" means something not already asked — 2023 refused credit for repeating the distance question already in the figure.

subsections.heading: OS maps: grid references, scale, distance, direction and relief
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4.1 Cartographic skills · examiner's reports 2022 and 2024

  • Eastings before northings — along the corridor, then up the stairs. Always.
  • Four figures name a square, six figures name a point — the extra digits are tenths of a square, so 100 m.
  • Scale — at 1:50 000, 2 cm on the map is 1 km; at 1:25 000, 4 cm is 1 km.
  • Relief from contours and spot heights — close contours mean steep, wide spacing means gentle.
More detail

Reading a grid reference. Take the 2026 booklet's OS extract of the reservoir site: its eastings run 08 to 16 and its northings 36 to 44. A question asking "what is found in grid square 1337?" means the square whose south-west corner is easting 13, northing 37 — go along to 13, then up to 37, and the square is the one up and to the right of that corner. For a six-figure reference you divide the square into tenths: 134 376 means easting 13 and four-tenths across, northing 37 and six-tenths up. Two habits stop most errors: always write the easting pair first, and remember that the number you read is the line to the left and below your point, never the nearest line.

Distance. Count grid squares — each is 1 km — and estimate the fraction. For a straight line, use the edge of a ruler or the straight edge of the answer booklet against the scale bar; for a curved line, mark a strip of paper along the route in short straight sections. The multiple-choice versions (2022 and 2024) only need you to get within a kilometre, which counting squares does comfortably. For area, count the whole squares inside the shape, then count part-squares and treat roughly two halves as one — so the answer comes out in km².

Direction. Give the eight points of the compass, and say it from the right feature. 2024 asked the direction of Paddock Wood from the proposed development: the answer was east. Getting the two features the wrong way round is the standard way to lose this mark.

Relief and drainage, which is what "describe the physical geography" means. The 2024 mark scheme shows the two levels clearly: Level 1 is "high land and low land, and a river"; Level 2 uses the map "with some precision" — the slope, the direction of flow of rivers, the height of the land. So the answer that reaches Level 2 looks like: "The land is low-lying, rising slightly towards the north, with gentle, relatively flat slopes" — a statement about height, a statement about gradient, and a direction, each one traceable to something on the map.

What else AQA can ask from an OS map. The specification lists it: four- and six-figure references; scale, distance and direction including curved-line distance; gradient, contour and spot height; identifying landscape features and describing their characteristics; relating cross-sections to relief features; drawing inferences about patterns of relief, drainage, settlement, communications and land use; interpreting transects; describing coastal, fluvial or glacial landscapes from a large-scale map; and inferring human activity, including tourism, from map evidence. The 2019 paper asked you to complete a cross-section from a contour map and then describe the slope from a point to the river — so cross-sections belong in the unseen fieldwork section too.

Photographs. Ground, aerial and satellite photographs can all appear, and the skills are: describe the human and physical landscape in them, draw a sketch from one, and annotate rather than merely label — a label names a feature, an annotation explains it. A field sketch beats a photograph when you want to select: you can leave out clutter, exaggerate what matters and write explanation onto the drawing. A photograph beats a field sketch for accuracy and speed, and it cannot be accused of bias in what it includes.

  • Four figures name a square, six figures name a point — the extra digits are tenths of a square, so 100 m.
  • Each grid square is 1 km by 1 km — which makes it 1 km² and gives you distance and area for free.
  • Scale — at 1:50 000, 2 cm on the map is 1 km; at 1:25 000, 4 cm is 1 km.
  • Relief from contours and spot heights — close contours mean steep, wide spacing means gentle, a lone spot height still counts.
  • "Physical geography" means relief and drainage — height, slope, rivers, lakes, ponds, woodland. Not roads and buildings.

✗ 2022 Q2.2, "Using map evidence, describe the physical geography of the area surrounding the proposed incinerator": roads and specific buildings. The examiner's report says very few candidates appeared to understand the term "physical geography" at all.
✓ "The land is low-lying and flat — a single contour line crosses the area and there is a spot height of 4 m just north of the proposed site. There are streams, lakes and ponds nearby, so drainage is dense and the water table is likely to be high."

subsections.heading: Graphs and charts: choosing them, completing them, reading them
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4.2 Graphical skills · examiner's reports 2023 and 2024

  • Match the chart to the data type — categories, continuous, relationship, spread, location, flow, density.
  • Know the map-based ones — choropleth, isoline, dot, desire line, proportional symbol, flow line.
  • Justifying a choice needs two halves — why it suits the data, and why it suits the question.
More detail
TechniqueUse it whenLimitation to name
Bar chartComparing discrete or categorical data — EQS scores by category, land use counts, bi-polar totalsSays nothing about change over time or relationships; too many bars becomes unreadable
Divided bar chartShowing the composition of a total, especially several totals side by sideHard to compare the middle segments between bars
Line graphContinuous data — a beach slope profile, a trend over time, a river's long profileGets crowded with several lines; implies values between the points that you did not measure
Pie chartProportions of a single whole — the split of household water use, questionnaire response categoriesUseless for comparing two wholes of different size; small slices are hard to read; 1% = 3.6°
HistogramFrequency in equal class intervalsNeeds sensible class intervals, and the choice of interval changes the apparent shape
ScattergraphThe relationship between two variables — river width against depth, distance travelled against nights stayedShows correlation, not cause; a best-fit line can hide a weak relationship
Dispersion graphThe spread of repeated readings at each site — the 2024 river timingsShows spread but not relationship; crowded where many values repeat
Population pyramidAge and sex structure of a populationOne snapshot; says nothing about why the structure is as it is
PictogramSimple counts for a non-specialist audiencePart-symbols are imprecise
Choropleth mapDensity or rate shaded by area — house price bands by districtImplies uniformity within each area and sharp change at the boundaries; the class intervals you pick drive the story
Isoline mapJoining points of equal value — temperature across a town, contours, pressureInterpolation between readings is a guess; the 2023 report says most candidates could not construct one
Dot mapAbsolute numbers located in spaceDots merge where density is high, so the eye undercounts
Desire line mapMovement from origin to destination, one line per journey or personLines are straight, so they ignore the actual route; clutters at the destination
Flow line mapVolume of movement along actual routes, line width proportional to flowWide lines obscure the map beneath
Proportional symbol mapA total at each located point — EQS score per site, visitors per attractionLarge symbols overlap; the eye judges area badly
Land use mapWhat each plot or building is used for — the 2024 "survey of main functions"Categories are a judgement; mixed-use buildings do not fit
Word cloudQualitative responses where frequency matters — the Stratford three-words questionImpossible to compare sites rigorously; no numbers behind it
GISLayering data onto a digital map so spatial patterns emergeNeeds software and accurate locations; easy to make look authoritative when the underlying data is thin

Justifying a presentation technique (3 marks, 2024). Three things get three marks: name the technique and the data it shows; say why it suits that type of data; say what it let you see in relation to the aim. The Brighton line graph is the model — continuous data, shows how height and angle change from shoreline to sea wall, which is exactly what tells you whether the groyne trapped sediment.

Assessing effectiveness (6 marks, 2023). The examiner's report on this question is brutal: a significant proportion of candidates wrote about data collection instead of data presentation and scored nothing. Those who stayed on topic ranged from merely naming techniques up to assessing them on ease of construction, visual clarity, and usefulness for analysing the data — which are the three criteria to structure the answer around. Two PEEL paragraphs, one per technique, each with a limitation and an improvement.

  • The commonest 1-mark question in Section B is "which presentation method" — in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.
  • Completing a graph is a free mark, so attempt it — with a ruler; the reports say accuracy suffers without one.
  • Every technique has a limitation — name one, because the 6-markers ask you to assess effectiveness.

subsections.heading: Statistics, trends and distributions: the numbers and the words
subsections.html:
Spec 3.4.3 and 3.4.4 Numerical and statistical skills · mark schemes 2019, 2022, 2024, 2025

  • Percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100 — the original, not the new value, on the bottom.
  • Describe a distribution with location — where the high values are, where the low ones are, and the direction.
  • Describe a trend with shape and data — direction, rate of change, peaks, troughs and anomalies, with figures.
  • Describe a relationship with its strength — positive or negative, strong or weak, and name the anomaly.
More detail

The calculations AQA has actually set. 2019: fill in a table of percentage loss of countryside, given the original area and the area lost (24 of 240 = 10%; 160 of 320 = 50%; 84 of 420 = 20%). 2022: total an environmental quality score across a bi-polar table, then complete mean, mode, median and range for thirteen beach widths — the answers were mean 17.6, mode 17, median 17.5, range 4. 2023: total three components of cruise spending. 2024: a percentage from a frequency table (29 of 50 people = 58%), and a total and mean for an EQS column (4+4+4+3+4+5 = 24, mean 4). 2025: a mean of six river widths (1680 ÷ 6 = 280 cm) and the range of six maximum depths (46 − 24 = 22 cm), and a straight-line distance from a scaled diagram.

Percentage change. (new − original) ÷ original × 100. Water pollution incidents rose from 263 in 2020 to 325 in 2021: 62 ÷ 263 × 100 = 24%, which is the figure the 2026 booklet quotes. Running it the wrong way round — dividing by the new value — gives 19% and loses the mark. For a decrease, the answer is negative or stated as "a fall of n%", and the original is still the denominator.

Describing a distribution. A distribution is spatial, so the answer needs location words: where the highest values are, where the lowest are, and the direction of change between them. The model for the 2026 rainfall map: "The northern and western parts of the UK are the wettest, with over 2000 mm a year in the north-west of Scotland and parts of Wales, while the south and east are the driest, with under 800 mm in the south-east — so rainfall decreases from north-west to south-east." Three components: highest with a figure and a place, lowest with a figure and a place, and the gradient between them. The 2023 report adds the Level 2 refinement for a map: use direction and distance, and comment on the rate of change — "temperature falls with distance from the town centre, but more steeply towards the west".

Describing a trend. A trend is temporal. Give the overall direction first, then the rate, then the detail: "Recycling rates rose steeply between 2000 and 2010, then levelled off after about 2012, remaining close to 45% to 2019 — so although the long-term trend is upward, progress has stalled for the last seven years." Quote the start and end values, name any peak or trough with its year, and mention anomalies if there are any — and if there are none, the exam technique guide says do not worry about it.

Describing a relationship. Name the direction and the strength, then evidence both: "There is a weak positive relationship — generally the further visitors travelled the longer they stayed, with those travelling over 200 km staying 7 or more days, but the scatter is wide and one visitor who travelled 50 km stayed 8 days, which is a clear anomaly." The 2023 report says the highest marks went precisely to candidates who judged the strength and identified anomalies with data; "it is a positive correlation" on its own is a Level 1 answer. The specification also expects you to sketch a trend line or line of best fit, interpolate and extrapolate from it, and to identify weaknesses in selective statistical presentation — a truncated y-axis, a cherry-picked date range, a sample of five.

Anomalies. A 2-mark question in 2020 asked how anomalies in your data could affect your enquiry, so have an answer ready: an anomaly pulls the mean away from the typical value and inflates the range, so it can make a pattern look weaker or stronger than it is; identifying it, suggesting a cause, and quoting the median instead is what protects the conclusion.

  • Five measures, all examinable by calculation — mean, median, mode, range, interquartile range.
  • Measures of central tendency have limits — and a 4-mark question in 2019 was entirely about those limits.
  • Describe a distribution with location — where the high values are, where the low ones are, and the direction of change.
  • Describe a trend with shape and data — overall direction, rate of change, peaks and troughs, anomalies, with figures.

The five measures, worked on the 2019 housing quality data

Twelve areas scored for housing quality on a 1–10 scale: 4, 6, 6, 2, 9, 3, 10, 1, 5, 8, 10, 1. Sorted: 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 8, 9, 10, 10.

  • Mean — add them and divide by how many. 65 ÷ 12 = 5.41 (the mark scheme accepts "approximately 5.5"). Uses every value, which is its strength and its weakness: one extreme reading drags it.
  • Median — the middle value when ordered. Twelve values, so average the 6th and 7th: (5 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5.5. Unaffected by extremes, which is why it beats the mean on skewed data.
  • Mode — the most common value. Here 1, 6 and 10 each appear twice, so the data is trimodal and the mode cannot usefully be calculated — which is exactly the point the mark scheme wanted. Saying "there is no single mode, because the data is trimodal" is a credit-worthy observation, not a failure.
  • Range — highest minus lowest. 10 − 1 = 9. One number for the whole spread, but it is set entirely by the two most extreme readings.
  • Interquartile range — upper quartile minus lower quartile. Lower half (1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) gives Q1 = 2.5; upper half (6, 6, 8, 9, 10, 10) gives Q3 = 8.5; IQR = 6. It describes the spread of the middle 50%, so it ignores extremes — which is why the 2019 mark scheme names it as a measure that "might be more useful".

The 2019 question was "Assess the usefulness of measures of central tendency… in analysing the housing quality data" [4], and the mark scheme's key indicative point is the one students miss: measures of central tendency have limited use here, because the enquiry is really about identifying differences and patterns between areas — an average of twelve different areas hides exactly what you went to find out. Two or more measures must be discussed for all four marks; one measure discussed clearly reaches low Level 2; and evidence of correct calculation alone is capped at one mark.

The facts you cannot sit the paper without

Paper 3: 1 h 15, 76 marks, 30%. Section A Issue evaluation 37 marks, Section B Fieldwork 39 marks. 6 SPaG marks, 3 on each section's 9-marker. Pre-release booklet issued about 12 weeks before (2026: Thursday 19 March); you get a clean copy in the exam. Heavily AO3 (judgement) and AO4 (skills).

Section A shape: three figures — the general problem, the possible solutions plus the site map, then the specific proposal with stakeholder views. Short skills questions on the figures, two or three 6-mark discussions (some general, some place-specific — read which), one 9+3 decision question. Copying = Level 1; developing = Level 2; linking across the booklet = Level 3.

2026 booklet (method practice, not your content): UK water supply and demand. 16 bn litres/day supplied; surface water 64% of England's supply, 93% of Wales'; rainfall over 2000 mm NW to under 800 mm SE; effective rainfall 2500 mm NW to under 200 mm E; summer demand +20%, June 2020 +70%; household use +70% since 1985; demand +4 bn litres/day by 2050 (South East 50% of the rise); supply −7% by 2045; drought restrictions twice as likely 2020–2050; 140 litres/person/day now, target 122 by 2038 and 110 by 2050, EA thinks 100 achievable; people estimate 57 vs actual 140; toilets 30% of household use, washing 25%, washing machines 21%; leakage over 3 bn litres/day ≈ 20% of supply; Thames desalination 140–150 m litres/day; pollution incidents 263 (2020) → 325 (2021), +24% → 307 (2022).

Lincolnshire reservoir (Anglian Water): SE of Sleaford, between Scredington, Helpringham and Swaton. Takes winter water from the Trent and Witham. 55 million m³; up to 166 million litres/day; 500 000 homes; £2.6 bn investment; supports 175 000 planned homes. Against: 2000+ petition signatures, 50+ families lose homes, farmland flooded, construction road closures. Stakeholders: Anglian Water, Environment Agency, Natural England, local authorities, farmers/NFU, residents, local businesses. NFU is on both sides — supports expanding supply, warns about local harm.

Brighton (physical): "Evaluate the success of groynes as a method of coastal management on Brighton beach." East Sussex, ~80 km south of London; LSD west→east; 3 adjacent concrete groynes of a ~3 km stretch; slope profiles at 2 m systematic intervals; bi-polar −3 to +3 on vulnerability to erosion, aesthetic value, lifespan, disturbance to habitats; presented as line graphs (profiles) and a bar chart (bi-polar). Result: sediment built up west, depleted east → groynes work. Limits: one October day, 3 groynes only, concrete only, subjective bi-polar, ruler shorter than the drop.

Stratford (human): "To what extent has the Olympic Regeneration of Stratford been successful?" Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, East London, 45–60 min from school; brownfield; Games 2012; former Athletes' Village = East Village. 5 sites A–E, EQS on buildings, traffic, open space, general quality; Site B London Blossom Garden +23 highest; Site A near Hackney Wick station lowest for buildings. Questionnaire: 3 questions, 3 people per site; Q2 75% "a lot", 100% "a lot"/"somewhat". Presented as 4 bar charts + word clouds. Limits: tiny sample, one sunny weekday, no stratification, subjective EQS (fixed by group averaging), mostly qualitative — needed BRES and deprivation data.

Six enquiry strands: 1 suitable question · 2 selecting, measuring, recording data · 3 processing and presenting · 4 describing, analysing, explaining · 5 reaching conclusions · 6 evaluation.

Statistics: mean = sum ÷ n · median = middle when ordered · mode = most frequent (can be bi- or trimodal, or absent) · range = max − min · IQR = Q3 − Q1 · percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100 · pie chart 1% = 3.6°. Set answers to learn: 2022 beach widths mean 17.6, mode 17, median 17.5, range 4; 2019 housing quality mean 5.41, median 5.5, trimodal (1, 6, 10), range 9, IQR 6; 2024 EQS business park total 24, mean 4; 2024 cleanliness 29/50 = 58%; 2025 mean width 280 cm, depth range 22 cm.

OS maps: eastings then northings; 4 figures = a 1 km square, 6 figures = 100 m within it; 1 grid square = 1 km = 1 km²; 1:50 000 → 2 cm = 1 km; 1:25 000 → 4 cm = 1 km; "physical geography" = relief and drainage, i.e. height, slope, rivers, lakes, woodland.

The 9-mark frame

Two different 9-markers, two different frames. Both are level-marked, both carry +3 SPaG, and both are lost by not deciding anything.

Section A — the decision question. Tick the box first if there is one.

  1. One-sentence introduction. Define the key term — usually sustainability: meeting the needs of the present without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own. State your overall position in the same breath.
  2. Social. Benefits with figures from the booklet, developed; then the short-term local cost; then which outweighs which and why.
  3. Environmental. The same shape. The strongest move here is scale: local habitat loss now against regional climate adaptation for decades.
  4. Economic. The same shape again. Reach for the stakeholder who is on both sides — in 2026 that is the NFU.
  5. Two-sentence conclusion. Reiterate the judgement, refer to long-term impacts, and say whether the scheme actually solves the problem Figure 1 set out.

Section B — the fieldwork question. Name the enquiry on the title line, then PEEL × 3 plus a conclusion.

  1. Frame the judgement. "To evaluate whether my conclusions are valid I need to judge how accurate my data collection was, and how reliable my results were — whether I would get the same results on a different day."
  2. Paragraph 1 — the quantitative method. Beach slope profiles: what made them reliable (complete profile shoreline to sea wall, 2 m intervals, three adjacent groynes), then the limitation (3 groynes of 3 km, concrete only, one day), then what it does to the validity of the conclusion.
  3. Paragraph 2 — the qualitative or subjective method. Bi-polar analysis: what it allowed (comparing groynes with the sea wall on four variables), then the limitation (subjective, wide variation between groups, judgements like lifespan need secondary data), then the effect on reliability.
  4. Paragraph 3 — how the methods interact. Do they support each other or leave a gap? At Stratford the questionnaires agreed with the EQS, which strengthens validity; at Brighton the bi-polar survey adds a dimension the profiles cannot measure but cannot be relied on alone.
  5. Conclusion that decides. "Although the data is a snapshot in time, which limits reliability, I am confident it provides evidence that the groynes at Brighton are a successful method of coastal management — they stop longshore drift and build a protective beach."

Sentence starters that carry the marks: "One major strength/limitation of the beach profiles was…" · "Another useful method was the bi-polar survey, which…" · "When combined, these methods allowed me to…" · "This suggests we can have relative confidence in the validity of our conclusions, that…" · "However, if we had repeated this on a different day with different weather…" · "Overall, the data was partially/mostly effective because…" · "In conclusion, my fieldwork has enabled me to reach some valid conclusions, although…"

subsections.heading: Figures to learn
subsections.html:
Geography's version of quotations: in this module the marks live in precise figures about the pre-release scheme and precise detail about John's own two enquiries. The front of the card names the source and what the figure is, so you can test whether you can produce the number from the prompt alone.

Lincolnshire reservoir — capacity and supply55 million cubic metres of water; up to 166 million litres a day; supplying 500 000 homesUsed to argue: the scheme's scale is the whole case for it — this is the figure that outweighs 50 families losing their homes in any sustainability judgement
Lincolnshire reservoir — why Lincolnshire needs it175 000 new homes planned in Lincolnshire in the next five years, in one of the driest parts of the UK with a rapidly growing populationUsed to argue: demand is not hypothetical — link this to the 500 000 homes figure and the social sustainability paragraph writes itself
Lincolnshire reservoir — the economic case£2.6 billion of direct and indirect investment, plus thousands of visitors a year using sailing, wind surfing, cycling and walking facilitiesUsed to argue: the long-term economic benefit is regional and lasting, against short-term local losses to farms and leisure businesses
Lincolnshire reservoir — the oppositionOver 2000 local people signed a petition; more than 50 families lose their homes; roads closed during construction on narrow country lanesUsed to argue: the costs are real, concentrated and immediate — quote it, then immediately set it against the regional scale, which is what moves the answer from Level 1 to Level 3
Lincolnshire reservoir — how it worksTakes water from the River Trent and River Witham in winter when flows are highest, stores and treats it for the hotter summer months, with an overflow drain reducing winter flood riskUsed to argue: this is climate-change adaptation, not just supply — and the overflow drain is a second benefit most candidates miss
Lincolnshire reservoir — the NFU's double positionFully supports expanding water supply infrastructure and says farms will benefit, but warns large-scale schemes significantly harm local farm businesses and communities, and insists local people be involved at all stagesUsed to argue: even the opponents accept the need, so the dispute is about this scheme at this scale — the single most useful source in the booklet because it supplies both halves of a paragraph
UK water — the central mismatchNorthern and western parts of the UK receive over 2000 mm of rainfall a year; the south-east, the most heavily populated part, receives under 800 mm — and takes 50% of the projected increase in demand to 2050Used to argue: the UK's water problem is distribution, not total quantity — the opening sentence of any 6-marker on managing UK water
UK water — supply falling, demand risingTotal supply predicted to fall 7% by 2045 from climate change, while demand rises about 4 billion litres a day by 2050; a year with drought restrictions is twice as likely between 2020 and 2050Used to argue: the gap is opening from both ends at once, which is why demand reduction alone cannot close it
UK water — personal consumptionThe average person uses 140 litres a day; government targets are 122 litres by 2038 and 110 by 2050; a 2023 survey found people estimated their own use at 57 litresUsed to argue: behaviour change is hard precisely because people do not know what they use — the strongest point for awareness campaigns and smart meters
UK water — where household water goesFlushing toilets 30%, personal washing 25%, washing machines 21%, washing up 8%, garden 7%, drinking 4%, other 5%Used to argue: rainwater harvesting into an underground tank for flushing targets the largest single slice, so it beats appeals to shorter showers
UK water — leakageOver 3 billion litres a day lost to leakage in England, approximately 20% of supplyUsed to argue: the cheapest water available is the water already paid for — the residents' strongest argument against needing a reservoir at all
UK water — pollution, and a percentage change325 category 1 and 2 pollution incidents in 2021, up 24% from 263 in 2020; 307 in 2022. Untreated sewage and agricultural slurry were the commonest pollutantsUsed to argue: polluted water is lost supply, not just an environmental problem — and it is the booklet's worked percentage change: 62 ÷ 263 × 100 = 24%
Brighton — the method, in one sentenceBeach slope profiles measured at 2 m systematic intervals from just above the breaking waves inland to the sea wall, on three adjacent concrete groynes along a 3 km stretch, plus a bi-polar survey scored −3 to +3 on vulnerability to erosion, aesthetic value, lifespan and disturbance to habitatsUsed to argue: this is the 3-mark "justify one primary data collection method" answer — the method, the interval, and why that interval suits the aim
Brighton — the result and the conclusionMarkedly more sediment on the updrift (west) side of the groyne and a clear deficit downdrift (east), because longshore drift running west to east was interrupted and sediment trappedUsed to argue: the groynes are successful — they stop longshore drift and build the protective beach, which was the stated test of success
Brighton — the honest limitationThree groynes out of a 3 km stretch, all concrete, measured on one day in October when destructive waves are strongest and beaches steepestUsed to argue: the conclusion has internal validity for this beach but not external validity for all beaches, and is a snapshot rather than a seasonal picture — the sentence that reaches Level 3 on the 9-marker
Stratford — the method, in one sentenceEnvironmental quality surveys at five sites A–E scoring buildings, traffic, open space and general quality, plus a three-question questionnaire — an age band, a closed question on how much the area had benefited, and an open question asking for three wordsUsed to argue: the closed question gives categorisable data and the open one gives a sense of place, which is why both were needed
Stratford — the resultSite B, the London Blossom Garden, scored highest at +23; Site A near Hackney Wick station scored lowest for building quality; 75% of questionnaire responses said the area had benefited "a lot" and 100% said "a lot" or "somewhat"Used to argue: regeneration has been successful but uneven — the inside-the-park sites gained far more than the fringes
Stratford — the honest limitationThree people per site, one sunny weekday in the middle of the day, no stratification by age — so locals were probably at work and tourists over-representedUsed to argue: the sample was not representative, so the social conclusions are weaker than the environmental ones; a group average of EQS totals removed outliers and partly rescued the accuracy
Statistics — the five measuresMean = sum ÷ n · Median = middle value when ordered · Mode = most frequent value · Range = highest − lowest · Interquartile range = upper quartile − lower quartileUsed to argue: the mean uses every value but is dragged by extremes; the median ignores them; the mode can be absent or multiple; the range is set by two readings; the IQR describes the middle 50% and is usually the better measure of spread
Grid references — the ruleEastings before northings. Four figures name a 1 km grid square by its south-west corner; six figures divide that square into tenths, so the fifth and sixth digits locate a point to 100 mUsed to argue: nothing — this one is simply never to be got wrong, and "along the corridor, then up the stairs" is the mnemonic that stops the reversal

equations.formula: 325 category 1 and 2 pollution incidents in 2021, up 24% from 263 in 2020; 307 in 2022. Untreated sewage and agricultural slurry were the commonest pollutants
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: polluted water is lost supply, not just an environmental problem — and it is the booklet's worked percentage change: 62 ÷ 263 × 100 = 24%

equations.name: Brighton — the method, in one sentence
equations.formula: Beach slope profiles measured at 2 m systematic intervals from just above the breaking waves inland to the sea wall, on three adjacent concrete groynes along a 3 km stretch, plus a bi-polar survey scored −3 to +3 on vulnerability to erosion, aesthetic value, lifespan and disturbance to habitats
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: this is the 3-mark "justify one primary data collection method" answer — the method, the interval, and why that interval suits the aim

equations.name: Brighton — the result and the conclusion
equations.formula: Markedly more sediment on the updrift (west) side of the groyne and a clear deficit downdrift (east), because longshore drift running west to east was interrupted and sediment trapped
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the groynes are successful — they stop longshore drift and build the protective beach, which was the stated test of success

equations.name: Brighton — the honest limitation
equations.formula: Three groynes out of a 3 km stretch, all concrete, measured on one day in October when destructive waves are strongest and beaches steepest
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the conclusion has internal validity for this beach but not external validity for all beaches, and is a snapshot rather than a seasonal picture — the sentence that reaches Level 3 on the 9-marker

equations.name: Stratford — the method, in one sentence
equations.formula: Environmental quality surveys at five sites A–E scoring buildings, traffic, open space and general quality, plus a three-question questionnaire — an age band, a closed question on how much the area had benefited, and an open question asking for three words
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the closed question gives categorisable data and the open one gives a sense of place, which is why both were needed

equations.name: Stratford — the result
equations.formula: Site B, the London Blossom Garden, scored highest at +23; Site A near Hackney Wick station scored lowest for building quality; 75% of questionnaire responses said the area had benefited "a lot" and 100% said "a lot" or "somewhat"
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: regeneration has been successful but uneven — the inside-the-park sites gained far more than the fringes

equations.name: Stratford — the honest limitation
equations.formula: Three people per site, one sunny weekday in the middle of the day, no stratification by age — so locals were probably at work and tourists over-represented
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the sample was not representative, so the social conclusions are weaker than the environmental ones; a group average of EQS totals removed outliers and partly rescued the accuracy

equations.name: Statistics — the five measures
equations.formula: Mean = sum ÷ n · Median = middle value when ordered · Mode = most frequent value · Range = highest − lowest · Interquartile range = upper quartile − lower quartile
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: the mean uses every value but is dragged by extremes; the median ignores them; the mode can be absent or multiple; the range is set by two readings; the IQR describes the middle 50% and is usually the better measure of spread

equations.name: Grid references — the rule
equations.formula: Eastings before northings. Four figures name a 1 km grid square by its south-west corner; six figures divide that square into tenths, so the fifth and sixth digits locate a point to 100 m
equations.symbolKey: Used to argue: nothing — this one is simply never to be got wrong, and "along the corridor, then up the stairs" is the mnemonic that stops the reversal

subsections.heading: Definitions marked to the word
subsections.html:
TermAccepted wording
Issue evaluationAssessing a contemporary geographical issue using secondary sources, considering the views of the stakeholders, appraising the advantages and disadvantages, and justifying a decision
SustainabilityMeeting the needs of people in the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
StakeholderAny person, group or organisation affected by or able to influence a development — residents, farmers, businesses, the Environment Agency, the water company, the local authority
SynopticDrawing together knowledge, understanding and skills from across the whole course, and making links between different aspects of an issue
AdaptationChanging our behaviour or infrastructure to cope with the effects of climate change, rather than reducing its causes
GroundwaterWater that infiltrates and percolates through soil into rock and is stored in aquifers
Surface waterWater that remains on the surface and flows into rivers or streams, including water stored in lakes and reservoirs
Water transferThe artificial movement of water, using pipes and pumps, from an area of surplus to an area of deficit
Effective rainfallThe rainfall left after evaporation and use by plants — the amount actually available for water supply
Geographical enquiryAn investigation with a suitable question underpinned by geographical theory, answered using data the student collects and presents, leading to an evidenced conclusion and an evaluation
Primary dataOriginal data collected for the first time — by you, in the field
Secondary dataData already available from existing sources — council websites, OS maps, GIS, census and government data, newspapers, previous years' results
Quantitative dataData that can be measured, counted and expressed as a number, so it allows statistical analysis; usually objective
Qualitative dataDescriptive data capturing concepts, experiences, emotions and behaviours, often from open questions; usually subjective
Random samplingSelection based purely on chance, so every member of the population has an equal probability of being chosen — which minimises bias
Systematic samplingTaking readings at regular intervals — every 2 m, every tenth person — which guarantees even coverage
Stratified samplingDividing the population into groups and sampling each in proportion, so every group is represented
AccuracyHow close a measurement is to the true value — affected by equipment and by whether everyone measured the same way
ReliabilityThe consistency or repeatability of a measurement — whether returning on a different day would give the same result
ValidityWhether the conclusion is genuinely supported by the data collected, given its accuracy and reliability
RepresentativeWhether the sample reflects what is actually happening in the wider population or area
BiasSystematic distortion of results by the way data was collected or judged — subjective scoring, an unrepresentative sample, a leading question
AnomalyA reading that does not fit the pattern of the rest of the data
Bi-polar surveyScoring an observation between two opposite statements on a scale such as −3 to +3, which turns a subjective judgement into a number that can be plotted

MeanThe sum of the values divided by how many there are
MedianThe middle value when the data is placed in order; with an even number of values, the mean of the two middle ones
ModeThe most frequently occurring value; data can be bimodal or trimodal, or have no mode at all
RangeThe highest value minus the lowest
Interquartile rangeThe upper quartile minus the lower quartile — the spread of the middle 50% of the data, which ignores extremes

Choropleth mapA map using shading of areas to show density or rate, with darker shades for higher values

DrainageThe pattern of water on the land — rivers, streams, lakes, ponds, marsh, and the direction of flow

questions.promptHtml: If you get the pre-release booklet twelve weeks early and a clean copy in the exam, what is there left to prepare?
questions.answerHtml:
Not the facts — they are in front of you. What you cannot do in the exam is think, because 37 marks in roughly 35 minutes leaves no time for it. So the twelve weeks are for the three jobs that have to be done in advance.

Annotate. Know where every statistic lives, so that when a question needs a figure you turn to the right page instead of hunting. Categorise. Sort the proposal's impacts into social, economic and environmental, positive and negative — the A3 evaluation grid. Rank. Number the points within each box from most to least significant, which means you walk in already holding a judgement.

The exam point: a Level 3 answer makes links across the booklet. Links are the thing you cannot improvise under time pressure, which is why the ranking step matters more than it looks.

questions.promptHtml: Why is copying the right sentence from the booklet only worth Level 1?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the question is not testing whether you can find the evidence — it is testing AO3, which is interpreting and evaluating it to make a judgement. Selecting an appropriate quotation shows you understood the question; it does not show you understood the geography.

The ladder is explicit in the mark schemes. Level 1: points identified, largely copied, mainly from one figure. Level 2: the same points developed — "this means that…", "as a result…". Level 3: points from across the booklet linked, with evaluative observations throughout rather than only in the conclusion.

The exam point: the cheapest upgrade available is to follow every quoted figure with a sentence beginning "this means that". It converts Level 1 material into Level 2 material without needing any extra knowledge.

questions.promptHtml: Some Section A questions are about the specific place and some are general. Why does getting this wrong cost marks even when the answer is good?
questions.answerHtml:
Because the mark scheme for a general question rewards breadth of understanding across the specification, and a place-specific answer cannot supply it. The examiners call this self-limiting: you have not written anything wrong, you have simply closed off most of the available marks.

The 2023 report gives both directions. Questions 2.2, 2.4 and 3 were tied to the Cayman Islands. Questions 1.4 ("To what extent can tourism create opportunities for economic development?") and 2.6 were broad discussions of tourism and development, where answers drawing on wider learning — economic leakage, seasonality, the multiplier effect, ecotourism — scored highest. In 2022 the mirror-image error: candidates answered the general question on waste as a resource entirely through the Cambridge incinerator.

The exam point: check for a place name in the question stem. No place name means the question wants the topic, so bring the rest of the course in.

questions.promptHtml: Why did the school choose questions for the two enquiries rather than hypotheses?
questions.answerHtml:
Because a hypothesis forces a verdict and a question permits a "partly". A hypothesis — "the beach gets wider from west to east" — is either supported or not, and real fieldwork data is usually mixed. A question — "to what extent has the Olympic regeneration of Stratford been successful?" — lets the honest answer be "largely, but unevenly", which is exactly what the data showed.

That matters for the 9-marker, because the wordings include "to what extent did your results and conclusions answer the enquiry question or hypothesis" (2024). A nuanced conclusion is easier to defend than a binary one, and nuance is what the Level 3 descriptors reward.

The exam point: write the title exactly as it was — "Evaluate the success of groynes as a method of coastal management on Brighton beach", "To what extent has the Olympic Regeneration of Stratford been successful?" — because the examiners say the answers must visibly reflect the aim in the stated title.

questions.promptHtml: What is the actual difference between accurate, reliable and valid, and why does the 9-marker need all three?
questions.answerHtml:
They are three links in a chain, and the 9-marker is about the chain rather than the links.

Accuracy is about the measurement: how close your reading was to the true value. A one-metre ruler used on a drop of more than a metre, down a groyne edge that was not straight, is an accuracy problem. Reliability is about repeatability: would you get this again? Three groynes on one October day, when destructive winter waves steepen beaches, is a reliability problem. Validity is about the conclusion: given the accuracy and the reliability, is the conclusion actually supported?

The chain runs one way. Inaccurate measurement produces results you cannot trust; unreliable sampling produces results that may not generalise; and the two together determine whether the conclusion is valid. The 2023 report found that most candidates described their results or their limitations well but never linked either to the validity of the conclusion, and so stalled at Level 2.

The exam point: write the chain explicitly. "We sampled at 2 m intervals, which was accurate enough to show the sediment difference. However we only sampled three of the groynes along 3 km, on one day, so the result is not reliable across the whole coast or across seasons. Therefore my conclusion is valid for these three groynes but cannot be extended to the whole beach."

questions.promptHtml: Both of John's enquiries used a subjective scoring survey. Is that a flaw in the fieldwork, or something to use?
questions.answerHtml:
Both. It is the single most useful thing in either enquiry, because it hands you a genuine evaluation point in every question type.

The strength is that a bi-polar or environmental quality survey converts a qualitative impression into a number that can be plotted, compared across sites and totalled. That is why the Brighton bi-polar survey could compare groynes with the sea wall on four variables, and why the Stratford EQS could rank five sites — neither comparison is possible with words alone.

The limitation is that the number is still a judgement. Classmates scored the same Stratford sites differently; Brighton groups' bi-polar scores showed a great range of variation. Some of the Brighton categories — lifespan, vulnerability to erosion — cannot honestly be judged by eye at all without secondary data.

And there are two fixes, which is what turns the limitation into a mark: take a group average of totals, which removes outliers (the Stratford answer), or run a standardisation survey at one agreed point and adjust everyone's scores to the average before starting. The 2024 mark scheme adds more: describe what each score means, widen the range of criteria, avoid an odd-numbered scale so the middle value is not a default.

The exam point: "it was subjective" is one mark. "It was subjective, which is why we took a group average of the totals to remove outliers, improving accuracy and reliability" is the Level 2 or 3 version.

questions.promptHtml: In the unseen fieldwork section you know nothing about the place. So what is actually being tested?
questions.answerHtml:
AO3 and AO4 only — interpretation, analysis, evaluation, and the selection and use of skills. Nothing in Question 4 rewards place knowledge, which is why it is the most learnable part of the paper: the skills recur, and so do the criticisms.

Three things make the difference. Read the stem, because it names the aim or hypothesis and every judgement has to be made against it — not against the data in general. Attempt every completion question, because the examiner's reports note year after year that significant proportions of candidates leave pie charts, isolines and scattergraphs blank "across the ability range", and these are 1-mark gifts. Criticise the method systematically, using a fixed checklist: sample size, number of sites, one day or one time, subjectivity, narrow scale, limited criteria, equipment.

The exam point: the same criticisms that evaluate John's own fieldwork evaluate a stranger's. The vocabulary transfers completely, which is why learning Brighton and Stratford properly also prepares Question 4.

questions.promptHtml: Why would the interquartile range sometimes be a better answer than the mean, and when would none of the measures of central tendency help?
questions.answerHtml:
The mean uses every value, which makes it sensitive to anomalies: one reading of 10 among a set of 2s and 3s drags it upwards and misdescribes the typical case. The median is immune to that, because it only cares about position. The range has the opposite problem to the mean — it is set entirely by the two most extreme readings, so a single anomaly defines it. The interquartile range describes the spread of the middle 50% and therefore ignores both extremes, which is why the 2019 mark scheme offers it as a measure that "might be more useful".

But the deeper answer, and the one the 2019 question was really after, is that sometimes an average is the wrong tool altogether. The housing quality enquiry surveyed twelve different areas of a town in order to find differences between them. Collapsing twelve areas into one number of 5.41 destroys exactly the information the enquiry existed to collect. The mark scheme says it outright: measures of central tendency "have limited use in the context of the data since it is really about identifying differences and patterns".

The exam point: when a question asks you to assess the usefulness of a statistical measure, the strongest point is not about the arithmetic. It is about whether the measure answers the enquiry's question.

questions.promptHtml: A student interviewed 50 people about their local bus service. Of the 50, 29 rated cleanliness as "reasonable". What percentage of the people interviewed considered cleanliness to be reasonable? (1)
questions.answerHtml:
58%. 29 ÷ 50 = 0.58, × 100 = 58% 1

The shortcut worth knowing: out of 50, double the count. Out of 25, multiply by four. Out of 20, multiply by five. These are the sample sizes AQA actually uses, and the arithmetic is quicker than the calculator. (AQA 2024, Q4.1.)

questions.promptHtml: Students measured a river at six sites. Widths were 180, 342, 210, 258, 320 and 370 cm. Maximum depths were 24, 42, 31, 34, 39 and 46 cm. Calculate the mean width of the river and the range of the maximum depth. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
Mean width = 280 cm. 180 + 342 + 210 + 258 + 320 + 370 = 1680; 1680 ÷ 6 = 280 1

Range of maximum depth = 22 cm. Highest 46 − lowest 24 = 22 1

Two habits that save the marks: write the units the table uses, and check the row you are being asked about — the table in 2025 already gave a mean of 190 for one column and a range of 36 for another, and candidates filled in the wrong cells. (AQA 2025, Q4.2.)

markScheme.point: Range of maximum depth = 22 cm. Highest 46 − lowest 24 = 22

questions.promptHtml: Study a map of annual average rainfall in the UK, 1991–2020, shaded in bands from "over 2000 mm" to "under 800 mm". Describe the distribution of average rainfall in the UK. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
The north and west of the UK are the wettest, with over 2000 mm a year in north-west Scotland and parts of Wales 1

The south and east are the driest, with under 800 mm in the south-east, so rainfall decreases from north-west to south-east 1

✗ "Scotland is wet and London is dry." No figures, no direction, and the second mark is for the gradient, not a second place name.
✓ Highest with a figure and a place, lowest with a figure and a place, then the direction of change in one clause. If there is an anomaly, name it; if not, the exam technique guide says do not worry about it.

markScheme.point: The north and west of the UK are the wettest, with over 2000 mm a year in north-west Scotland and parts of Wales
The south and east are the driest, with under 800 mm in the south-east, so rainfall decreases from north-west to south-east

questions.promptHtml: Study the Ordnance Survey extract of the proposed reservoir site. Give the name and six-figure grid reference of one farm that would be flooded by the proposed reservoir. (2)
questions.answerHtml:
One mark for naming a farm that lies inside the outlined site area — read the name off the map rather than from a nearby square, and check it is within the boundary, not just close to it 1

One mark for a correct six-figure reference: eastings first, then northings, each taken to tenths of a grid square. On this extract the eastings run 08–16 and the northings 36–44, so a reference inside the site looks like 134 376 — easting 13 and four-tenths across, northing 37 and six-tenths up 1

Work it with the booklet open: this is the question where the mark is lost to the mechanics, not the geography. Four figures name the whole square (1337 = easting 13, northing 37); six figures locate a point to 100 m. Along the corridor, then up the stairs — and the line you quote is always the one to the left of and below your point, never the nearest one.

markScheme.point: One mark for naming a farm that lies inside the outlined site area — read the name off the map rather than from a nearby square, and check it is within the boundary, not just close to it

One mark for a correct six-figure reference: eastings first, then northings, each taken to tenths of a grid square. On this extract the eastings run 08–16 and the northings 36–44, so a reference inside the site looks like 134 376 — easting 13 and four-tenths across, northing 37 and six-tenths up

questions.promptHtml: Using the Ordnance Survey map, describe the physical geography (relief and drainage) of the area around the proposed development. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
Relief — height. The land is low-lying, with few contours crossing the area; quote a spot height or the single contour value you can see, and say where the land is slightly higher 1

Relief — slope. The contours are widely spaced or absent, so the slopes are gentle and the area is relatively flat; where contours tighten, note the steeper ground and which way it falls 1

Drainage — features. Name the water on the map: rivers, streams, drains and dykes, ponds, lakes, areas of marsh — and, in a low-lying fenland area, note how dense the drainage network is 1

Drainage — direction and inference. Give the direction of flow of the main watercourse, and infer from the flat relief and dense drainage that the water table is likely to be high 1

✗ Roads, railways, settlements and named buildings. The 2022 examiner's report says "very few candidates appeared to understand the term physical geography" and most wrote about human features.
✓ Level 1 is "high land, low land, a river". Level 2 needs precision: the slope, the direction of flow, the height of the land. Three sentences, each traceable to something on the map.

markScheme.point: Relief — height. The land is low-lying, with few contours crossing the area; quote a spot height or the single contour value you can see, and say where the land is slightly higher

questions.promptHtml: Identify one potential risk in your physical geography fieldwork and explain how the risk was reduced. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Enquiry: "Evaluate the success of groynes as a method of coastal management on Brighton beach."

Risk. The waves approaching the coastline at Brighton were powerful destructive waves, so there was a risk of being caught by a breaking wave while measuring near the water 1

We carried out all measurements at a safe distance from the breaking waves, starting the slope profile from just above the point where they broke rather than at the water's edge 1

Our teachers had also checked the tide times in advance, so that we worked on a falling tide with enough safe beach exposed for the whole profile 1

Equally acceptable, and worth the same three marks: the steep pebble beach risked slipping, so we wore appropriate footwear, and worked sensibly in small groups when taking measurements at the groynes. (AQA 2019, Q5.2.)

✗ "It was dangerous so we were careful." One mark at best. The structure is one named risk, then two specific mitigations — or one mitigation explained in two steps.

questions.promptHtml: Justify one primary data collection method used in your physical geography enquiry. (3)
questions.answerHtml:
Enquiry: "Evaluate the success of groynes as a method of coastal management on Brighton beach."

Method: beach slope profiles. We measured the build-up and depletion of sediment on the updrift (west) and downdrift (east) side of each groyne, because if the groynes were stopping longshore drift there would be more sediment on the updrift side 1

We measured from just above where the waves broke, for safety, inland towards the sea wall, so that we captured the complete profile and not just part of it 1

questions.promptHtml: Students tested the hypothesis "the velocity of a river increases downstream" by timing a ball over 10 m, five times at each of three sites 1 km apart. Times in seconds — Site A (upstream): 26, 24, 22, 24, 25. Site B: 22, 23, 18, 20, 24. Site C (downstream): 20, 18, 20, 18, 19. To what extent does this data support the hypothesis? Use the data to support your answer. (4)
questions.answerHtml:
The data broadly supports the hypothesis. Mean times fall downstream — Site A 24.2 s, Site B 21.4 s, Site C 19.0 s — so velocity rises from 10 ÷ 24.2 = 0.41 m/s to 10 ÷ 21.4 = 0.47 m/s to 10 ÷ 19.0 = 0.53 m/s 1

That is an increase of about 29% from upstream to downstream, and it is consistent with the Bradshaw model, in which velocity increases downstream as the channel becomes smoother and more efficient 1

However the support is only partial, because the ranges overlap. Site A spans 22–26 s and Site B spans 18–24 s, so the fastest reading at Site A (22 s) is faster than two of the five readings at Site B 1

Site B also contains the single fastest reading of the whole investigation at 18 s, equal to the fastest at Site C, which is an anomaly — so while the means show a clear downstream trend, the individual readings do not cleanly separate the sites, and three sites with five readings each is a small basis for the conclusion 1

✗ "Yes, because the times get smaller." Level 1 — a basic reference to the data with no measure of strength.
✓ Level 2 needs "appears to support but": calculate something, state the trend with figures, then test it by looking at the spread and naming the anomaly. And note the trap in the arithmetic — a shorter time is a faster velocity. A manipulated calculation with the wrong conclusion is capped at Level 1. (AQA 2024, Q4.11.)

questions.promptHtml: Using Figure 1, "Water supply and demand in the United Kingdom", explain why it is increasingly difficult to manage water resources in the UK. (6)
questions.answerHtml:
Two or three developed paragraphs; marked in three levels, so develop rather than list.

Paragraph 1 — the mismatch between where the water is and where the people are. Figure 1 shows the north and west receive over 2000 mm of rainfall a year while the south-east, the most heavily populated part of the UK, receives under 800 mm 1; the gap is wider still in effective rainfall, which runs from more than 2500 mm in parts of the north-west to less than 200 mm in parts of eastern England, so the driest regions have least water actually available for supply and depend on costly transfers or on groundwater that is already being over-abstracted 1

Paragraph 2 — demand is rising, unevenly, and in the wrong place. Average household use is up 70% since 1985 and total demand is forecast to rise by about 4 billion litres a day by 2050 1; crucially the increase is not spread evenly — the South East alone accounts for 50% of the projected growth to 2050, against 6% for the North — so demand is growing fastest exactly where the resource is scarcest, which means national averages conceal the real problem and a region cannot simply be left to balance its own books 1

Paragraph 3 — supply is falling and becoming less predictable. Total supply is predicted to fall 7% by 2045 because of climate change, groundwater use has to be reduced for environmental reasons, and between 2020 and 2050 a year with drought restrictions is twice as likely as in the past 1; on top of that, demand peaks in summer when rainfall is lowest — up over 20% in a normal summer and over 70% in the hot, dry June of 2020 — so managers are being asked to meet a larger, spikier demand from a smaller and less reliable supply, which is why the Environment Agency warns of shortages within about 20 years 1

✗ Listing six statistics from Figure 1. The command is explain, so every figure needs a "which means that…" after it.
✓ Three linked reasons, each with a figure and a consequence, and at least one explicit link between paragraphs — the point that demand is growing fastest in the driest region is worth more than either fact alone.
